sources.title: How Cody Schneider runs a Claude Code agent marketing stack: bulk ads, outbound and autonomous growth
sources.originalTitle: Claude Code & MCPs built my $145K marketing machine
sources.summary: Cody Schneider shows a live demo of running many parallel Claude Code instances wired to marketing APIs. They generate bulk Facebook ad variations from real customer pain points, scrape and cold-email podcast hosts, auto-respond on LinkedIn, and then deploy workflows to Railway. He also argues API quality is now the key criterion for buying software and that domain vocabulary is the real moat.

principles.text: Put all your API keys in one repo's env file and run your whole growth stack from it via Claude Code.
principles.quote: it just holds all of your API keys that you're basically going to be working with.

principles.text: Buy software based on how robust its API is, since agents work through APIs, not UIs.
principles.quote: how I buy software in particular is how robust the API is.

principles.text: Generate ad creative as React components rendered to PNG so you can mass-produce variations cheaply, then find winners before spending on polished creative.
principles.quote: everything in here is just it's just react components like that. This is this is just a react component and entirely built by code. And so, I can make an infinite amount of these at scale

principles.text: Base ad copy on real public pain points and outcomes, and find formats by copying proven ad layouts from competitors in the Facebook Ads Library.
principles.quote: the best ads that I'm seeing perform right now are basically you're selling outcomes or you're you're talking to the pain points, right?

principles.text: Run a continuous test-and-promote loop: a test campaign with new creative, a daily cron turning off losers, and winners bumped into their own ad sets with dedicated budget.
principles.quote: I would have a cron job that's on a daily basis basically going and turning off the low performers. And then the high performers, they get bumped up into their own ad sets with their own dedicated ad budget

principles.text: Agents analyzing ad data need a data warehouse and pipeline; plain MCPs hit pagination and rate limits and show only a fraction of the data.
principles.quote: there is literally no way that you're going to be able to analyze this data without a data pipeline and a data warehouse.

sources.title: Cody Schneider: Building marketing agents for LinkedIn-signal cold outbound and organic content
sources.originalTitle: Marketing Agents Masterclass (GROW your startup)
sources.summary: Cody walks through two marketing agents. One scrapes engagers from niche LinkedIn influencer posts, runs waterfall enrichment, and cold emails or DMs them. The other turns real conversations into LinkedIn posts for a whole team. His core view is that an agent is just code on a cron job with an optional LLM thinking loop, not tokens burned per action.

principles.text: Target people who engaged with niche content; engagement is a hand-raise signal beating firmographics.
principles.quote: you have to look for signals or triggers that basically show that people are hand raising um saying hey I want I want this thing.

principles.text: Track only 10-20 outlier creators in your niche; they cover most of the audience.
principles.quote: If you just monitor those outliers, you're actually going to get, you know, 80% surface area coverage for that entire industry.

principles.text: Waterfall enrichment: start with the cheapest, most accurate data source, then fall through to pricier ones.
principles.quote: you're starting with what is the cheapest, most accurate and then moving your way down into the more expensive uh uh validation tools.

principles.text: Send cold email from separate burner domains and inboxes to protect your core domain's deliverability.
principles.quote: you're buying inboxes and domains that are burner domains that enable you to send cold email um not from your core domain.

principles.text: Pay for software that does the job, not tokens on every action; use inference only where needed.
principles.quote: Build the software that does the solution for you, not tokens burning every time that you're trying to do the action.

principles.text: Source social content from real human conversations, then find winners and remix them on a recurring cadence.
principles.quote: source this from real human conversation because that's where these original ideas are coming from.

sources.title: How Cody Schneider builds marketing agents that run Facebook ads on live business data
sources.originalTitle: Marketing Agents Are Too Good Now
sources.summary: Cody defines a real marketing agent as unified data in a warehouse, autonomous decisions on a cadence, and cloud hosting. He walks through a full Facebook ads agent (research, creative, publishing, culling winners) and an AI-for-WordPress startup idea to market with it.

principles.text: A real marketing agent needs unified data, autonomous decisions on a cadence, and cloud hosting; a linear automation workflow is not one.
principles.quote: you have to solve the data problem to like give the agent unified data clarity of like the whole pipeline.

principles.text: Put all channel data (ads, analytics, CRM, Stripe) in one warehouse so the agent can tie a specific ad to revenue.
principles.quote: A data warehouse is a way to unify all of your data sources into a single location so that your agent has the ability to understand all of the data in context

principles.text: Use the Facebook marketing API only for writes (publish, turn off, promote); bulk pulling data breaks TOS and gets accounts banned.
principles.quote: So, how you actually use the Facebook ads API is you use the API only for rights, like only to publish content to the Facebook ads account

principles.text: After Andromeda, skip interest targeting: make creative about a specific pain point and Facebook finds the buyers, making it a strong B2B channel.
principles.quote: Facebook has turned into the best B2B ads channel and that exists right now.

principles.text: Run a test-and-cull loop: publish ads daily, let them run 2 to 3 days, kill losers, and pool winners to compete for budget.
principles.quote: The winning ad sets, they go into a winners pool, and they're competing against each other for the ad budget that's available.

principles.text: Marketing is continuous, not campaign-based; fast feedback loops mean you must observe trends and keep adjusting.
principles.quote: Like how marketing actually functions now is like you're continuously doing this and because the feedback loops are so fast

sources.title: How Cody Schneider runs GTM as a one-person Claude Code growth system
sources.originalTitle: Claude Code Replaced My 20-Person Marketing Team (Here's How)
sources.summary: Cody shows his live workflow for replacing a marketing team with Claude Code, APIs and templates: bulk Facebook ad variants, templated landing pages, cold email pipelines and shared internal tools. His core argument is that volume is now cheap, so the edge is domain knowledge, clear outcomes and the data to see what works.

principles.text: GTM engineering is the same growth job as before; only the tooling changed. The work is finding distribution arbitrage and positioning.
principles.quote: I'm basically trying to find marketing and distribution arbitrage within the system like figure out the positioning for my company so that the audience is receptive to it and then I'm going to go and basically like build out processes to go execute on that

principles.text: Domain expertise translated into code is the real leverage. Deep knowledge plus systems beats generic AI use.
principles.quote: if you have a deep expertise in one thing and you can you understand the systems and the processes for that, if you can translate that into code, which is like literally what we're doing, and then use this as a system like to go and do activities for you, like that's where the real like power of this comes from.

principles.text: Test positioning with high-volume ad variants built from your buyer's own language (Reddit, pain points), then remix the winning message into other formats.
principles.quote: I'm using the language of my target customer. Like here's their actual pain points and the actual uh um, you know, outcomes that they're looking for that I'm then going to go incorporate into the bulk production of this ad creative content.

principles.text: Structure ad testing in stages: test creatives on cheap clicks first, then move winners into a conversion campaign with dedicated budget.
principles.quote: I'll test all the ad creative against each other in a click campaign and then I'll look at what has the cheapest CPC and I can run, you know, we'll do like a $100 over a three-day period to see which gets the cheapest CPC.

principles.text: Match the landing page to the winning ad angle with templated pages that only swap the headline and hero copy, to lift conversion.
principles.quote: when we align the ad and the landing page that we're sending them to, we can increase the uh conversion rate that's happening there.

principles.text: Output quality comes from your own source material and vocabulary, not a generic prompt. Monologue your opinions and add what ranks, then generate.
principles.quote: if I interview myself say I'm an expert at whatever this topic is I'm going to like do a transcription where I talk for 10 minutes. Like I just monologue about the topic, my opinions, my views. I use that as source material.

sources.title: How Cody Schneider uses Claude Code agents to automate SEO, content refreshing and growth workflows
sources.originalTitle: How Cody Schneider Uses AI Agents to Automate SEO, Ads & Growth
sources.summary: Cody explains his Search Console feedback loop for refreshing content, how he writes bottom-of-funnel articles from SERP source material plus personal input, and why he favors custom Claude Code agents over OpenClaw. He also covers citation link-building for AI search, publishing velocity risks, and data-warehouse context design.

principles.text: Use Search Console data as a feedback loop: add the keywords Google already hints at to existing articles, then build supplementary articles if needed.
principles.quote: you're going to find keywords that you're accidentally ranking for that you don't even have on the page. Uh if you add a section or figure out how to weave those in, like you can get a lift typically in like 10 to 20% like overnight

principles.text: SEO content must be relevant to the product; traffic that doesn't lead to a user action is worthless.
principles.quote: it's not just about getting traffic it's like it's not just about getting impressions it's like purely about like the user lands on that page and then what's the user action that I can get to occur

principles.text: AI content quality comes from source material plus your own opinions: scrape page-one results, add a 30-minute personal interview, then write.
principles.quote: I'll put that into the context window and then I'll interview myself for like 30 minutes talking about that specific category with my personal opinions, with my personal experiences

principles.text: For AI search visibility, get your brand mentioned on the citations already being pulled; treat it as targeted outbound link building.
principles.quote: just go and look at the keywords that you want to rank for and the citations they're pulling from and then you email all those citations and you're like, "Yo, I want to get my like self added.

principles.text: Give agents boundaries and just the right context at the right time rather than stuffing everything in; fewer tools work better.
principles.quote: the more tools you have the like worse it gets right so it's like what are the least amount of tools that we can give it to like do the action that we're trying to the outcome that we're trying to get

principles.text: Build specific custom agents in code on a cron job instead of broad tools like OpenClaw; they're more malleable, safer, and cheaper.
principles.quote: it's probably going to be way more effective to build a really specific solution to a specific problem and also it's more malleable

sources.title: How to build an AI-native marketing team: Cody Schneider's marketing engineering playbook
sources.originalTitle: How we’d build an AI-native marketing team from scratch | Eric Siu & Cody Schneider
sources.summary: Cody Schneider live-demos "marketing engineering": a coding agent plus a data and API infrastructure layer does the middle work of a marketing team. He runs parasite SEO, AI-avatar ad creative, and LinkedIn-engager cold outbound in parallel, and explains why agents should run as code rather than as chat.

principles.text: Marketing is turning into code: ads, analysis and publishing are just JSON, API calls and SQL an agent can run.
principles.quote: all marketing is now just going it's turning into code, right?

principles.text: Do the task manually with the agent first, then turn that session into a repeatable cloud job on a cadence.
principles.quote: I'm gonna take a task that I'm doing manually right now. I'm gonna co-work with cloud code to be like cool like I get the outcome that I get out of that.

principles.text: Build agents as software with a live data stream, not a chat model told to go do work. Skip token maxing.
principles.quote: that agent is just software with a thinking loop with a live data stream right it's not like God in a box is managing a Google Ads account.

principles.text: On Facebook, target broadly and let the creative (script plus avatar) do the positioning instead of interest targeting.
principles.quote: we are targeting all of Facebook and then we're making the creative basically be the positioning element.

principles.text: Gate agent output with brand style guides and a second vision model, then get humans out of the approval bottleneck.
principles.quote: humans are actually they need to get out of the way for a lot of this work.

principles.text: Keep spend at roughly 80% on proven creative and 20% on new tests, since every winner decays.
principles.quote: I'm always just trying to think about like how am I 80% is what I know is working 20%'s always testing

sources.title: How Cody Schneider uses Claude Code agents to run marketing, ads, SEO and cold outreach
sources.originalTitle: How Cody Schneider Built AI Agents That Run His Entire Marketing Team | FULL INTERVIEW
sources.summary: Cody explains how he hands "middle work" to Claude Code agents wired to his stack's APIs, with a data warehouse underneath. He covers agent loops for Facebook ads, a cold-email PR sprint, rolling this out to a team, and why API quality now drives software choices.

principles.text: Hand off the middle work to agents; you become the curator who supplies the idea up front and the polish at the end.
principles.quote: all of the middle work. So, me touching a keyboard and a mouse is now I'm trying to hand off to an agent entirely.

principles.text: Any task you repeat becomes an agent, which is just a small-scope employee running your old SOP.
principles.quote: when you think when you hear agent just think like employee with small scope of work that does a specific thing.

principles.text: Give agents a data pipeline and warehouse instead of raw API access, or you get rate limits, pagination errors and bloated context.
principles.quote: you have to basically create a data stream. Otherwise the agent is going to try to interact directly with the API, and you're just going to run into challenges.

principles.text: Close the loop on ads: publish, analyze, kill losers, promote winners, and feed results into the next round of creative.
principles.quote: The losers get automatically turned off. The winners automatically get promoted to their own adsets with their own dedicated budget.

principles.text: Set the outcome and the 'nos' rather than prescribing steps; boundaries give the agent surface area to say yes in.
principles.quote: It's way easier to be like here are all the nos that you can't do and then that suddenly that creates surface area for it to live in

principles.text: Your domain vocabulary and expertise are the superpower; specific, expert prompts beat generic ones and produce top-tier output.
principles.quote: the language that you have becomes your superpower like the vocabulary and deep under technical knowledge that you have becomes the most valuable asset that you own.

sources.title: Tournament ad testing: how Cody Schneider runs 10,000+ ads/month with agents
sources.originalTitle: 10,000 Ads/Month: The Tournament System Replacing Media Buyers | Cody Schneider Interview
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains how Grafft runs 10,000-15,000 ads a month with agents acting as media buyers. He maps competitor messaging onto a pain-point matrix to find uncovered angles, runs ads in a tournament that kills losers in 2-3 days, and buys cheap impressions through TikTok real-phone farms.

principles.text: Map emotional triggers by situations into a matrix, overlay competitor ads, and make creative for the empty cells.
principles.quote: Everybody's talking about the product in the exact same way, but there's really like, you know, 10 different ways that I could talk about this and then nobody is.

principles.text: Compete angle to angle, not capital to capital: zig when the big brands zag.
principles.quote: if you zig when they zag and you're talking about completely other things, that's a way to compete with them, not not capital to capital. It is just angle to angle.

principles.text: Run ads as a tournament: ads compete inside ad sets, losers turn off in 2-3 days, winners enter a pool that fights for budget.
principles.quote: The ads compete against each other over like a two to three-day window. Losers automatically turn get turned off.

principles.text: A media buyer is a loop you can code: a data stream, an agent that thinks over it, and the ability to make new creative.
principles.quote: It's a software with a thinking loop and some type of data like feedback, right? And like that's all it is.

principles.text: AI output regresses to the average unless you give it source material and a defined direction.
principles.quote: This is what north looks like. You can go northwest, you can go northeast, I don't care, but you have to go north in some capacity.

principles.text: TikTok real-phone farms with slideshow posts buy impressions at roughly $2-3 CPM versus about $10 on paid, so use them for brand reach.
principles.quote: the CPM on that ends up being about two to three dollars. >> That's nice. >> on Tik Tok is like you know in the range of $10 right?

sources.title: How Cody Schneider builds marketing agents that replace four hires (ads, SEO, cold email)
sources.originalTitle: How To Build AI Agents That Do the Work For You | Cody Schneider
sources.summary: Cody explains what a real AI agent is (software running a repeatable job with a thinking loop), why agents need live revenue data, and how Graft deploys Facebook Ads, Google Ads, SEO and cold outbound agents. He also gives an adoption path for non-technical owners: co-work first, automate later, one workflow at a time.

principles.text: Agents only work if they get live data on what drives revenue, not just lead counts.
principles.quote: to actually like make, you know, an agent run for a company, you basically have to have like a live data stream of what's actually driving revenue.

principles.text: Automate a human's existing process rather than expecting an agent to "run everything"; most "run your whole account" claims are snake oil.
principles.quote: the only way to actually get these things to function and work is you basically take like what is the process that a human was doing? Okay, how do I go and basically, you know, repeat that process like with having an agent run that?

principles.text: Adopt in stages: co-work with Claude Code/Codex on daily tasks first, then make proven workflows autonomous. Don't start by automating the whole business.
principles.quote: Don't try to jump initially to like I'm going to build an agent that entirely, you know, automates my whole business. It's I think that that's a mistake and it's it's kind of a tar pit that people fall into accidentally a lot of the times.

principles.text: The ads loop mirrors top media buyers: test lots of creative daily, kill losers, promote winners, repeat, optimizing to a real conversion action.
principles.quote: 10 new pieces of creative go into testing every day. Losers get turned off, winners get promoted to a winner's campaign, the winners are competing for budget for like, you know, who's the best performer.

principles.text: Give AI boundaries (brand guides, banned language) and your own domain knowledge; unbounded or generic prompts produce average slop.
principles.quote: if you're like, "Hey, here is, you know, 30 minutes of me talking about some specific thing that's happening within my category." You give it that context. ... The output quality that you're going to get out of that is going to be like top 1%, right?

principles.text: Drive AI adoption in a team with a weekly lunch-and-learn that spotlights one person's automation, not token quotas.
principles.quote: the best way I've seen to incentivize people is to have like a weekly lunch and learn where somebody on your team shows what they did with like this AI tooling

sources.title: Cody Schneider (Graphed): Building AI marketing agents that actually work in production
sources.originalTitle: Cody Schneider (Graphed): What It Takes to Build AI Marketing Agents That Work
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains how to build teams of specialized AI marketing agents with feedback loops, evals and safety guardrails rather than one generalist agent. He covers choosing businesses by search intent, why data ontology and good signals decide whether agents succeed, and why buyers want outcomes, not tools.

principles.text: Pick businesses by real demand: search intent and a problem people already try to solve.
principles.quote: or it's just like based off of search intent.

principles.text: A business is what the market wants to buy and how you get in front of it. Use that as first principles.
principles.quote: a business at its core is always the simplest thing. Like it's it's basically like what does the market want to buy and like how you know, how do I sell it?

principles.text: Growth is engineering: an outcome, limited time/money/energy, and a system distributing resources toward it.
principles.quote: I have an outcome that I'm trying to get. I have limited resources of time, money, and mental energy.

principles.text: Agents fail when they optimize the wrong metric. The AI SDR got leads, but poor quality ones; fix the signal fed back.
principles.quote: if you have the wrong signal going back to it, then that's like it's not the agent's fault. It's just it's doing its job, right?

principles.text: Vibe coding gets you to 80%; production needs evals, feedback loops and narrow agent roles.
principles.quote: vibe coding from 0 to 80% is pretty cool. 80 to production and live is is like a chasm.

principles.text: Agents guess at raw data columns, so teach them the data's ontology; decisions on bad data are the worst failure.
principles.quote: unless you're teaching them the ontology of the underlying data, it becomes a massive problem.

sources.title: How Graphed's CEO runs GTM with Claude Code agents: owned media, agent harnesses, token abundance
sources.originalTitle: Graphed CEO Cody Schneider on an AI-First Approach to GTM
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains how he automates go-to-market with Claude Code agents: a podcast-booking cold email agent, bulk Facebook ad generation, and a LinkedIn comment-to-lead loop. He also argues for owned media, solving the data pipeline before agents make decisions, and ideas plus polish as the only human work left.

principles.text: Go straight to code instead of workflow tools; agents in a repo are malleable and can be fixed from market feedback fast.
principles.quote: friends don't let friends do n right? Like you just go straight to code now because it's so much more malleable than all these other workflow tools.

principles.text: Start an agent setup with a local folder and an environment file holding all your stack's API keys, then have Claude interrogate you.
principles.quote: You add all of your API keys for your entire stack of your business into that environment file. That's it.

principles.text: Treat ad ops as an agent loop: generate variants, test, kill losers, promote winners, remix winners, repeat.
principles.quote: I turn off the losers. I promote the winners to more budget and then the winners I like remix those over and over again with new new creative.

principles.text: Agents making ad decisions need a data pipeline and warehouse; raw APIs hit rate limits, truncation and context bloat, causing hallucinated decisions.
principles.quote: You literally can't do this with the APIs because you run into rate limits.

principles.text: Own media is how you keep customer acquisition cost flat as paid CPCs rise in a maturing market.
principles.quote: as a market matures more people come and compete in that market and so the CPC increases over time only way to combat that is you have to invest in owned media that gives you organic reach

principles.text: With the middle work automatable, the only human jobs left are good ideas and polish (taste); give agents boundaries of nos.
principles.quote: Like having good ideas the hardest part. The middle work can be solved and then the polish is like like you know people call it taste

sources.title: Marketing engineering: let a coding agent do your marketing ops via a data warehouse and unified API
sources.originalTitle: Marketing Engineering Crash Course with Claude Code
sources.summary: Cody explains marketing engineering: using a coding agent like Claude Code to do the manual middle work of marketing. He lays out the infrastructure it needs (pipeline, warehouse, server, storage, crons, APIs) and demos ad creation, Facebook uploads, SEO, lead enrichment and dashboards. The video is sponsored by graph.com, his own product.

principles.text: Marketing engineering means having a coding agent do the manual middle work marketers used to do by hand.
principles.quote: In marketing engineering, what that is is having your coding agent do all of the middle work that you used to have to do by hand as a marketer.

principles.text: Pipe all marketing data into one warehouse and let the agent query it, instead of hitting platform APIs directly.
principles.quote: Joining data across these sources in the agent is extremely hard and you're going to find that it hallucinates.

principles.text: Read from the warehouse and use platform APIs only to write (upload ads, toggle ads), to avoid rate limits and TOS bans.
principles.quote: I'm only using the APIs to write to those platforms.

principles.text: Tie ad data all the way to revenue outcomes; a single source like Facebook Ads misrepresents what is happening.
principles.quote: I need to be able to tie the Ads all the way into what is actually producing outcomes.

principles.text: Agents need real infrastructure to be effective: server, storage, databases, crons, hosting, auth, Git and an API gateway.
principles.quote: You have to give it the right resources for it to be able to do these actions.

principles.text: Build a workflow once, then deploy it to the cloud on a schedule and run several agent tasks in parallel.
principles.quote: Once I build the system, once I build this process, I then go and deploy this into the cloud so that it can run on its own cadence without me having to jockey or manage it.

sources.title: GTM engineering with Claude Code: hand the middle work to agents and conduct
sources.originalTitle: GTM Engineering with Claude Code Crash Course
sources.summary: Cody Schneider defines GTM engineering as using Claude Code to do the hands-on work across marketing, sales and product. He shows the minimal setup (a folder, an env file, a CLAUDE.md), then runs keyword research, writes and publishes an SEO article, and tracks and improves it with Search Console data.

principles.text: Hand the middle work to AI agents; your role becomes having ideas and being the polish at the end.
principles.quote: all that middle work you hand off the Claude code, and then you're the polish, you're the endpoint.

principles.text: Run several agent terminals in parallel and act as the conductor and curator of their output.
principles.quote: you are just that conductor and that curator of the actions that it's doing.

principles.text: Set up the foundation once: an environment file for all API keys plus a CLAUDE.md telling the agent to store every new key there.
principles.quote: anytime I provide an API key, add it to that environment file so that all of these get stacked together so they can be reused in the future.

principles.text: Base SEO articles on what already ranks on page one, since Google signals what a good result looks like.
principles.quote: Google is basically signaling this is what we think a good search result looks like.

principles.text: For the best content, combine scraped sources with your own perspective (from an AI interview), tone of voice and a style guide.
principles.quote: you basically have an AI interview you for like 30 minutes. You take that transcript, and it's your perspective, your opinions, your point of view

principles.text: AI content quality is a guardrails problem, not an AI problem; give the agent a definition of good content.
principles.quote: You can 100% get good content to come out of this. You are just not providing it guardrails of what good content looks like.

sources.title: How Cody Schneider builds a Facebook Ads AI agent that researches, makes, publishes and prunes ads
sources.originalTitle: LIVE CLASS: Build a Facebook Ads AI Agent
sources.summary: Cody walks through the full stack for an agent that runs Facebook ads: conversion tracking, Reddit-sourced pain points, AI-generated statics and UGC video, API-based uploads, a test/winners campaign structure, and a data warehouse for analysis. Key ideas: creative is the targeting under Andromeda, move conversion events down-funnel, and qualify leads in real time with server-side events.

principles.text: Under Andromeda the ad creative is the targeting, so make many ads across many personas.
principles.quote: how Andromeda functions is the ad creative itself is actually the targeting mechanism.

principles.text: Source ad angles from the language customers already use on forums like Reddit, not from guesses.
principles.quote: You're not trying to guess what are the pain points and the outcomes that I or the desired outcomes that I'm trying to um you know use for for this ad creative.

principles.text: Start with an upfunnel conversion event, then move deeper as volume builds; keep to a handful of events.
principles.quote: you want to start with a conversion action that is upfunnel and then work your way down as close to revenue as you possibly can get.

principles.text: Qualify leads in real time with enrichment and send a good-lead signal back via server-side conversion events instead of waiting weeks for closed deals.
principles.quote: you can have an agent give a score to a lead that's 1 to 10. And you can basically qualify that lead.

principles.text: Use the ads API only for writes (upload, pause, promote); do analysis from a data warehouse to avoid API abuse and bad data.
principles.quote: The only thing that you're using to touch the API is for that rights to the ad uh to the to the ad channel. You're using for the analysis, you're only ever using the data warehouse.

principles.text: Run a survival-of-the-fittest loop: test ads in a testing campaign, promote winners, trim losers, then remix winners and inject outside inspiration to avoid repetition.
principles.quote: every ad has a shelf life, especially it's way faster in Andromeda, especially in B2B now.

sources.title: Digital gravity: start with transactional channels, then build brand mass as CAC rises
sources.originalTitle: Digital Gravity Explained: How Startups Can 10x Brand Growth with AI, SEO & Creator Flywheels
sources.summary: Cody explains how startups should use transactional channels (paid ads, cold email) for fast revenue, then invest in content, creators and SEO to build brand mass before arbitrage disappears and acquisition costs climb. He also covers AI search as a scrape of Google's top results, and automating only after a manual process is proven.

principles.text: Early on, use transactional marketing (paid ads, cold email, DMs) that turns into revenue tomorrow.
principles.quote: you're looking for like some type of arbitrage in the beginning that has uh like a direct I call transactional marketing so like tomorrow it revenue, right?

principles.text: Arbitrage channels get crowded and cost per acquisition rises, so build a content flywheel for branded discovery.
principles.quote: when you find that arbitrage, right, like cold email or uh like paid ads, um other people are going to identify that same arbitrage, that arbitrage is going to go away.

principles.text: Cost per signup can balloon fast; one example went from $1 to $5 in 12 months.
principles.quote: we were getting dollar signups and 12 months later that same signup was costing us $5, right?

principles.text: Goal of digital gravity: maximize your brand's surface area wherever your target customer spends time online.
principles.quote: all you're trying to do is make as much mass on the internet related to your brand in the niche that you are as possible

principles.text: For software SEO, bottom-of-funnel keywords (X vs Y, alternatives, best X for Y) drive signups and feed AI answers.
principles.quote: bottom of funnel keywords are super effective at making signups, right? What are those? It's like X verse Y product, X alternative product

principles.text: Do things that don't scale first, find what works, then automate it; agents are automations with AI making the decisions.
principles.quote: do things that don't scale exactly figure out what works right and then go and basically automate away as much of this as possible.

sources.title: Productized AI services beat AI automation agencies: 6 niches to $50K/mo
sources.originalTitle: The 6 Best AI Agency Niches to Make $50K/mo (Data-Backed)
sources.summary: Cody argues AI automation agencies are a bad business (one-time project revenue, hard sales, 12-18 month lifespan) and that productized monthly services delivered with AI tooling are better. He walks through six niches (med spas, beauty e-commerce ads, nutrition coach social, webinar lead magnets, data analytics, voice agents) with delivery stack, pricing and acquisition plays.

principles.text: Automation agencies are a weak business: high-ticket sales, one-time project revenue, no recurring base. Build a productized monthly service instead.
principles.quote: the business composition or the biology of the business for an automation agency is just really hard like you have to be really good at getting like top offunnel leads you have to be really good at sales

principles.text: Aim for recurring revenue and remote delivery so you aren't fighting for lead volume every month just to cover payroll.
principles.quote: something that has recurring revenue that's happening month over month so you're not fighting, you know, tooth and nail to get make sure that you have enough lead volume

principles.text: Sell a fixed monthly deliverable and tie reporting to leads or revenue to prove the service is worth its price. The closer to revenue, the easier to validate.
principles.quote: the closer you are to revenue, the easier it is to validate that work.

principles.text: Generate ad hooks from raw customer language (Reddit, reviews), not competitor ads. Copying competitors gives you no differentiation in a crowded feed.
principles.quote: you scrape a Reddit forum and you find this random quote, you know, about acne cream and like somebody describes it in this funny way or a different way and like you extract that using Claude and you're like, "Oh my god, like that's the hook, right?"

principles.text: Win clients by doing the work in public: YouTube case studies and LinkedIn 'comment to get the asset' posts create inbound leads.
principles.quote: Literally just talk your book and that's going to create the lead volume uh that you're looking for for this agency.

principles.text: Show your work before they hire you. Make a lead magnet from the prospect's own content (e.g. an ebook from their webinar) and send it as the pitch.
principles.quote: for them, you you you basically show your work before you they're even working with you.

sources.title: Digital gravity: Cody Schneider's B2B and consumer playbook for making a company famous
sources.originalTitle: He Built a Startup using AI That Prints Money (Full Tutorial)
sources.summary: Cody argues the marketing funnel is the wrong model and proposes "digital gravity": build mass through continuous content and ads everywhere your customer is, so people orbit and eventually convert. He walks through a B2B stack (scraped lists, custom-match ads, cold email, podcast as media business) and a consumer stack (UGC ads, influencer arbitrage, programmatic SEO).

principles.text: Think digital gravity, not funnels: build mass through constant content so buyers orbit and touch down later.
principles.quote: what you're doing is like you're building Mass digital Mass on the internet and The more mass you have the more influence you have within the niche or the sphere that you're in

principles.text: Marketing is continuous, not a campaign. Never start and stop; keep running and testing.
principles.quote: you don't start in stop you you're not you didn't do marketing you're marketing like you're you're constantly doing marketing

principles.text: Volume is a surface-area game: more swings at the plate beats fewer, more polished ones.
principles.quote: if I hit 300 right which is like decent and I go up to the plate but I only swing once like strong likelihood I don't even touch the ball but if I swing 10 times I get on base

principles.text: In B2B, scrape your small target list's emails, then hit them with custom-match ads and cold email at once.
principles.quote: we're touching them in these two different places simultaneously

principles.text: Test many ad variations, then put most budget on the winner while a slice keeps testing.
principles.quote: say 80% goes to those best performing 20% is always running in the background doing testing

principles.text: Turn customer conversations into a podcast to build a media arm that gains leverage and can pay for growth.
principles.quote: it turns it from a cost center into a profit Center

sources.title: How to run creator marketing on short form: zero-follower creators beat influencers on CPM
sources.originalTitle: Apps make $50K/mo like THIS (I shouldn't share this)
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains why For You page algorithms make creators with no followers cheaper and more effective than influencers. He covers the CPM math, how to find and manage creators, the tool stack, which products fit, and how it lifts branded search.

principles.text: Pay creators who talk about your niche consistently, not influencers, because purchases follow creators.
principles.quote: people do not make purchasing decisions largely off of like influencers. They make them off of creators that are consistently talking about these things.

principles.text: Creator retainers beat influencer posts and paid ads on CPM, since the For You page ignores follower count.
principles.quote: I'm getting a CPM by working with these creators. I'm getting a CPM that's cheaper than what I could pay on Facebook.

principles.text: Hire creators to start brand-new accounts from zero followers; the algorithm gives them reach anyway.
principles.quote: because it's again this for you page content they can get this reach like they never could previously.

principles.text: Work with 5 to 10 creators and share the outlier formats across all of them to compound learning.
principles.quote: you don't work with just one creator. You work with like five to 10 of them. And there's this compound learning effect that happens.

principles.text: Turn organic winners into paid ads, and make ads look native, like they were edited on an iPhone.
principles.quote: So you find the winners, pull those out, put ad spend behind them.

principles.text: This works best for impulse-priced, one-killer-feature mobile products with no learning curve.
principles.quote: it has to be an impulse purchase decision that can happen on a mobile device

sources.title: YouTube creators plus affiliate commissions: how to get first customers with underpriced creator videos
sources.originalTitle: What Vibe Coders Wish They Knew Sooner
sources.summary: Cody Schneider walks through a step-by-step playbook: scrape emails of YouTube creators in your niche, cold-email them for a 3-video package plus affiliate commission, find the underpriced ones, and put the winners on retainer. It works because creator attention is mispriced and affiliate links make ROI trackable.

principles.text: YouTube creator videos with affiliate links are product demos in disguise, and a top way to get first customers for SMB or single-feature products.
principles.quote: YouTube creators plus affiliate marketing is like one of the best ways to go about getting your first customers. And the reason for that is it's basically a product demo that's in disguise, right?

principles.text: Creator pricing is an inefficient market: small creators underprice themselves, so contacting many creates marketing arbitrage.
principles.quote: if I reach out to enough YouTube creators, they don't know how to price themselves, right? Like we'll see this all the time, especially with smaller creators that are like 10,000 to 50,000 subs.

principles.text: Ask for a three-video package plus an affiliate commission; commissions give trackable ROI and lock in pricing as the creator grows.
principles.quote: it creates this lock in with the creator so that long-term they won't increase their prices on you because they're like, "Oh I'm making 10 grand a month in affiliate commissions from this company."

principles.text: Rank creator quotes by cost per subscriber or view to find the underpriced ones, then negotiate down.
principles.quote: I would take the cost of the three video package divided by the amount of subscribers that they have. You could also do like average views per video.

principles.text: Choose creators already succeeding in your category over raw CPM; an engaged niche audience converts like a video sales letter that lives forever.
principles.quote: I'm way more focused on like is this creator making content already within the category because that means that they understand the audience

principles.text: Hire existing creators who know the algorithm rather than training someone from zero, and scale by retaining the 2-3 winners of each cohort.
principles.quote: don't hire somebody for this find somebody that's already doing this and work with them because they've already figured out like the algorithm for that specific category

sources.title: Cody Schneider: finding pain points on Reddit and building AI-powered one-person service businesses
sources.originalTitle: A New AI Gold Rush Just Started. Don’t Miss This One. (+4 Ideas)
sources.outlet: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
sources.summary: Cody Schneider walks through several one-person business ideas: an AI avatar UGC ad agency for supplement brands, webinar-to-ebook lead magnets, and city-specific flight deal newsletters. The common thread is mining real customer pain points, niching down, and selling to buyers who already spend money on the problem.

principles.text: A business is something people want plus the ability to sell it by speaking to their most painful problems.
principles.quote: A business is two things at its core. It is you have something people want to buy and you can sell it,

principles.text: Sell to people already addicted to a channel like ads; don't try to convince non-buyers to start.
principles.quote: You're not going to convince people to start running ads. You want to find people that already know that ads work and offer them something better.

principles.text: Mine real public conversations (Reddit via Perplexity/ChatGPT deep research) to uncover pain points, then build the offer around them.
principles.quote: So, this is basically like how you can uncover based off of the real conversations that people are having in these public forums. What are their pain points?

principles.text: Unsexy, boring businesses are where the money is; competitors rarely bother and budgets are large.
principles.quote: this is where you make money on online businesses is doing stuff like this that is like super high value

principles.text: With AI, creative volume replaces scarcity: generate many variations and act as curator, picking winners to test.
principles.quote: The job of the human is like you're just a curator. You're just like picking the winners.

principles.text: Niche down deeply within an industry so your outreach and social proof carry weight with that specific category.
principles.quote: go deep on like you only do biotech or you only do you know cyber security

sources.title: Cody Schneider on growth flywheels, underpriced attention and building Graph
sources.originalTitle: Growth Flywheels, Underpriced Attention & Building Graphed.com | Cody Schneider
sources.summary: Cody Schneider recounts scaling Rupa Health by layering growth channels, then explains how to find underpriced distribution (paid creative testing, creator posts, programmatic TV) and why early startups should do transactional marketing first. He also pitches Graph, an AI marketing analytics agent.

principles.text: Layer growth channels like flywheels: pour everything into one until it plateaus, then add the next.
principles.quote: you figure out a channel and you test five things, see traction with one of them, focus all of your like mental energy, money, resources, like everything basically gets f focused there until you start to see the um the ceiling occurring on that growth channel.

principles.text: Early on, do transactional marketing (paid ads, cold DMs, cold email) that produces revenue tomorrow, not long-term SEO.
principles.quote: when you're an early early stage company, you focus on transactional marketing. So like something that is going to make an action happen tomorrow. So re revenue tomorrow, not revenue six months from now.

principles.text: Validate ideas before building: put up a landing page, run ads, and see if anyone will give a credit card.
principles.quote: stand up a landing page with claude code run ads to it see which you get the cheapest signups for like or if somebody can would even pay you like go through the flow or start a free trial

principles.text: Look for channel arbitrage: underpriced or hard-to-access inventory not yet saturated by advertisers.
principles.quote: typically you're looking for an arbitrage that isn't being exploited currently. The best way to find those arbitrageages is like look where people spend time online that like isn't really saturated yet

principles.text: Testing paid social: mass-produce creative, find cheapest clicks, then run winners as conversion campaigns on payment events.
principles.quote: our strategy is like you build like a hundred pieces of creative. Um, you take uh the um like cheapest C, you run those as CPC campaigns to see which ones get the cheapest clicks.

principles.text: Judge acquisition by lifetime value and payback, not first-month profit; losing money on month one can be fine.
principles.quote: the customer lifetime value was like $600, right? So, you'd basically like pay the 89 to make 600, but you would lose money off of it the first month.

sources.title: Digital gravity: build sustainable, high-volume content and email distribution
sources.originalTitle: Cody Schneider: Every Founder Needs To Build Digital Gravity
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains his "digital gravity" view of marketing: pick repeatable channels (X, email nurture, newsletters, podcasts, short-form clips), publish at high volume, read the data, and double down on winners. He covers recycling top tweets, growing newsletters from social, pairing podcasts with newsletters for trust, and setting a North Star metric per channel.

principles.text: Think of marketing as building digital mass: more content creates more gravity and a larger natural inbound over time.
principles.quote: you're trying to build like digital Mass on the internet so that you have more digital gravity within your sphere

principles.text: Choose marketing you can sustain indefinitely, as a lifestyle choice rather than a campaign; consistency beats short bursts.
principles.quote: think about it as okay this is a lifestyle choice that I'm going to choose and for the next whatever it is you know five years I'm going to do this every week every day

principles.text: Run content as a volume-plus-data loop: publish a lot, check what works, do more of it and less of what doesn't.
principles.quote: do a bunch of stuff look at the data to see what works do more of what's working un less of what isn't and you're going to create a growth flywheel

principles.text: Recycle your top-performing posts every six to eight weeks; audiences have short attention spans.
principles.quote: I don't write new tweets anymore I basically just go and look at the top performers and I cycle them in every six to two months or six weeks to two months

principles.text: Pair a weekly podcast with a newsletter: repeated long-form listening builds deep trust so prospects arrive sales-ready.
principles.quote: you just build this such deep trust that by the time they come to sales they're like oh I'm buy ready like I know your whole stick

principles.text: Define one North Star metric per channel up front and get everyone to agree on it.
principles.quote: defining that Northstar goal from the beginning and having everybody agree on that that's how uh you like build good marketing organizations

sources.title: Cody Schneider on AI UGC ads, bottom-funnel SEO, and small-scope apps
sources.originalTitle: How to make $60k/mo in 2025 w Cody Schneider
sources.summary: Cody lays out several AI-era arbitrage plays: mass-testing AI avatar ad variations, bottom-of-funnel programmatic SEO with early CTAs, and tiny-scope apps or exact-match-domain tools that undercut high-ticket services. He also explains why he prefers B2B over B2C and how he spins killer features into standalone products.

principles.text: Use AI UGC to test ad variations at a scale that was never affordable before, then hand winning scripts to real humans.
principles.quote: it's like it's about I test the variations at a scale that I couldn't previously

principles.text: Bottom-of-funnel SEO tied to your core product wins; put CTAs early in the article, not at the bottom.
principles.quote: the call to action to join the software is at the bottom of the page of a 2,000w article

principles.text: Build tiny-scope products in proven categories at a price point that undercuts incumbents.
principles.quote: things that have very small product scope that have already proven um like spaces that they're working in at a high price point that we can then undercut

principles.text: Package formerly high-ticket coaching as an affordable AI product with voice for an impulse purchase.
principles.quote: if you can figure out a coaching mechanism that's an AI that used to be a high ticket thing

principles.text: B2B is a better entry point than B2C: less price sensitive and easier pain points, while B2C demands elite marketing.
principles.quote: if you aren't God at marketing there is zero% chance that you're going to make it in BDC

principles.text: Spin standout features out of a larger app into standalone products with their own exact-match domains.
principles.quote: when you build these apps you're going to find like killer features within the like larger app that you built that is actually more valuable to the market than what you initially thought

sources.title: Cody Schneider on AI-scaled SEO, distribution moats and growth stacks for podcasts and newsletters
sources.originalTitle: Hacking Marketing & Growth w/ Cody Schneider (MI293)
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains how he learned growth by doing, why distribution beats product, and how AI makes long-tail SEO content nearly free. He also covers his Twitter system and a layered growth stack (podcast SEO, iOS Facebook ads, email/SMS newsletters) for podcast growth.

principles.text: Learn marketing by running a real loop: a blog, traffic, then a sale. Doing it puts you in the top 1%.
principles.quote: make a Blog about a topic you're interested in figure out how to get traffic to it figure out how to sell something to that traffic and you're in the top one percent of marketers if you can do that

principles.text: Distribution beats product. Owned media and proprietary customer data are the only moats left.
principles.quote: I see worse products win all the time because they have better distribution

principles.text: When AI makes content nearly free, target low-difficulty, low-competition long-tail keywords at scale and rank fast.
principles.quote: I find all the low KB low competition keywords related to that topic

principles.text: Publish first, polish later. Add images, CTAs and internal links only once an article gets traffic and data.
principles.quote: publish all of this like if nobody's seeing it it doesn't matter if it's not perfect as soon as people are seeing it again we're just looking at the data then we go back in

principles.text: Treat every channel as a system: pick it, run it consistently, measure, and double down on what works.
principles.quote: figure out a channel turn it into a system and then look at the data to see what's working and do more of what's working and less of what isn't

principles.text: Grow a podcast by stacking podcast SEO, iOS-only Facebook ads and newsletters so each lever feeds the others.
principles.quote: the things that you layer together are podcast SEO Facebook ads to iOS only devices and then newsletters

sources.title: Cody Schneider on bootstrapping Swell AI and stacking growth channels with podcasts and AI
sources.originalTitle: A Napier Podcast Interview with Cody Schneider at Swell AI
sources.summary: Cody explains how podcasts act as a sales and content engine, why feeding AI human expert source material beats generic prompting, and how he layers every growth channel (cold email, paid, programmatic SEO, TikTok networks). He also shares his "can we do this forever?" marketing filter and career advice to start a blog, get traffic and learn technical skills.

principles.text: Ground AI content in unique human expert source material, not generic prompts, to stand out from average LLM output.
principles.quote: When you create that source file that is unique, from that expert point of view, that's where you can create this differentiation within the content.

principles.text: Early-stage companies should launch a show: inviting target customers is sales in disguise and builds relationships.
principles.quote: Podcasts are one of the most effective sales tools that exist currently, so, and I see this especially for early stage companies like I always advocate for them to create a show.

principles.text: Layer every growth lever wherever your target customer is; stacking channels compounds results.
principles.quote: take every growth lever that exists, like, wherever your target customer is, like, you need to meet them there, and then what you need to do is basically layer on all of these growth strategies onto each other, and that's how you break the laws of physics.

principles.text: With for-you-page algorithms, volume matters: more posts means more at-bats at going viral.
principles.quote: if I hit 100 times, right, like, I'm gonna get on base 20 times. And so it's the same idea with content now

principles.text: Only start marketing activities you can sustain indefinitely; think repeatable cadence, not campaigns.
principles.quote: Can we do this for two years, every week, every month, every day, whatever that ends up being from a cadence standpoint, if the answer is no, don't even start the thing because it won't make impact for your company.

principles.text: To learn marketing, start a blog, drive traffic, sell from it, and get technical by prompting AI to write scripts.
principles.quote: Start a blog, figure out how to get traffic to it. Figure out how to sell something to them. From that traffic. If you can do that, you're in the top 1% of marketers in the world.

sources.title: Cody Schneider: Distribution, owned media and "digital gravity" as the only moat in the AI era
sources.originalTitle: AI, Brand Moats, and the Power of Owned Media with Cody Schneider (MDE644)
sources.summary: Cody argues that as AI drives feature parity and the cost of building software toward zero, distribution and brand are the only durable moats. He covers owned media (a16z, Arrow Electronics, Red Bull, Rupa Health's podcast), tracking branded search, bottom-up AI adoption, guardrails and domain vocabulary for AI output, and using social as a public idea-testing ground.

principles.text: With feature parity, the product with better marketing and distribution wins every time.
principles.quote: if I have a product A and product B, and their feature there's feature parity, right? But product A has better marketing and distribution than product B, product A is going to win every time, full stop.

principles.text: Build owned media that speaks to one well-defined target customer; it gives distribution, defensibility and negotiation leverage.
principles.quote: you have to make media that is selling to your target customer. And if you're like, our target customer is everyone, like you're going to create terrible media.

principles.text: Track brand as the compounding moat: measure branded searches in Search Console month over month.
principles.quote: are the brand volume searches increasing month over month?. And I think for growing companies, this is, for example, this is my, like, one of my biggest metrics for 2026

principles.text: Content marketing fights rising ad costs: as CPCs climb, organic content drives acquisition toward zero.
principles.quote: it basically is how you fight that increased, you know, advertising costs that's going to naturally happen within a market.

principles.text: Build 'digital gravity': enough content mass that you catch prospects at every stage of a messy, non-linear funnel.
principles.quote: you basically need to build digital mass on the internet so that you create digital gravity within your, your space.

principles.text: Roll out AI bottom-up: give individuals tooling to automate tasks they hate, then reward sharing with status.
principles.quote: I think the best way to do this is to give your individual contributors the tooling that they can, or that they need to automate as much of their own daily workflows or jobs as possible.

sources.title: Cody Schneider on AI content repurposing: turn long-form expert conversations into a distribution flywheel
sources.originalTitle: #121: AI Content Creation Strategy with Founder Cody Schneider
sources.summary: Cody explains how solopreneurs and creators can build trust and revenue with long-form content (podcast, newsletter, YouTube) fed by short-form clips, and how to use AI as a task automator grounded in expert source material rather than generic LLM knowledge. He also covers high-volume posting on "for you" feeds and remixing top performers.

principles.text: Use short-form content for top of funnel, then pull people into long-form and email, where trust and sales happen.
principles.quote: use short form content for top of funnel. That leads into some type of own media where it's like email long form content.

principles.text: Content builds 'digital gravity': more content creates mass, which creates gravity, which pulls in influence and inbound.
principles.quote: the more content I make, the more digital mass I make, the more digital mass I make, the more digital gravity I make, and the more digital gravity I have, the more influence and inbound I get.

principles.text: High-ticket buyers arrive ready to buy after consuming your long-form content over weeks; they don't buy off one viral short.
principles.quote: when you have this longer form content, the the person is already ready to buy when you get on that sales call.

principles.text: AI is best at structuring unstructured data and getting you 80-90% there; ground it in expert source material, not its general knowledge.
principles.quote: it's great at taking unstructured data and structuring it.

principles.text: Audit your workflows and automate tasks, not whole companies; reserve human time for sales and client-facing work.
principles.quote: what are you doing currently? Like, which part of these tasks can AI automate? And then let's implement those solutions so that your team can focus on high impact things.

principles.text: For-you feeds mean saturation is outdated; post far more than you think, review the top 10% weekly and remix those ideas.
principles.quote: every week I go back and I look at the data over the last 3 months and I'm like, okay, what are the top performing pieces of content? Here's the top 10%. Let's just go remix those over and over again.

sources.title: Why businesses must become media companies: Cody Schneider on AI content engines and owned media
sources.originalTitle: Scaling Content Creation with Cody Schneider
sources.summary: Cody Schneider explains how he built an owned-media content engine at Rupa Health and turned it into Swell AI. He argues for interview-led podcasts chopped into clips, automating 5% of your process at a time with AI, and treating your content library as the differentiator while marketing becomes a profit center.

principles.text: Own your media channel: record expert conversations and distribute them yourself to cut through noise and get discovered.
principles.quote: we needed to create these owned media channels as a way to cut through the noise.

principles.text: Run one long-form interview weekly, chop it into clips, and schedule them daily across social to cover every discovery surface.
principles.quote: we did a, you know, long-form podcast on a weekly cadence. We would then chop that up into clips. All those clips get scheduled out to our social media platforms.

principles.text: Adopt AI incrementally: automate 5% of your current process, then scale to 10, 15, 30, 60%, instead of reinventing the company.
principles.quote: Just find 5% of your current process. that you can automate away with AI, automate that away, and then bump that up to 10%, and then to 15, and then to 30, and then to 60

principles.text: AI makes marketers curators instead of grunt labor, so small teams of strong marketers multiply their output.
principles.quote: if you have a team of five marketers that are 10X marketers and you give these tools to them, they suddenly turn into 100X marketers.

principles.text: Your proprietary content library will be the differentiator as products and distribution get easier to copy.
principles.quote: Your content library will be your differentiator.

principles.text: Owned media turns marketing from a cost center into a profit center via ad sales, leverage, and inbound.
principles.quote: it turns your marketing department from a cost center into a profit center.

sources.title: How Cody Schneider uses Claude Code for GTM engineering: parallel terminals, code over N8N, bulk ads and pages
sources.originalTitle: Claude Code is Fundamentally Changing GTM Engineering
sources.summary: Cody explains his Claude Code setup for growth work: one env file of API keys, five parallel terminals, and Claude building software to automate everything. He shares concrete builds: 100 landing pages in 30 minutes, 40 Facebook ads from code templates, and a LinkedIn engager to cold email pipeline built in 15 minutes.

principles.text: Run growth work from Claude Code with one env file of API keys, and have it build software for whatever you're working on.
principles.quote: I just have an environment file that contains all the API keys for my entire software stack that I use.

principles.text: Let AI do the "middle work": you supply the idea and the final polish, the AI materializes it in between.
principles.quote: That middle section. Number two. Claude now does all that for me.

principles.text: Skip no-code automation middleware; go straight to code and have Claude build and deploy the server.
principles.quote: Now when I'm building an automation, I just go straight to code. No N8N middleware.

principles.text: Build a dedicated landing page per converting Google Ads keyword to lift conversion rate, and generate them in bulk.
principles.quote: find the converting keywords and then build a landing page that's dedicated to that. This increases the conversion rate of this campaign.

principles.text: Treat design as code: build ad templates as React components and generate many variations programmatically.
principles.quote: I had the epiphany that all design is just code.

principles.text: Make many ad variations around different positioning and messaging concepts, and put winners in their own campaigns.
principles.quote: You basically make a ton of different variations focusing on different positioning and messaging concepts and the winners go into their own campaigns.

sources.title: Digital Gravity: win AI search with 1000x surface area on Google pages 1 and 2
sources.originalTitle: AI search is here, the only way to win is by making Digital Gravity
sources.summary: Cody argues AI answer engines mostly scrape Google's first two result pages, so brands must flood their niche with content and media placements to build "digital gravity". He also covers YouTube as the top social channel, free apps as lead gen for services, and cheap ad tactics.

principles.text: AI answer engines scrape Google pages 1 and 2, so rank and get media placements there to show up in AI search.
principles.quote: From our internal data we’ve found that AI answer engines are scraping page 1 and page 2 of Google.

principles.text: Aim for 1000x content volume, not 10x; surface area builds digital mass, gravity and niche influence.
principles.quote: And I’m not talking about 10x content, I’m talking about 1000x. You need surface area, a lot of surface area to show up in AI search engines.

principles.text: Mental model: more surface area creates more digital mass, which creates more digital gravity and influence.
principles.quote: more surface area makes more digital mass, more digital mass makes more digital gravity which makes more influence in your niche.

principles.text: YouTube puts you in people's living rooms on TV; invest in it as the most valuable social platform.
principles.quote: you can now be in a persons home, talking to them, daily weekly monthly

principles.text: Build small free apps as lead gen that funnel to a higher-priced services business.
principles.quote: They build tons of small scope Shopify apps and provide them for free all with the goal of creating lead gen for their main services

principles.text: Use TikTok ads with a $2 CPM bid cap for cheap top-of-funnel discovery instead of managing clippers.
principles.quote: when I tested this I got a $1.64 CPM

sources.title: Media is a terrible business unless you sell a product you own
sources.originalTitle: Media is a terrible business unless you do this...
sources.summary: Cody argues ad-supported media is a grind (constant outbound, budget cuts, advertiser management) and the real money comes from using media as a vehicle to sell a product you own. He gives B2B and DTC examples plus quick distribution ideas like short-form LinkedIn and AI-written long-tail blog posts from webinars.

principles.text: Ad-supported media is a grind; the money is in selling a product you own through the media.
principles.quote: Media is a terrible business… unless you’re selling a product you own

principles.text: Selling ads means constant outbound, managing advertisers, and budgets that vanish overnight.
principles.quote: You’re constantly outbounding for ads, managing advertiser expectations, budgets get cut overnight. It’s brutal.

principles.text: Treat media as the vehicle to sell something, not as the product itself.
principles.quote: Media isn’t the product. Media is the vehicle to sell something.

principles.text: Build niche podcasts, then build DTC brands or sell your own products on top of the audience.
principles.quote: Builds podcasts for consumers and then builds DTC brands on top of those podcasts.

principles.text: For short-form LinkedIn, pick a format and commit; new viral content resurrects old content.
principles.quote: just find a format and let it rip

principles.text: Turn a webinar transcript into 20 AI-written long-tail blog posts with the webinar embedded to drive recording views.
principles.quote: have ai write blog posts about each longtail keyword

sources.title: Cody Schneider: activation mirrors YouTube thumbnails, plus Twitter newsletter growth and local SEO
sources.originalTitle: YouTube videos teach us good software activation, newsletter growth
sources.summary: Cody argues software signup-to-paid activation works like a YouTube video: the homepage is the thumbnail/title promise and onboarding must deliver the lightbulb moment fast. He also shares concrete tactics: a high-volume Twitter plus DM automation that nearly doubled his newsletter in 4 weeks, a directory-link plus indexing playbook for local SEO, and a "Google Ads for XYZ" YouTube idea.

principles.text: Treat your homepage as a thumbnail/title: it makes a promise, and onboarding must deliver it immediately.
principles.quote: Your homepage is your thumbnail/title. You’re making a promise with it.

principles.text: Activation is the lightbulb moment; design the signup flow to get users there as fast as possible.
principles.quote: Activation happens when the user has the lightbulb moment as fast as possible.

principles.text: Failing to deliver on the marketing promise destroys trust instantly.
principles.quote: The promise is an opportunity for trust, if I don’t deliver on that promise it erodes all trust instantly.

principles.text: Grow a personal newsletter via Twitter: post ~10 times a day, add a delayed subscribe CTA thread to each post, and auto-DM new followers.
principles.quote: 70 Tweets a week, 10 per day, every hour from 7a to 5p

principles.text: Build local business links through cheap directory links, then use an indexing tool so huge directory pages actually get seen.
principles.quote: Directory links don’t get seen easily because the sites are huge.

principles.text: Target long-tail 'google ads for XYZ' keywords where YouTube videos rank on page one, then monetize with affiliates and service upsells.
principles.quote: Start a channel and make videos that target these keywords.

sources.title: Cody Schneider's hot takes: newsletter consolidation, creator-first founders, and cheap growth plays
sources.originalTitle: Newsletters value go to zero, ebook generator ai, agency for unlimited influencer reachout
sources.summary: A May 2024 newsletter issue where Cody argues newsletter values are crashing (a consolidation opportunity), that founders should build in public as media companies, and shares business ideas (an unlimited influencer outreach agency, an exact-match ebook domain) plus AI-written SEO articles and affiliate bounties.

principles.text: Newsletter values are heading to zero because supply is saturated; brands can buy them cheap and consolidate.
principles.quote:
There’s more ad inventory than people who want to buy.

This space is going to crash.

And there is a huge opportunity for brands to buy these on the cheap and consolidate.

principles.text: Founders who build in public gain a differentiator and leverage with customers, investors and partners; every company should become a media company.
principles.quote: Ride-alongs, build-in public, and vlogs of startup life are now a blue ocean strategy.

principles.text: Sell outsourced influencer outreach as a flat-fee agency: scrape creator emails, cold email from lookalike domains, handle negotiation and reporting.
principles.quote:
You do unlimited influencer research, reach out, negotiation, tracking and affiliate reporting.

Charge $3,000 a month.

principles.text: Spot agency opportunities by listening to founders' pain points: time-consuming marketing tasks they want done but can't.
principles.quote:
They told me they want to do this, but it’s super time-consuming.

Bingo.

Business idea.

principles.text: Find simple niche products via keywords: buy an exact-match domain, build links, rank, and get paid.
principles.quote: Buy exact match domain build links rank for that keyword get paid.

principles.text: Run affiliate bounties with a specific task, a deadline and quality expectations to get people making social content about your software.
principles.quote:
There’s a specific thing they want you to do.

There is a time limit which creates urgency.

sources.title: Cody Schneider: AI brand voice docs, long-tail SEO tool ideas, LinkedIn polls and cold email for signups
sources.originalTitle: AI Brand Voice Documents, xyz quickbooks integrations, LinkedIn polls for leads
sources.summary: Cody argues teams need an AI brand voice document just like a style guide, and pitches small-tool-for-big-ecosystem businesses built on long-tail keywords and programmatic landing pages. He also shares growth tactics: controversial hidden-result LinkedIn polls that convert to an email course, and cold email measured on signups rather than replies.

principles.text: Create an AI brand voice document so everyone on the team gets consistent, on-brand AI output.
principles.quote: Just how we have brand style guides, we need to have AI brand voice guides for our teams.

principles.text: Build the voice doc from existing brand content, then have AI define the persona and refine it.
principles.quote: Collect existing media your brand has already produced and then ask AI to help define your brand voice and persona based on this existing content.

principles.text: Include the brand's own vocabulary in the voice doc so AI output sounds human and on-brand.
principles.quote: Instruct the AI to include specific vocabulary from your brand’s existing content.

principles.text: Favor small tools for big ecosystems; long-tail keyword gaps like 'xyz quickbooks integration' reveal them.
principles.quote: My favorite businesses are small tools for big ecosystems.

principles.text: Marketplaces grow through millions of long-tail landing pages, which AI now makes cheap to produce.
principles.quote: This is how marketplaces actually grow. By making millions of long tail landing pages.

principles.text: Hide LinkedIn poll results to drive votes, then edit the post with an email course CTA when the poll ends.
principles.quote: And when they come back, I’ve edited the post to include a call to action to join my 7 day email course.

sources.title: Digital Gravity: Cloning a corporation's real-world size online, from brand to product to industry
sources.originalTitle: Digital Gravity: A Model to Think About Your Brand’s Online Footprint
sources.summary: Cody Schneider borrows startup tactics (be where customers look, solving problems) and applies them to large corporations with no digital footprint. His "digital gravity" model grows online influence in sequence: brand first, then product questions, then industry questions, so the internet recognizes a company as big as it is offline.

principles.text: Be present wherever your target customers look for information, and provide value there; this makes young companies feel bigger and more trustworthy.
principles.quote: This formula involves being where our target customers expect to get information about a company like us online.

principles.text: A company's real-world size doesn't carry online; you must deliberately build your digital footprint so the internet understands you're big.
principles.quote: You have to teach teach the internet you’re big. You have to create digital gravity but growing your digital footprint.

principles.text: Digital influence is earned and, unlike a planet's mass, can keep growing through brand, product answers, and industry answers.
principles.quote: Unlike the Earth, whose mass is finite, digital planets can grow. They grow through brand, answering questions related to product, and answering questions related to their industry.

principles.text: A website exists to market the brand. Optimize it first to make search engines and social platforms understand who, what and why.
principles.quote: Why does a website exist? To market brand. Period.

principles.text: Answer the questions people ask about your products, in forms both people and search robots can find and understand: text, video, audio, combined.
principles.quote: People ask questions in the real world, so we answer these questions online but make them both findable by people and the robots.

principles.text: Sequence content from specific to generic (brand, product, industry), and treat it as a grueling multi-year investment that can build an uncatchable lead.
principles.quote: By going from specific to generic, from brand to industry, we can clone the company’s real world size online.

sources.title: Marketing moats: build owned media as the bonds of your marketing portfolio
sources.originalTitle: The Power of Marketing Moats: How to Create Owned Media for Long-Term Success
sources.summary: Cody argues that the most important business moats are marketing moats built from owned media. He shows how he dominates the front page for a handful of keywords across blogs, YouTube and free tools, then backstops it with email. He frames marketing as a portfolio of risk-weighted bets, with owned media as the bonds.

principles.text: The moats that matter most are marketing moats, not product, scale or NPS moats.
principles.quote: But we are consistently talking about the least important moats. Moats around product, economies of scale, high-NPS… when we really should be talking about marketing moats.

principles.text: Find the few keywords that drive acquisition and own the whole front page for each, across many assets.
principles.quote: For this product, there are 10 keywords that create all the new customer acquisition. I tirelessly work to own the front page for every one of those keywords.

principles.text: Rank on multiple surfaces: separate-domain blogs, several YouTube channels, and free Chrome extensions.
principles.quote: Multiple blogs in separate domains ranking for them. YouTube videos from multiple channels ranking for them. Free chrome extensions that do a less better version of what the software accomplishes.

principles.text: Collect emails so you can reach your audience directly if Google or YouTube change their algorithms.
