principles.quote: So we focus on email collection for our audience as well so we can have direct coms when we want.

principles.text: Rented channels like paid ads are variable, risky and easy to copy, so a competitor entering can wreck your unit economics.
principles.quote: Channels you don’t own are variable, and higher risk. They’re also easier to duplicate, especially now with ad spy tools.

principles.text: Treat marketing as a portfolio of bets with risk premiums, and treat owned media as the bonds.
principles.quote: I want to challenge you to think about marketing as a portfolio of bets with risk premiums.

sources.title: FOMO marketing: bet on what's working, explore with 20%
sources.originalTitle: FOMO Marketing: How to Avoid Shiny Object Syndrome
sources.summary: Cody defines FOMO marketing as deciding based on what you could be doing instead of what is working. He frames marketing as a portfolio (80% on proven channels, 20% on exploration) and says to keep scaling a winning channel until returns diminish, using a 13x ROAS Google Search example.

principles.text: FOMO marketing means choosing based on what you could do, not on what is working.
principles.quote: FOMO marketing is when we make marketing decisions based on what we could be doing rather than what is working.

principles.text: Treat marketing as a portfolio: 80% on proven channels, 20% on exploring new ones.
principles.quote: I think about marketing as a portfolio, where 80% of resources is spent on what is working and 20% on an exploration of new initiatives.

principles.text: Scale a winning channel until diminishing returns show up before expanding elsewhere.
principles.quote: I told him literally put as much money into that channel until you see diminishing returns. Go to that ATM until it quits printing.

principles.text: Shiny object syndrome distracts marketing teams from their purpose: increasing revenue.
principles.quote: A lot of marketing teams get shiny object syndrome and which distracts them from why they exist: to increase revenue.

principles.text: Keep testing new things, but with only a small share of resources.
principles.quote: And I'm not saying don't test new things. But allocated a small percentage of resources.

principles.text: Make bets for both the short term and the long term.
principles.quote: We're making bets for the short term, and bets for the long term.

sources.title: Educational B2B content: host experts and remarket ungated demos to build buyer-ready leads
sources.originalTitle: The Power of Educational Content in B2B Marketing
sources.summary: Cody starts B2B engagements by asking what the sales team wishes prospects knew before the first call, then maps marketing tactics to those gaps. He pairs purely educational, team-hosted expert content (trust, brand) with ungated product demos remarketed to scraped customer-match lists (product understanding).

principles.text: Start B2B marketing by asking sales what they wish prospects knew before the first call, then build marketing to close those gaps.
principles.quote: When I’m working with b2b clients one of the first questions I ask is what does your sales team wish prospects knew before ever talking to you?

principles.text: The goal is buyer-ready leads who already know the product, the problem it solves, the company, and trust its people.
principles.quote: In other words, they want leads to be buyer ready.

principles.text: Make purely educational content with a strong CTA, not sales content in disguise.
principles.quote: focus on purely educational content with a strong call to action to learn more about your product.

principles.text: Giving value without expecting anything builds 'digital gravity' and influence in your market.
principles.quote: When you give without expecting, you create what I call digital gravity. When you increase your digital mass online, you get more influence in your target market.

principles.text: Bring in industry thought leaders and host their content: it offboards idea generation, elevates your brand, and builds an owned media library.
principles.quote: It is a way to “offboard” content idea generation. Your job no longer includes creating unique ideas, but instead curating and sharing those ideas.

principles.text: Don't gate demos; B2B buyers want to learn everything before talking to sales. Remarket demos to scraped-email customer match lists and pixeled site visitors.
principles.quote: An easy way to get these demos in front of your customers is to scrape all their emails, and import these list as customer match lists into all platforms people spend time online on.

sources.title: Why B2B brands should hire channel-specialist creators: a TikTok experiment
sources.originalTitle: Specialized Content Creators: Insights from a B2B TikTok Experiment
sources.summary: Cody recounts a friend's B2B SaaS experiment paying one creator $5K/month to run the brand's TikTok, yielding 375K views for $15K and a 3x ROAS. He argues for hiring channel-native specialists who build trust through consistency, tell product-in-the-journey stories, and are measured on channel growth, with simple referral-link tracking.

principles.text: Hire a dedicated specialist per channel (YouTuber, TikToker, Podcaster) who owns it entirely, rather than rotating UGC models.
principles.quote: brands starting to realize that having creators who are specialists for each channel creates more impact.

principles.text: Consistency of one face builds trust and lowers the ask when it's time to buy.
principles.quote: The more you see them keep providing value, the less the ask is when they want to buy.

principles.text: Mimic what naturally works on each platform and make content native to the channel, not one-size-fits-all.
principles.quote: When doing b2b marketing I challenge you to mimic what is naturally happening on channels and do a version that serves your business goals.

principles.text: Put a real personality on camera: faceless product-focused content underperformed videos featuring the creator.
principles.quote: Videos with the person included go viral 10x more.

principles.text: Make the customer's goal the story and the product an essential tool in the journey, not the subject.
principles.quote: The best performing videos always told a story where the product was included in the journey, rather than the journey being about the product.

principles.text: Prove ROI with a dedicated signup link per channel plus a required 'how did you hear about us?' field.
principles.quote: Creating a referral link for each channel is super easy way to measure ROI on hiring these people.

sources.title: How Cody Schneider grows a newsletter from a scraped cold list by promoting a podcast
sources.originalTitle: How to use podcasts to grow a thriving newsletter from a scraped email list
sources.summary: Cody argues the hardest part of a scraped email list is knowing what to send, and his answer is a podcast. A client's cold list, sequenced into an ESP and only promoting the podcast, got a 40% open rate and 5% CTR. The podcast hit 5K+ monthly downloads in 60 days because people see podcasts as education, not sales.

principles.text: The hard part of a cold email list is deciding what to send; a podcast solves that content problem.
principles.quote: But once you have these emails and you’ve validated them, what do you send them? This is one of the hardest challenges I’ve found with this distribution channel.

principles.text: Sequence the cold list into an ESP and only promote the podcast. This produced a 40% open rate and 5% CTR on a cold list.
principles.quote: For a client I’m working with we sequenced a cold list of their target audience into an ESP and all we did was promote their podcast.

principles.text: Keep the email educational and low-lift: a passive listen is a small ask for the target customer.
principles.quote: The content of the email is super educational and basically just “Go learn this today on this podcast”. For the target customer, the podcast is a small lift because it is passive.

principles.text: People treat podcasts as education, not sales tools, so a soft CTA inside one doesn't feel aggressive.
principles.quote: I believe this is working because people don’t view podcasts as sales tools yet. They look at them as educational vehicles, so the call to action is soft and doesn’t feel aggressive.

principles.text: Have clients interview their customers, so episodes are customer testimonials disguised as education.
principles.quote: What’s wild those is we instruct clients to interview their customers, which means that the podcast episodes are basically just customer testimonials disguised as education.

principles.text: Content quality matters less than existing and being distributed; the playbook works in any industry.
principles.quote: The content doesn’t have to be perfect, it just has to exist so it can be distributed.

sources.title: Lead validation with GPT-3: qualifying a scraped prospect database by reading each company's website
sources.originalTitle: Lead Validation with GPT3
sources.summary: Cody argues every B2B software company should own a database of all its target customers, then use GPT-3 to qualify leads instead of relying on brittle keyword matching or manual SDR review. The workflow is simple: scrape each lead's site, feed the text to a yes/no prompt, and loop over the list. He frames AI as making top performers 100x rather than replacing people.

principles.text: Own a database of every target customer, sourced from directories, Google Maps scraping and similar places.
principles.quote: Every b2b software company should have an owned database of all their target customers sourced from anywhere they can collect them. Think directories, scraping google maps etc.

principles.text: A startup with a full list of its target customers at raise time impresses investors.
principles.quote: if you’re an early-stage startup and have a list of all your target customers when you’re raising you A, investors will be stoked.

principles.text: With tens of thousands of leads, the real problem is deciding which ones sales works first.
principles.quote: But say you collect 50K leads, which do you prioritize your sales team working?

principles.text: Keyword matching is too limited for qualification because people describe the same thing differently; an LLM reads meaning instead.
principles.quote: But keywords are super limited because people talk about the same thing differently pretty often.

principles.text: Validate leads by scraping each prospect's site, asking GPT a yes/no fit question about the text, and looping over the whole list.
principles.quote: Use python to request a potential leads URL; Ingest all the text on the persons site; Then use a gpt3 prompt like “Does this company have multiple mental health professionals or are they a solo practitioner?”

principles.text: Use AI to make your best people far more productive, not to replace them.
principles.quote: I think it will make 10x people 100x people.

sources.title: Email as a personal search engine: measure email on a CPC basis and treat it like SEO
sources.originalTitle: A Modern Way to Think About Email Marketing
sources.summary: Cody argues email should be judged by cost per click, including labor and CRM costs, rather than as a transactional blast channel. Because people return to old emails months later, email works as a user's personal search engine and database, so every relevant email you send seeds long-term, SEO-like assets in their inbox.

principles.text: Measure email on a cost-per-click basis, like search and display ads.
principles.quote: We should be measuring email clicks on a CPC basis and we should be thinking about email clients as a people’s personal search engines.

principles.text: Compute true email CPC by including setup labor and CRM cost, not just the sender fee.
principles.quote: Email CPC = Initial labor setup costs + (CRM cost \* months) / Total clicks in time frame

principles.text: A higher email CPC than paid ads can be worth it because people revisit emails months later.
principles.quote: Say we were spending $0.10 on paid ads, now we have to make the decision of whether this premium for a CPC is worth it. It’s worth it because people were revisiting the emails months later.

principles.text: People use their inbox as a searchable database, so sending email adds your brand and content to it.
principles.quote: when we send emails to users we’re adding our brand, content and ideas to their database — a database that they search later on.

principles.text: Any email-capture moment (PDF download, newsletter signup, purchase) is permission to seed their inbox with relevant content.
principles.quote: when people share their email with your organization through a PDF download, a newsletter signup, or when they make a product purchase they’re giving us permission to add to their database.

principles.text: Treat email as a long-term compounding strategy like SEO, not a transactional campaign.
principles.quote: email is not a transactional campaign, but rather a long term marketing strategy similarly SEO.

sources.title: A-through-Z testing: let the platform eliminate losing ads instead of A/B testing
sources.originalTitle: Stop A/B testing, Start A-through-Z Testing
sources.summary: Cody argues digital ads should work like evolution: a process of elimination, not a search for one right answer. Instead of A/B testing single components, combine many photos, headlines and body copy into hundreds or thousands of ad units and let CPC and conversion data show the winners. He also ties this to AI-built ads drawn from media libraries.

principles.text: Search for what doesn't work rather than what does; use process of elimination like nature.
principles.quote: Digital advertising should use the same process of elimination — search for what doesn’t work rather than what does.

principles.text: Digital ad inventory is effectively unlimited, so test every creative idea instead of one ad per audience.
principles.quote: No longer do we have to run a single ad to an audience, but rather every ad creative idea we can think of.

principles.text: Treat a combined ad as its own unit; dissecting components (photo, copy, CTA) in isolation misleads.
principles.quote: when you combine the different aspects of creative it creates a whole new piece of media.

principles.text: Combine components into many ad units and let the platform's data pick the winner on CPC and conversions.
principles.quote: imagine you combine ten different photos, ten different headlines and ten different body texts for Facebook ads. This would create 1K combinations.

principles.text: Let the audience tease out the message they want rather than forcing one on them.
principles.quote: In this way we’re not forcing a message on the audience, but rather teasing a message out of the audience with the message they want to engage with most.

principles.text: AI will generate ad units from media libraries, testing thousands and telling creative teams what media to make next.
principles.quote: Firms will be able to test thousands of ad units and advise creative teams on what media they should make next for the media library.

sources.title: Think of your marketing budget as a financial portfolio, not time-boxed campaigns
sources.originalTitle: Think About Your Marketing Budget as a Financial Portfolio
sources.summary: Cody argues digital marketing should drop campaigns with start and end dates (a military idea from Madison Avenue) and instead run an always-on portfolio. Spread resources across short and long term assets, favor things that compound, and simply do more of what works and less of what doesn't.

principles.text: Eliminate start and end dates; digital feedback loops are instant, so don't flight ads.
principles.quote: We need to eliminate start and end dates. I mean this as bluntly as I can, if your agency is flighting digital ads you should fire them.

principles.text: Treat the marketing budget like a financial portfolio with both short and long term initiatives, favoring what compounds.
principles.quote: Financial portfolios have both short and long term initiatives, and your marketing budget should as well.

principles.text: Don't reset your marketing to zero each year; build initiatives that grow in value over time.
principles.quote: Let’s build digital marketing initiatives into marketing portfolios that mitigate risk and grow in value over time.

principles.text: Match risk tolerance to digital maturity: early-stage digital companies can risk more, mature ones have more to lose.
principles.quote: companies who are in the early phases of adopting digital have less to lose so they should have a higher risk tolerance.

principles.text: Treat SEO as the long-term compounding investment, like income you put into accounts that compound.
principles.quote: SEO is our long-term investment. It’s our 10% yearly income that goes into accounts that have compounded growth.

principles.text: Run everything open-ended: stop what isn't working, do more of what is.
principles.quote: We don’t flight ads, we don’t do unnecessary work, we just do more of what’s working and less of what isn’t.

sources.title: Storytelling marketing: make the product a character inside a problem-journey-solution story
sources.originalTitle: Storytelling Marketing
sources.summary: Cody argues that storytelling marketing hides the product inside a narrative where it is a character, letting people sit in someone else's problem and see how the product improves life. Every story needs a problem, a journey and a solution, and it works across Facebook ads and email by tapping the human urge to share stories that make us feel.

principles.text: Storytelling marketing makes the product a character in a narrative, not the headline.
principles.quote: Storytelling marketing is the process of creating story narrative where the product is a character.

principles.text: Let people sit in someone else's problem and see how the product makes life better.
principles.quote: helps people to sit in someone else shoes, in someone else’s problem and see how a product will make their life better.

principles.text: Every marketing story needs three parts: a problem, a journey and a solution.
principles.quote: Storytelling marketing is always composed of three things, a problem, a journey and a solution.

principles.text: Stories are a shortcut to capturing interest, illustrating a problem and showcasing the product as the solution.
principles.quote: storytelling is a cheat for capturing a persons interest, illustrating a problem, and showcasing a solution to that problem in the form of a product or service.

principles.text: On Facebook, ads that show people overcoming a challenge with a product get the cheapest traffic.
principles.quote: Ads that employ the model described above by casting a vision of people facing a challenge and overcoming that challenge with a product will get the cheapest traffic from Facebook.

principles.text: Email storytelling works by tapping the natural urge to share stories that make us feel.
principles.quote: we can use email marketing for storytelling by tapping into this natural desire to share stories that make us feel.

sources.title: Branding Increases Mental Switching Costs: Why You Keep Branding After Winning the Association
sources.originalTitle: Branding Increases Mental Switching Costs
sources.summary: Cody explains that when a customer won't buy within about 48 hours, your marketing goal is branding: owning an association in their mind. Continued branding raises mental switching costs by deepening the customer's emotional relationship with you, making it very hard for a competitor to uproot.

principles.text: If the customer won't buy within ~48 hours, your marketing goal is branding, not conversion.
principles.quote: If your customer won’t make a purchase within the next 48 hrs your marketing goal is branding.

principles.text: Branding means owning an idea or need in the customer's mind so they think of you the moment it arises.
principles.quote: What branding does is associate your company name with an idea.

principles.text: Clients usually underestimate how long their customers' purchase cycle really is.
principles.quote: One thing I’ve noticed with clients is that their estimation of a customer purchase cycle is less than what it should be.

principles.text: Mental switching costs exist alongside physical ones, because people form relationships with brands like they do with people.
principles.quote: But what’s often forgotten is that mental switching costs exist.

principles.text: Keep branding after you win the association; it deepens the relationship and raises mental switching costs.
principles.quote: Because **banding increases mental switching costs.**

principles.text: Speak to customers regularly with what they want to hear, so your brand-idea association is hard to uproot.
principles.quote: But when we develop customer relationships, when we grow the level of affinity and speak to our customers more regularly with things they want to hear, we make it hard if not impossible to uproot the brand and idea association.

sources.title: The V3 SEO Model: Pick keywords by Value, Verge and Volume for fast organic gains
sources.originalTitle: The V3 SEO Model
sources.summary: Cody Schneider describes the V3 SEO Model his agency used on powerful, aged domains to find keywords worth targeting. By combining Value, Verge and Volume, the team built landing pages for search intent and reports a client gaining 51% more organic clicks and 29% more impressions in 30 days.

principles.text: Target keywords that create business value: products, buyer-journey information, and brand identity terms.
principles.quote: Keywords that can create value for the organization. For example, keywords that are related to products, information prospects search for at different stages in the buyer’s journey or keywords important to brand identity.

principles.text: Treat keywords on page two or three as 'verge' keywords: Google signals what you can rank for, and a little work lifts them to page one.
principles.quote: Google signals to us what we can rank for. Keywords on page two and three can often be lifted to page one with just a little work.

principles.text: Only chase keywords with enough search volume for your industry to actually move your analytics.
principles.quote: Our keywords must have the potential energy necessary to create impact to our current search analytics.

principles.text: The sweet spot is the intersection of value, verge and volume (V3 keywords).
principles.quote: When we combine these three ideas, we get The V3 SEO Model.

principles.text: After picking V3 keywords, build landing pages that best answer the search intent of each target keyword.
principles.quote: Once we’ve identified V3 keywords, we then build landing pages that best answer search intent for our new target keywords.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider shows a live demo of running many parallel Claude Code instances wired to marketing APIs. They generate bulk Facebook ad variations from real customer pain points, scrape and cold-email podcast hosts, auto-respond on LinkedIn, and then deploy workflows to Railway. He also argues API quality is now the key criterion for buying software and that domain vocabulary is the real moat.

chunks.heading: Environment file as the foundation for a growth-agent workspace
chunks.text:
- Cody starts by creating one folder he "lives out of" (his is called "Graft Growth Agents"). All work starts there.
- First file: an environment file holding API keys for every tool in his daily go-to-market stack: Intercom, SendGrid, HubSpot, cal.com, Perplexity, Facebook Ads, MillionVerifier, Instantly, Phantombuster and others.
- The point is to interact with everything he does day to day through APIs, from a single repo (just a folder of files), with Claude Code doing the work.
- Recommended extras: a transcription tool like Super Whisper so he can speak his instructions instead of typing, and optionally the Claude Code front-end design skill so generated UIs look decent.
- He shows a blank "demo" folder he wipes before each presentation, to demonstrate going from zero to one.

chunks.heading: Buying software based on API quality (APIs over UI)
chunks.text:
- Cody now evaluates software mainly by how robust its API is. A friend told him Salesforce, though a clunkier CRM, is the better foundation for AI than HubSpot because its API lets you do more.
- He is close to churning a tool because something critical can be done in its UI but not its API: "it feels archaic for me to go and interact with your UI."
- In his view the UI/SaaS becomes the nice-to-have; what matters is the output, and agents running 24/7 against the API.
- His company Graft debates whether to build a UI at all, or just the tooling that works inside any harness (Claude iOS, ChatGPT desktop, Claude Code, Cursor) and gives the same outputs everywhere. Its MCP serves a live data feed from the warehouse, e.g. "show me my Google Ads and Facebook Ads paid ad spend", usable by the whole team.
- He is losing sleep over how agents discover and pick your infrastructure when they build something.

chunks.heading: Running many Claude Code instances in parallel ("agent jockeying")
chunks.text:
- Cody runs a separate Claude Code window per project, starts each in plan mode, then moves on to the next while it works. In the session he had about ten going.
- Workflow: describe the job by voice, put Claude in plan mode, answer its questions, let it run in the background, check back.
- Examples running at once: a LinkedIn auto-responder, a bulk Facebook ad generator, a podcast outreach pipeline, a LinkedIn engagement scraper, a Notion giveaway doc writer, a dashboard builder.
- A LinkedIn responder agent (using the Claude Chrome extension and a custom skill) replied to everyone who asked for his email-triage giveaway asset, with the Notion doc link, and ran about 15 minutes unattended.
- Downside he admits: context switching between windows is hard ("what was this one doing again?"), and he is considering a new computer for more RAM. He has worked this way for about six weeks, starting at 2-3 windows and now comfortable with far more.
- His framing of GTM engineering: the term was coined by Clay for cascading data-enrichment workflows for outbound. He sees it as everything that used to be "middle work" at the keyboard now passed to an agent harness. His job becomes having ideas, handing them off, and polishing the end product.

chunks.heading: Bulk Facebook ad creative generator built from React components
chunks.text:
- Format: 1080x1080 images, built entirely as React components and exported to PNG with html-to-canvas, with a UI to preview and a downloadable zip.
- Finding a starting template: browse the Facebook Ad Library for competitors' ads in your category. His template came from a before/after format he found there.
- Messaging comes from research: he has Claude (via the Perplexity API) pull pain points and desired outcomes from Reddit, YouTube and Twitter, e.g. growth marketers who can't get analyst bandwidth, find BI tools too complicated, or can't unify data in one place. Ads speak to pain points and sell outcomes.
- Cost: roughly "a thousand tokens" to produce many variations; "we can create a thousand ad variations right now and it literally costs nothing."
- Why code instead of Nano Banana: Nano Banana images can drift off-brand. Code gives a fast way to test messaging angles. Once an angle wins, remix it into other templates or formats (e.g. a UGC video via the HeyGen API). For bulk Nano Banana generation he points to Kai AI.
- Strategy: find the winning format or angle first, then remix it a thousand ways.

chunks.heading: Bulk-uploading, analyzing and pruning Facebook ads with agents
chunks.text:
- Steps shown: generate variations, tell Claude to bulk upload them as drafts into a given Facebook ad set via the Facebook Ads API, build a dashboard in Graft (clicks over time, cost and CPC lines, spend and click scorecards, impressions by age bar chart), then pull ad-level data through the Graft MCP and pause the worst performers.
- Example: he pulled ads with the highest CPM and told Claude to turn off those ads by name using the Facebook Ads API.
- Why a data warehouse: he argues a direct Facebook Ads MCP hits pagination and rate limits, and people end up seeing "only like 5% of the data that I think I'm actually seeing." With volume, analysis without a data pipeline and warehouse isn't possible.
- Where he is taking it: a test campaign constantly trying new creative; a daily cron that turns off low performers; winners promoted into their own ad sets with a dedicated CPA budget; a dashboard tracking it; and a morning chat briefing on KPIs (e.g. yesterday's homepage users via the Graft MCP plus GA4), including from his phone.
- He frames this as an early version ("weeks of realization") of autonomous marketing running 24/7.

chunks.heading: Cold email pipelines: podcast outreach and LinkedIn engager scraping
chunks.text:
- Podcast booking pipeline: scrape podcast host emails (from Rephonic, in the marketing category), verify them with MillionVerifier, push them into an Instantly campaign, then have an agent respond to replies and book him on the podcast. It "ends up turning into way better performing than I expected."
- LinkedIn engager pipeline: a Slack command (`/linkedin post`) where anyone on the team drops a LinkedIn post URL. It uses the PhantomBuster API to extract engagers, enriches the profiles with the Apollo API, verifies emails with MillionVerifier, and adds them to an Instantly campaign.
- Instantly is the cold email software in his stack. The manual workflows he used to run are now daisy-chained APIs built by Claude.
- He describes an always-on agent that crawls LinkedIn for his ICP, enriches, writes a personalized email and cold emails them.

chunks.heading: Deploying agents and on-demand infrastructure with Railway
chunks.text:
- Once a workflow works locally, he tells Claude Code to deploy it to a server on Railway (or Vercel) so the team can use it and it runs in perpetuity, e.g. the LinkedIn queue where teammates drop posts that flow into cold email.
- He found Railway's API robust and picked it because he saw a tutorial.
- Example of throwaway infrastructure: instead of downloading data into Excel and building pivot tables (about 5 hours historically), he had Claude spin up a Postgres database through the Railway API, loaded the data, analyzed it with Claude, pushed the outputs where he needed them, and then spun the database down. Done in about 20-30 minutes.
- His takeaway: "on the fly UIs, on the fly databases, on the fly software" will become standard for people at the forefront. He emphasizes custom jobs-to-be-done workflows rather than giving a general agent access to everything.

chunks.heading: Domain knowledge, vocabulary and who wins from AI marketing
chunks.text:
- Cody's point: just because something can be built doesn't mean you can build it, because you may lack the vocabulary. His co-founder Max gets top-1% output from coding agents thanks to precise technical vocabulary.
- Example: he couldn't describe a TV-like texture for an ad background until he found someone's description with the right terms, after which it one-shotted. A designer with 20 years of experience would have the same edge in design.
- He believes the old "deep T with one or two skills" still applies, amplified: deep domain expertise plus these tools is what makes people valuable.
- A hosted question about his predictions: he expects rapid, real job loss. He cites a startup founder friend planning to cut 50 people (about 70% of the team), believing agent swarms can do their jobs. His definition of an agent swarm: agents doing specific tasks with an agent managing the system, which he says he has already built.
- He is excited because domain experts become far more capable.
- He is building a free, public course at gtmengineeringcourse.com, with a waitlist of about 100, documenting his step-by-step process. He also mentions Chrome extensions one-shotted by Claude Code and an agent that ran an Etsy shop until it was banned.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody walks through two marketing agents. One scrapes engagers from niche LinkedIn influencer posts, runs waterfall enrichment, and cold emails or DMs them. The other turns real conversations into LinkedIn posts for a whole team. His core view is that an agent is just code on a cron job with an optional LLM thinking loop, not tokens burned per action.

chunks.heading: Cody's definition of a marketing agent: software with a thinking loop, not "God in a box"
chunks.text:
- Cody says "marketing agents are the new coding agents": deploying them gets customers "on autopilot."
- His definition: an agent is "code. It's maybe some thinking loop and it's a live data stream." What makes it an agent is that it does a job to be done (find leads, outbound to them, answer replies), not that it uses a particular framework.
- He rejects "everybody tried to put God in a box and give it access to a Facebook ads account." The right approach is to copy what a top human did (a media buyer researches angles, makes creative, tests, prunes losers, promotes winners) and write software that runs that exact process.
- He argues against paying token tax on every marketing action: "You should not be paying Anthropic... to do an API call. You should be paying them to make the software that uses CPU to do the API call." Use inference only when you need it.
- His view: "the only agent is a coding agent." Everything else is software the coding agent makes.
- He says agent frameworks are usually bloat for finite problems; a very simple setup works.
- The build tools are Claude Code or Codex; the hard part is strategy (who you target, why, and the tool stack).
- Deployment: take the local script and put it on a server (Railway, for example), which is "just a computer that is on all the time somewhere else," running on an hourly or daily cron. For the data pipeline and warehouse feeding agent decisions he suggests ClickHouse; his company Graft combines the warehouse and the server.
- Risk example: if an LLM agent like Hermes runs your Facebook ads freely, it may "absolutely nuke the account." Custom software that mimics a human process is safer and higher quality.
- Marketing is code: an image is a JSON prompt, an AI avatar video is an LLM scraping Reddit and writing a script, then an API call to Kai AI.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn engager outbound agent: sourcing leads from hand-raisers
chunks.text:
- Context: Cody says cold email reply rates are down, and "every marketing channel is down right now" because AI slop is flooding the zone. His way to stand out is to target signals or triggers where people hand-raise, instead of firmographics, demographics or psychographics.
- The signal: someone liking or commenting on content their target customer would engage with shows interest in the topic.
- Step 1: find 10-20 LinkedIn influencers or business accounts in the niche (e.g. AI marketing, Clay) and keep them in a spreadsheet. He does this manually from his own For You feed, because the feed already shows what is relevant. The company usually already knows who its customers engage with.
- Why 10-20 is enough: there are a handful of outliers per niche and everyone engages with them. Monitoring them gives roughly "80% surface area coverage" for the industry, and the marginal return of chasing the rest is poor.
- Step 2: use Apify (a scraping API; one key covers LinkedIn, Twitter and more). He likes the LinkedIn actors from "API Maestro" because they are the most stable and maintained. The ones used are the profile post scraper, post comments and post reactions.
- Step 3: have the coding agent write a script that takes a post URL and extracts all engagers. In his demo, one post gave 63 raw profiles.
- Step 4: deploy the script to the cloud on a daily cron: pull net-new posts from each tracked profile, then extract their engagers.
- Optional LLM step: before enrichment, have an LLM research the person and company (employee count, etc.) and check ICP fit, so you only pay to enrich and email qualified people.
- Compliance caveat: he says buying contact data from data brokers is legal and "pretty far on the white hat side," but compliance rules (CAN-SPAM, EU) differ and people should do their own research. He is not a lawyer.

chunks.heading: Waterfall enrichment for emails and phone numbers
chunks.text:
- Cody's rule: start with the cheapest, most accurate source and fall down to more expensive ones for the leftovers.
- Stack he names: getleads.io first (a B2B contact database with an API), then Apollo for what's missing, then tools like Prospeo or Origami (he praises Origami's team and says it aggregates the waterfall; you send a LinkedIn profile and it cascades through providers). LeadMagic is one he uses a lot, especially for mobile phone numbers.
- Worked example: of 50 LinkedIn URLs, getleads finds 32 emails; the remaining 18 go to Apollo, which finds maybe 10; the last 8 go to Prospeo/Origami. This is how you reach an "80% find rate," and you can chain as many providers as budget allows.
- Validation: run every email through MillionVerifier (good / risky / catchall / bad) and cold email only valid ones, because invalid addresses cause deliverability problems. He says to double-check even for Apollo and getleads output.
- In the demo he had Claude Code call the getleads API on the scraped LinkedIn URLs.

chunks.heading: Cold email infrastructure and costs
chunks.text:
- Never cold email from your core domain. Sending e.g. 10,000 cold emails from it can "nuke the deliverability" of the business domain.
- Keep separate domains for each purpose: cold email, email marketing, transactional email (e.g. password resets), and the main business domain the team uses.
- Buy burner domains plus inboxes from Inboxkit, Instantly's pre-built inboxes, or Hypertide (the partner Cody's team uses and has a partnership with).
- Cost: about 10,000 cold emails per month for about $100/month in inbox infrastructure with Hypertide. Inboxkit pricing is similar, and it runs frequent sales.
- Sending software: Instantly, with a $97/month tier. Total to get started is roughly $200 for sending software plus inboxes.
- LinkedIn DMs: HeyReach and Botdog both have APIs and run DM campaigns from LinkedIn accounts. He also knows people seeing "incredible success" right now using LinkedIn InMail.

chunks.heading: An SDR in a box: an agent that manages the inbox
chunks.text:
- Instantly's API lets an agent monitor and manage the whole account. The agent can write per-person copy and variables, which get pushed into Instantly.
- Instantly webhooks fire on a positive reply and send it to the agent on a cloud server. The agent gets a base prompt with the context and a goal: get the person to schedule a demo at your link. It answers questions and pushes them deeper.
- Long-term follow-up: program it to re-reach people who went cold, for example every six months.
- Plug in a scheduler (Calendly or Cal.com) so the agent can check whether a contacted person actually booked a discovery call, the action being optimized.
- Whole chain: find people by social engagement, find emails, write emails, decide ICP fit, send via the sending platform, then manage replies. Under the hood it is "code with an LLM attached."

chunks.heading: Organic LinkedIn agent: interviews to posts to scheduling to analytics
chunks.text:
- Problem: companies (for example sales teams of seven wanting to post daily) need unique posts from many people. Cody says "write good LinkedIn content" from nothing yields mid content that wastes readers' time and risks being flagged as AI slop by LinkedIn.
- The fix is real source material: a weekly one-on-one interview ("tell me everything you've learned this week"), sales call or Gong transcripts, Slack sales channels, Notion, the codebase, or a podcast transcript. A customer saying why they did not buy can become an "unbelievable piece of content." The same works with someone else's podcast as source.
- Pipeline: transcript, then insights, then an LLM API call to write posts (Claude Sonnet is "probably good enough" for writing), then schedule via Ordinal's API or MCP. Ordinal, a partner, supports multiple connected LinkedIn accounts that can interact with each other.
- Feedback loop: Ordinal's analytics for every account feed back to the agent, so the next round of writing leans on what got impressions. He uses the words "snowball" or "remix" to push it to build on winners.
- The social media manager's job (prospect ideas, make content, publish, read data, build a recurring calendar) can be done by an agent. He says the "real meta" is one person managing 10, 20 or 100 accounts across channels with agents.
- His own content: "the exact same thing remixed every 90 days." He has posts he has reused for two years, and "every time I post it, I know it's going to go viral."

chunks.heading: Content and product principles: mine what the market already wants
chunks.text:
- Cody's mindset: find ideas or winners, then reuse them as often as possible. Building a corpus of data shows what will already go viral.
- Same logic for products: ask "what do people want to buy that they currently can't, and can I build and sell it?" rather than trying to invent a new idea.
- For content, mine posts that already had a viral moment, then add your own spin or angle.
- Ad creative entropy fix: a looping agent keeps producing the same ideas. Instead, track about 10 human creators on Instagram, look for outliers, and pull new hooks or topics to remix.
- Earned media value: LinkedIn impressions cost about $22 per thousand on average, so a post with 1,000 impressions from a 500-follower account is roughly $20 of free value. "I get paid to build lead pipeline."
- Platforms also pay creators, such as YouTube, on top of the earned reach.

chunks.heading: Where to follow up
chunks.text:
- Cody is active on Twitter and LinkedIn. His company Graft offers a platform for deploying these agents and forward-deploys software engineers to implement them for fast-growing companies.
- He offers to teach on request, such as direct mail at scale by scraping Google Maps, TV advertising, or cheaper LinkedIn clicks. He has a crash-course video on go-to-market engineering that covers the Claude Code setup in about 10 minutes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody defines a real marketing agent as unified data in a warehouse, autonomous decisions on a cadence, and cloud hosting. He walks through a full Facebook ads agent (research, creative, publishing, culling winners) and an AI-for-WordPress startup idea to market with it.

chunks.heading: What Cody counts as a real marketing agent
chunks.text:
- Cody says a marketing agent needs three things: unified data on the whole pipeline, autonomous decision-making on a cadence with a thinking loop, and the infrastructure to host it.
- That infrastructure is a data pipeline, a data warehouse, and agents hosted in the cloud.
- He rejects "some Zapier automation workflow that's linear". His version is "code in the cloud that's making decisions off of your live business data".
- He doesn't want a free-roaming AGI-style agent. He wants one that runs a defined process, looks at the returning data, and improves from it.
- He is skeptical of claims that an agent runs a whole marketing stack end to end.
- Where it does work today is a single channel. An agent can run Facebook ads entirely: research pain points and outcomes, make on-brand statics and AI avatar UGC, publish to the ads account, turn off losers, promote winners, and feed results back into new creative.
- He describes the result as a "virtual employee" focused on one channel.
- His view on jobs: marketers become "agent jockeys" who turn their domain knowledge into code.
- He says a semi-technical person can set this up by giving Claude Code a transcript like this one and asking it to walk them through the build.

chunks.heading: The data stack: pipeline, warehouse, and hosting
chunks.text:
- **Why a warehouse:** it unifies every data source so the agent sees all channels in context with each other. For Facebook ads, Cody lists the data needed: Facebook Ads, Google Analytics, PostHog, the CRM (e.g. HubSpot) and Stripe. With all of it in one place, you can tie a specific ad to revenue.
- **Pipeline:** Airbyte is a self-hosted data pipeline with pre-built connectors that pipes sources into the warehouse.
- **Warehouse:** ClickHouse, which is also open source and self-hostable. He offers both as accessible options, not the only ones.
- **The loop:** data sources feed the warehouse, the agent reads the warehouse and acts in the channel (e.g. Facebook Ads), and the channel's results flow back into the warehouse. That cycle is what makes the system learn.
- **Conversational analytics:** the same warehouse lets an owner query business data from Claude Code or Codex. His example question: "we're having trouble hitting payroll this month, what is going wrong?" The answer might be accounts receivable. It also supports custom dashboards.
- **Hosting:** agents don't need a local Mac mini (the OpenClaw-style setup). They can be deployed to any cloud, such as Heroku or Railway.
- **What an agent is:** "just code under the hood", a decision tree over a live data stream with an LLM thinking loop, optimized for an outcome, which for most companies is more revenue.

chunks.heading: Facebook ads after Andromeda
chunks.text:
- Andromeda is Facebook's ad algorithm. It reads the ad creative (image, text, video content and script) and the landing page, and uses that to decide which ad goes to which person.
- Because of this, Cody says interest-based targeting is no longer needed. Before, he would have targeted a WordPress interest.
- Now you make creative that speaks to the pain points or outcomes of the buyer, then send people to a landing page that explains the product.
- He claims "Facebook has turned into the best B2B ads channel that exists right now". Very obscure ads, possibly relevant to only about 10 people in the US, still get found and produce qualified B2B leads.
- Set the conversion event on a deeper funnel action such as signup or payment.
- Sample script angle for the WordPress idea: "I used to be paying my agency a thousand dollars a month to maintain my WordPress site... I just found this plugin that makes it so I can chat with AI to change my website and it includes all these plugins I used to pay extra for."
- He argues for paid ads over relying on organic or word of mouth. You can test a thousand creatives and know within 48 hours what the market responds to.
- He calls it the one system where "I put a dollar in and $5 can potentially come out the other side".
- Founders shouldn't impose positioning on the market ("we're not Don Draper"). Put creative into the market and let the data pick. He also says a competitor-negative angle (an "anti-Yoast" ad) might work and is worth testing.
- Quitting after a few ads is a common mistake. Marketing is continuous, not campaign start/stop, because trends now move roughly 10x faster than 20 years ago.

chunks.heading: The creative pipeline for an agent-run ad account
chunks.text:
1. **Research:** scrape Reddit for pain points and outcomes of the target customer. He used Perplexity live in the demo. Reddit works because it is real people complaining, though he notes it is being eroded by people manipulating it for LLM ranking.
2. **Rank:** have the model rank the most-referenced pain points and make the top ones the ad themes. In his WordPress example the top pains were plugin sprawl, performance and speed, and security and maintenance.
3. **Statics:** use Kai AI, which puts the image and video models in one place, with Google Nano Banana for images. Feed it an existing ad from a competitor or adjacent industry as the example to adapt.
4. **Brand check:** run a vision model over the outputs to check brand style guides (fonts, colors, readable text).
5. **Video:** HeyGen for AI avatar UGC still gives great results. He is testing Seedance, but stitching it into 30-second videos is hard because clips are capped at roughly 9 seconds (he says not to quote that exactly).
6. **Publish:** use the Facebook Marketing API, with the constraint below.
7. **Judge:** turn off losers, promote winners, and feed what worked back into creative.

chunks.heading: Facebook API rules, test cadence, and the winners pool
chunks.text:
- **API TOS:** accounts get banned for spamming the API by pulling "hundreds of millions of rows" of data from the ads account, not because an agent was used. Cody's rule is to use the Facebook API only for writes (publishing, turning off, promoting). Read performance data from the warehouse instead.
- **Example cadence at a client:**
  - 2 ad sets per day, 5 ads each.
  - Ads upload automatically based on prior research and warehouse data on what has worked.
  - Let them run 2 to 3 days to get initial signal, then turn off the worst performers.
  - Winning ad sets go into a winners pool and compete for the available budget.
- **Learning from creative:** he keeps a database of every ad made, including the JSON prompts sent to Nano Banana and the scripts sent to HeyGen or Seedance. The agent analyzes this to get better at making creative that produces outcomes.
- Human in the loop is fine at the start.
- The time claim: producing around 100 ads and getting them into Facebook was about 2 weeks of work historically. Now a founder can have the system running in roughly an hour and a half.

chunks.heading: Solving entropy so the agent doesn't stagnate
chunks.text:
- Entropy is when "the agent gets stuck thinking in the same way". Cody says people who claim set-and-forget agents "have never set up anything", since results feel good on day one and degrade after.
- **Fix 1:** pull competitors' ads from the Facebook Ads Library to inject new "DNA" alongside the original research.
- **Fix 2:** pull YouTube and podcast transcripts and extract insights from them. For WordPress there are hundreds of channels. Run ads off the aggregated insights.
- **Fix 3:** use a trend tool such as Viral Loop (it has an API and scrapes TikTok, and possibly Instagram Reels, which he isn't sure of). Ask for the most viral posts in a category over the last week and use the formats and concepts to shape creative.
- Because the market moves fast, he says you need observability of what is happening and must keep adjusting ads, positioning and go-to-market. Short-form social is where trends originate before they trickle down.

chunks.heading: Business idea: AI for WordPress, and where agents would go
chunks.text:
- **The idea:** "Lovable or Anything.com but for WordPress". Users vibe code their site on the WordPress platform.
- **Bundle:** the product includes forms, a CRM and the other plugins people normally hodgepodge together. Cody argues the aggregate of about 10 plugins is replaced by one package at a tenth or fifth of the cost.
- **Pricing:** token-based. His example is a base tier at $29 a month for a set amount of tokens.
- **Why this market:** he says no one is building for WordPress. He cites that 43% of websites indexed by Google are WordPress, calls it "blue ocean", and says he has pitched it to three founders who got into YC and didn't know what to pivot into (they passed).
- **Go-to-market:** Facebook ads and Google ads first.
- **Other agents he says he can build or has seen:**
  - Google Ads agents that run the account end to end.
  - Influencer outreach: research influencers, cold email them, negotiate pricing, and flag good ones.
  - Cold email: find customers and their emails, send, and manage the inbox to book meetings.
  - TikTok reel farms: about 10 cloud accounts posting slideshows about the product, with views aggregated.
  - SEO: keyword research, research, writing on-brand with a distinct point of view.
  - AI search: build citations and do outreach to get listed where AI answers already cite.
  - Social management for LinkedIn and Twitter.
  - Podcast-based newsletters: research, write the script, read it with ElevenLabs voices, and build lead magnets to grow the email list (his example is an e-commerce industry).
- He mentions companiesgraph.com as where his team does this work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody shows his live workflow for replacing a marketing team with Claude Code, APIs and templates: bulk Facebook ad variants, templated landing pages, cold email pipelines and shared internal tools. His core argument is that volume is now cheap, so the edge is domain knowledge, clear outcomes and the data to see what works.

chunks.heading: Cody's definition of GTM engineering and how it has evolved
chunks.text:
- Cody says GTM engineering started around 2023 as an outbound discipline, and Clay solidified it as a job function. The idea was to treat distribution as trackable, attributable systems and processes rather than one-off campaigns, like a software engineering function: weekly sprints, analyze the data, repeat what works.
- He says it has since expanded to everything: outbound, inbound, paid ads, SEO, organic content. It now covers sales, marketing, customer experience and revops.
- He argues the name is just a new label for the same person who has existed for 10-20 years (growth hacker, head of growth). The job is unchanged: find marketing and distribution arbitrage, nail the positioning so the audience is receptive, build processes to execute, and put data analysis on top to track it. Only the tooling changed.
- Some teams are building these systems into the core company codebase, so a side project (e.g. one running the whole blog and organic content strategy) becomes an agent that works continuously in the background.
- On his career leverage: "you're a person with 30 agents behind you." You bring your own personal software and systems to a company, which is a salary-negotiation lever.
- His claim: what one person can do in a day with Claude Code, APIs, GitHub, Railway and skill files is what a Fortune 500 team would do in a year. He says he's done more work in two weeks than in the period since October. He is explicit that he is sharing what he's experimenting with and seeing work, not claiming universal results.

chunks.heading: Setup: how Cody works day to day in Claude Code
chunks.text:
- He keeps one local folder (in Documents) that he lives out of, deliberately unorganized ("it works for me").
- First step: create an environment (.env) file holding the API keys for every tool in the stack. Claude Code uses these to interact with each tool.
- He `cd`s into the folder and starts Claude Code. Claude understands the file structure and prior work in it.
- He spins up multiple Claude agents in separate desktops/workspaces and moves between them while others work. He calls it "jockeying" agents. Alex frames it as multi-threaded work, not multitasking.
- He dictates prompts with Super Whisper (voice transcription).
- He uses plan mode for new builds: Claude asks what it needs (API keys, permissions) and walks him through where to get each one. Errors are fed back to Claude, which loops to fix them (e.g. reading Railway logs to fix a failed deploy).
- Claim: you don't need engineering knowledge, just clear thinking. If you don't know something (what an API is, how to get one, how to share a tool), ask Claude.
- He installed a Claude Code UI design skill (search "UI design") to improve visual output quality.
- He found most tools via Twitter and YouTube, where this is happening in real time. Practical method: ask Perplexity "what are the five best tools for X." He says there's no good educational material and the meta changes weekly; everything he showed happened over the previous two weeks.
- He used to build workflows in n8n but now skips it and writes code directly. Example: a post-sales-call workflow where a Notion recording triggers a follow-up email draft, run from Slack. He gave Claude his Railway API key and it set up a Node Express server, deployed the software and pushed the repo to GitHub.

chunks.heading: Bulk Meta ad creative: template, research and testing
chunks.text:
- Build: he gave Claude an example ad and had it make a bulk ad generator in about 20 minutes (the template took roughly two prompts; the bulk generator took more back and forth). Design is just code, so the ad is a React component exported to a downloadable PNG with the HTML-to-canvas library.
- Variation workflow:
  1. Use Perplexity to find the pain points and desired outcomes of the target buyer (his example: an AI data analyst for GTM teams), pulling in real Reddit conversations so the copy uses the customer's own language.
  2. Feed that into Claude: "brainstorm 40 ad titles and supporting paragraphs based on the source material."
  3. Claude bulk-generates a zip of image variations.
  4. Upload to Facebook Ads. He was still building the connector so Claude Code can upload the zip into a specific campaign (as drafts), edit destination URLs and subject lines at scale, and tell him which ads perform best.
- Why: he doesn't know what will work, so testing angles is how he finds the positioning the audience responds to.
- Test structure (his way, "a million ways to do it"):
  - Test all creatives against each other in a click campaign, about $100 over three days.
  - Pick the lowest-CPC winners, which he says is historically a leading indicator of cheaper cost per action later.
  - Move winners into their own conversion campaign with a dedicated budget.
  - Goal: test around 200 creatives a month and always refresh the ads platform with new winners. Google Ads works the same way, tracking keywords that produce conversions or the cheapest CPC.
- Example results he showed: CPC of 30 cents on a winner versus 53 and 85 cents on others.
- He says spend so far is small: the company is early stage and he settled on its positioning about two weeks earlier, narrowing from "AI business intelligence software" to "AI data analyst for GTM teams" for 10-50 person companies that don't want to hire a data engineer.
- Remixing winners: take a winning message and recreate it in other formats, e.g. bulk UGC ads via the HeyGen API. His loop: generate ads in HeyGen, test, take the winner and try to make a better version in Veo 3 with the same script, and only then hire a human to read the script if needed.
- On quality: "the concept is what you're testing"; the medium can change. Creative doesn't need to be perfect first; humans can polish winners later. He says AI avatar UGC ads have been among his best performers and he moves faster than when a human is in the loop.

chunks.heading: Landing pages at scale with Strapi and Claude Code
chunks.text:
- Stack: Strapi, an open-source, self-hostable CMS with an API endpoint, used for graft.com. He creates content formats in Strapi and Claude Code hits the API to create and upload blog and landing page content. Any CMS (e.g. WordPress) would work; he chose Strapi because it scales cheaply (he cites a possible 100,000 blog posts).
- Landing page template: a copy of the homepage where only the title (H1) and supporting paragraph in the hero change.
- Reason: aligning the ad with the landing page it sends to increases conversion rate, because the funnel feels cohesive.
- Two sources of angles: winning Facebook ad angles, or keywords that convert in Google Ads (the ones creating signups or payments). He used to do this manually; now Claude does it in bulk.
- Keyword demo: use Keywords Everywhere to pull long-tail keywords for a topic (his example: "AI dashboard generator"), download them, and tell Claude "make a landing page for each of these." Seven pages were created in draft mode with URLs to review before publishing.
- Indexing: have Claude find the sitemap, submit it via the Google Search Console API, and for pages not getting indexed use Google's web indexing API to manually request indexing.
- He can also test different landing page formats against each other without engineering resources.

chunks.heading: Blog content quality: interview yourself plus SERP scrape
chunks.text:
- He says "write a blog post about X" yields "the most average thing you've ever seen."
- His fix: record a roughly 10-minute monologue of his own opinions on the topic and use the transcript as source material. Also scrape what ranks on page one of Google and add that as source material. Then ask for a post using both and the vocabulary from the transcript. He says this lands output in the top 10% to 1% of quality.
- Same principle for design: the hard part is having the language to describe what you want. Example: he didn't know to say "grain overlay" (an SVG grain with adjustable opacity) and kept asking for "texture." He says domain knowledge is the real bottleneck, which is why experts get more out of these tools. His technical co-founder describes outcomes with far deeper vocabulary.

chunks.heading: Cold outbound and LinkedIn engager workflow
chunks.text:
- Cody calls cold email "super underrated": scrape data from the internet and send customized bulk email at scale.
- Infrastructure: Hypertide.io for domain and inbox setup. He runs about 2,000 inboxes inside Instantly and several campaigns at once. Current campaigns: pitching himself to podcasts, pitching YouTubers for creator/influencer marketing, and traditional cold email to his ICP.
- Live build, from one prompt in plan mode: take engagers from a LinkedIn post, enrich them with the Apollo API, validate emails with MillionVerifier (to avoid damaging sending domains), and add them to an Instantly campaign. He says the workflow is built in about 20 minutes. He tells Claude to read keys from the .env file and ask for any it's missing. He also names PhantomBuster for scraping LinkedIn comments and engagers.
- He extends it into a Slack command (a `/linkedin`-style slash command): drop a LinkedIn post URL from his phone and the whole pipeline fires into the cold outbound campaign.
- Sourcing ideas: use Apify or RapidAPI to extract the most viral content in the category automatically. He is building a version that scrapes LinkedIn engagers on incumbent competitors' CEO posts, treating people who engage as a signal that they're in a buying motion, then reaching out to them.
- Lead gen assets: he wrote scripts and software to give away as LinkedIn lead magnets.

chunks.heading: Data analysis is the bottleneck and the origin of Graft
chunks.text:
- Core point: producing a thousand ads or pages is now easy; understanding what is actually working is the hard part. "If you don't have an outcome you're moving towards or a way to measure this, there's no point."
- This is the origin of his company, Graft: he says an MCP or the Facebook API can't handle the volume. One customer's Facebook ads produce about 25 million rows of data a month at about $180K monthly spend.
- Graft provides an AI data analyst that builds dashboards. Demo: paste a Facebook ad set ID, ask Claude "make a dashboard about this ad set," and get spend, conversions and placement breakdown. He can chat with the dashboard to change chart styles and share it internally to build buy-in with KPI evidence (e.g. showing a 20% CPA reduction from ad velocity testing).
- On sharing and team use: deploy tools like the bulk ad generator to a URL, or use a shared GitHub repo where merges keep everyone on one instance. You can ask Claude how to do either.
- On quality control and brand risk: test ideas on burner or satellite accounts and promote winners to the main account. He does this with organic social. Paid ad spend on a winner is the filter before it reaches main channels. He says to get buy-in, show the KPI dashboard.
- His advice on tools: "The tools don't matter anymore." Focus on the outcome, then polish and measure what works for the company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains his Search Console feedback loop for refreshing content, how he writes bottom-of-funnel articles from SERP source material plus personal input, and why he favors custom Claude Code agents over OpenClaw. He also covers citation link-building for AI search, publishing velocity risks, and data-warehouse context design.

chunks.heading: Using Search Console data as a feedback loop for content refreshes
chunks.text:
- Cody treats Google as telling you what it wants you to rank for. His starting point: look at pages two and three of results, where an active SEO effort has "hundreds of keywords that Google's basically pointing at you."
- Loop: find long-tail phrases tied to the product, check top-performing articles for keywords they rank for accidentally, then add a section or weave those phrases in. He says this typically lifts traffic "10 to 20% overnight."
- If the article still doesn't reach page one for that phrase, write a supplementary article and link to it from the original page. The original then helps it rank.
- Track the refreshed batch (e.g. 100 articles) in a dashboard, measure organic lift, and repeat. He calls refreshing "the most valuable thing to be doing in this AI era of content."
- Mechanics: he pipes Search Console data into Claude Code. At large volume the API hits rate limits, pagination truncation and context limits, so he builds a data pipeline and warehouse. The open-source version is Airbyte writing into ClickHouse, hosted on Railway. Duplication errors are common when writing to ClickHouse or combining sources.
- Content must be maintained. He cites an AI spreadsheet tool ("how to Excel" keywords) he took from zero to 400,000 clicks a month in 12 months. After the person running it left, it "falls off a cliff because nobody's maintaining it." A site is "a living breathing thing."

chunks.heading: Writing bottom-of-funnel SEO content with AI
chunks.text:
- Relevance to the product matters more than traffic. He says HubSpot's correction came because most of its content was random business articles, while what still ranks relates to CRM and its integrations. Everything should push toward a purchase or signup action.
- Target keyword types: "X vs Y," "X alternative," "X review," and other bottom-of-funnel phrases tied to other products.
- Process:
  1. Pick the target keyword and scrape what ranks on page one (he mentions Cloudflare's new scraper that returns full HTML sites as JSON).
  2. Put that in the context window.
  3. Interview himself for about 30 minutes on the category: opinions, experiences, where the market is going.
  4. Write the article from both sources.
  5. Run an agent loop for internal linking and for a link to the homepage in the last paragraph.
- Place CTAs at the first paragraph and at 25%, 50% and 75% scroll, with varied CTAs sending to the signup flow.
- Put a TL;DR callout above the fold in a different background colour, with the CTA directly below it. He says this also lifts AI search because the answer is easy to pull.
- For better quality, have the model build an outline from the ranking sources (skyscraper style), write section by section, then run a "what did we miss" improvement pass. Newer models often manage it in one try.
- On "AI content is terrible": generic prompts like "write me a blog post" produce average output. Giving the role ("top 1% direct response marketer"), a sandbox of source material and the "nos" produces far better output. "It's not that you don't know what you're doing. It's you don't know how to explain it."

chunks.heading: Tracking signups from content and sending engagement signals
chunks.text:
- Set up a custom conversion event in Google Tag Manager for signup (push to the data layer), then use GA4 and Looker Studio to filter landing pages containing "blog" and see signup events. This shows which topics convert, e.g. Facebook ads articles at 2x the rate of Search Console articles.
- His target for a blog post is about 5% of traffic turning into signups. Landing pages are usually better for conversion than blog posts.
- Signals he believes help: scroll tracking firing every 10% (he saw "lift sites overnight"), downloadable assets with a promise, and clicks into deeper pages like a form. He reads these as trust signals back to Google.
- He uses brandable domains for social. Example: gtmengineeringcourse.com (as spoken: "gtmineeringcourse.com"), which he mentions in videos. Free assets are "the most slept on thing in the world."

chunks.heading: Velocity, sites and risk
chunks.text:
- Only go high velocity on sites with branded search that grows month over month. A site that looks like a real business: about page, privacy policy, LinkedIn and Twitter, real people.
- He will publish around 10,000 articles in a month to a newish site with some backlinks, dumping them at once. Once impressions and clicks start to curve, he moves to a monthly rewrite cycle on the best and the declining articles. He noindexes or 301-redirects content that no longer belongs, rather than leaving 404s.
- Content is tightly relevant (e.g. integrations of the product). A team member spent about three weeks filtering the keyword set, using Claude Code and a database to cluster it.
- He has intentionally had many sites penalised while finding the threshold. His warning: "If SEO drives 80% of your revenue, do not do this." He also says manual penalties are a real risk.
- Example: a Chrome extension that extracts emails from websites, backed by Google and Facebook ads remarketing, to drive branded search.
- Exact-match domains: he has bought "XYZ generator" domains, built a tool on the homepage, bought about 10 DA50 backlinks and reached page one in about 30 days.
- Keep a marketing mix of two to three channels. After an algorithm update hit a channel he leaned on, he had no fallback. Facebook ads referral traffic also reads as a real-business signal.

chunks.heading: Link building, tools, newsjacking and AI citations
chunks.text:
- Link exchange via Twitter ads: global targeting, max CPC 1 cent, link clicks at about 3 cents, landing on a form (name, email, company URL). He keeps the highest-value sites and does three-way exchanges across his portfolio rather than direct swaps.
- Tools: calculators and generators are the biggest AI-era opportunity and also work as link magnets that pass value to money pages.
- Newsjacking: write an article on a current topic before the SERP settles, promote it on social, and you can reach page one. Combining PR and social with SEO beats SEO alone. Example: a friend with an AI-image-detection tool checks viral news images, then pitches journalists.
- AI search: look at the query fan-out and citations. If you email the pages being cited most and pay (e.g. $500) to be added, you can see impact fast. He says to rank-stack the top 10 most-cited sources and prioritise by how often a source appears in the fan-out. He considers it "link building, but very strategic citation link building."
- Hub pages (e.g. /uses or /tools) get the links and distribute to each bottom-of-funnel landing page. With a new site, focus links on three to five landing pages.

chunks.heading: Agents, harnesses and data for marketing
chunks.text:
- A harness beats the raw model. Claude Code reportedly has about 38 tools, and he says the same model performs far better inside it than via the bare API. Claude has an SDK for the harness.
- Cost hack: swap in an open-source model trained on Opus 4.6 outputs (he names MiniMax 2.5, at about 1/20th the cost of Opus) inside the harness, and run it in the cloud.
- Hallucination: give the right context at the right time, not everything. Graph's agent pulls pieces of an ontology through a vector database on demand. Fewer tools is better, as Claude Code's team deliberately limits them.
- Graph: AI data analyst for growth teams with a semantic layer. Facebook ads alone has 42 tables, and the agent confuses "link clicks" with "post link clicks" (12 variants) without definitions. They run agent evals on SQL retries (e.g. seven attempts) to make future queries one-shot. Switching between OpenAI and Anthropic models forced a retool.
- On OpenClaw: he hasn't seen a use case a simple scoped agent can't do. An agent is "a loop on a cron job" with an LLM. Build narrow software, deploy it on Railway via its API key, and keep the surface area small.
- Examples: a podcast-booking agent got 112 yeses from about 2,000 contacted and booked 35 calls in a week; a Facebook ads agent (research, make UGC and statics, publish, kill losers, promote winners) he expects to finish in about a week.
- Daily workflow: email triage via Claude Code, Notion meeting notes into follow-up drafts, SendGrid product emails, and a LinkedIn post-engager → Apollo or LeadMagic → MillionVerifier → Instantly cold email flow built in about 30 minutes. His line: "friends don't let friends do n8n."
- Result he cites: 39,000 organic users in a month as one person across channels.

chunks.heading: Content strategy, channels and background
chunks.text:
- Long form beats short form for conversions. He does an hour-long podcast to reach thousands, and finds short form hard to track and best for top of funnel with a CTA to something longer.
- His YouTube formula: the thumbnail and title make a promise, deliver in the first 30 seconds, then do the thing.
- Social algorithms care about retention, not how content is made. "Good content is good content."
- Background: print on demand (Etsy, Amazon, Redbubble) in high school and his early 20s; a digital strategy role at a Fortune 500 manufacturing marketing firm with long sales cycles; early employee at Rupa Health, which grew from a $20M to a $110M valuation in about six months; Chrome extensions paying rent for about 10 years; now founder of Graph.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider live-demos "marketing engineering": a coding agent plus a data and API infrastructure layer does the middle work of a marketing team. He runs parasite SEO, AI-avatar ad creative, and LinkedIn-engager cold outbound in parallel, and explains why agents should run as code rather than as chat.

chunks.heading: Mapping the AI-native marketing stack ("marketing engineering")
chunks.text:
- Cody describes "marketing engineering" (or GTM engineering when it touches a CRM or sales) as a new role: using a coding agent to do all the "middle work" a marketer used to do by hand. That covers ad creative research and generation, media buying, and channel execution.
- His claim is that a team that once needed about 25 people can now run on one person with a Claude Code Max subscription.
- He expects around 70% of a non-engineer's work to be done by AI. Anything that touches a keyboard should be tested with "can an agent do this?"
- Infrastructure his team found necessary over 18 months:
  - a data pipeline and data warehouse (open-source options he names: Airbyte, ClickHouse)
  - a cloud server to run code, and media storage for images and videos
  - databases the agent can spin up to log its own work (for example, the JSON used to generate an ad, tied back to Facebook ads data)
  - cron jobs for recurring runs, app authentication for private dashboards, and a git manager so several people can work at once
  - an API gateway to every tool the agent needs
- His thesis is "all marketing is now just turning into code." A Seedance video is a JSON file sent to a GPU API, an ad upload is software publishing content, and analysis is an SQL query the agent writes against the warehouse.
- Unifying Google Ads, Google Analytics, PostHog, the CRM and the payment processor lets you see which search terms lead to higher customer lifetime value.

chunks.heading: Turning a manual task into a deployed agent
chunks.text:
- Method: do the task by hand with Claude Code, keep the session log, turn it into a repeatable process, then deploy it to the cloud on a daily, weekly or monthly schedule. Marketers then stack these processes on top of each other.
- SEO example:
  1. Research target keywords.
  2. Scrape what ranks on page one.
  3. Write an article from that.
  4. Add brand voice from a founder transcript.
  5. Publish via the CMS API (his blog runs on Strapi).
  6. Refresh on a 30-day cadence from live data.
- Scaled output he cites: 30 new Facebook ads per week, 20 new LinkedIn ads, and Google Ads optimized continuously from the live data stream.
- He argues against "token maxing" and against God-in-a-box agents. He found that having the coding agent write discrete software with a thinking loop and a live data stream beats pointing a general agent like Hermes at an account.
- He treats this as converting a standard operating procedure into code, then giving the coding agent the data it needs to improve that code.
- His tools: Cursor and Claude Code daily (Cursor cloud agents are good for background work), and Codex more recently. He also uses DaVinci Resolve MCP for long-form video editing and says the output is "ridiculous."
- Rule he repeats: "Friends don't let friends do n8n." Go straight to code because it is more discreet and easier to modify.

chunks.heading: Parasite SEO on LinkedIn articles
chunks.text:
- Parasite SEO means borrowing a high-authority domain to rank a piece of content. His example publishes a LinkedIn Pulse article from a company page.
- Workflow:
  1. Pull page-one results for the target keyword with serper.dev.
  2. Extract the content with Exa or Firecrawl and put it in the context window.
  3. Have the agent write an article for that exact keyword.
  4. For a real client, record a 30-minute founder conversation about positioning and feed the transcript in alongside the scraped text.
  5. Publish the article on a LinkedIn page, using the keyword phrase as the exact title so it becomes the URL.
  6. Put the URL through Prime Indexer, which drip-pings it to speed up indexing.
- Rule: use Prime Indexer only on external sites, never your core domain, because the drip ping can hurt it.
- Results he cites:
  - A "Facebook ads for kitchen remodeling" article went live and was indexed by Google in about 38 minutes, ranking position one.
  - A "Facebook ads for orthodontists" article reached page one, position one, within 20 minutes of publishing.
  - He also has "Facebook ads for pet grooming" pages built the same way.
  - Pages carry calls to action at different commitment levels.
- The same indexing approach works for local map-pack SEO: put name, address and phone on many large directory sites (Foursquare, MapQuest) and use an indexer so Google sees those deep pages.

chunks.heading: Static creative at scale with Seedance and AI avatars
chunks.text:
- For Facebook, Cody targets all of Facebook and lets the creative do the positioning, not interest targeting.
- He explains that with Andromeda, targeting is driven by the ad creative, so the script and the avatar decide who sees the ad. He keeps five AI avatars across age groups and ethnicities.
- Three things must be realistic: the voice, the avatar, and the audio environment. A person shown in a car needs audio that sounds like a car, not studio quality.
- Script pipeline:
  1. Scrape Reddit (via Exa or Perplexity) for pain points and desired outcomes tied to the product.
  2. Take 10 proven Facebook ad hooks from a post he wrote.
  3. Combine them as hook, then desired outcome and pain point.
  4. Write 15 scripts, each 30 seconds, at a 12th-grade reading level, with an "economy of words."
