  5. Send the scripts to ElevenLabs for MP3 audio (he uses a voice called Natasha).
  6. Send the MP3 and an avatar screenshot to Seedance through Kai AI or Higgsfield, which lip-syncs the video.
- Cost: about $2.50 for a 30-second video on Higgsfield at the pricing his team has locked in.
- He uses a voice-to-text tool (Superwhisper) to give the agent instructions faster.
- Quality control:
  - He puts a brand-style-guide gate in the loop, where a separate vision model checks each ad, such as for a wrong font, and sends it back to the image model (GPT image) for fixes.
  - He says humans should get out of the way after an initial phase, because a person cannot approve 20 new ads a day, while an agent can reach roughly 99.9% quality.
- Scale reference: Rise Superfoods has about 5,100 active ads. Cody says the best companies test creative volume like this using AI plus creator networks. His team shipped about 11,000 ads across clients in July.
- Creator networks (Sideshift, Tribe): pay per video, for example $40 per UGC video. Another option is paying about 3% of the spend behind each ad the creator makes, so only winners cost more. These networks have APIs, so an agent can manage campaigns and review creative.

chunks.heading: Budget, testing cadence and results
chunks.text:
- Starting spend: about $100/day each on Facebook and Google ads. Typical cost per demo for software clients is $50 to $200.
- Timeline: his team usually has enough signal by week six, and sometimes within a week. They can run two to three creative loops per week (test, see what won, remix).
- Cost results he cites:
  - A wellness franchise (corporate level): Facebook cost per lead from $70 to about $16 in four weeks. Google Ads from about $82 to $35 in the same period. He jokes they are "day trading" the Facebook and Google ads algorithm.
  - A prosumer app: roughly 2,000 signups in June, then about 20,000 signups across Facebook ads, Google ads, SEO, cold email and LinkedIn DMs. The whole stack was set up in about three weeks, and signups were roughly doubling month over month.
- Creative decay: "everything has a half-life," so you need to introduce new DNA. His sources are viral organic social posts in the category.
- Explore/exploit split: about 80% on what works and 20% testing, rising to 20-30% net-new creative once cost per action hits a threshold.
- Competitive research: use a vision model (he mentions Gemini) to pull and describe every ad in a category. He did this for car detailing. If many advertisers in different regions run similar ads, that is a strong signal those ads work.

chunks.heading: Signal-based outbound from LinkedIn engagers
chunks.text:
- Workflow he demoed:
  1. Pick influencers in your product category and set up a daily check for their new posts.
  2. Extract the commenters and reactors from each post using an Apify actor (API Maestro's LinkedIn actors).
  3. Take the LinkedIn profile URLs and run a waterfall email enrichment (GetLeads, then LeadMagic).
  4. Verify the emails with MillionVerifier.
  5. Upload them to an Instantly campaign.
  6. Optionally send LinkedIn DMs via HeyReach.
- Do not automate your core LinkedIn account with browser-use agents. It risks a ban, so he scrapes through a third-party actor that handles proxies. He says his approach lives in a "white to gray hat" zone.
- Copy rule: two concise emails, subject like "saw your comment," referencing the post, then a short offer (for example, 80 new creatives a month with an agent running media buying).
- Qualification: have the agent score each person one to ten against an ICP markdown file. He also uses TAM mapping (find all target companies, firmographics, the decision maker) and layers signals: engagement, website visits (via a tool like Leadpipe), and job changes. A new job is a strong buying signal because "everybody buys new when they join another company."
- Best-performing offer: find an influencer in your category, record a live class with them, then DM people who engaged with the influencer: "saw you commented on X, we recorded a live class with Y, want the recording?" The recording is effectively a demo in disguise. He points to Nick Abraham, who sends about a quarter million LinkedIn DMs a month, for more.

chunks.heading: Cold email infrastructure and cost
chunks.text:
- Cody runs about 1,000 inboxes in Instantly through Hypertide, which manages Microsoft tenants.
- Hypertide groups two domains per tenant and about 100 inboxes per domain so a burned tenant doesn't hurt the rest. Microsoft deliverability suffers if you land in a bad tenant pool.
- Cost: about $125 of infrastructure per 10,000 emails a month, which he extrapolates to a million emails a month for about $8,000.
- Alternatives: InboxKit, and Instantly's own pre-warmed domains (good deliverability, but not branded to your company).
- He thinks of cold email as a one-to-one marketing channel.

chunks.heading: Team size and how Graph engagements work
chunks.text:
- Cody's company, Graph, has six people: him and a co-founder, three to four deployed engineers, and a head of sales.
- They sell a platform and forward-deploy engineers to build agents on it. Clients can later drop the engineer and keep the "virtual employee" running on usage-based pricing (rows synced, credits for enrichment and creative).
- He says the hard hire is someone with both software engineering and marketing knowledge. He sees 22-year-olds who have run AI consulting agencies fitting best.
- He says you can build the infrastructure yourself with a coding agent, but his team spent 18 months on it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains how he hands "middle work" to Claude Code agents wired to his stack's APIs, with a data warehouse underneath. He covers agent loops for Facebook ads, a cold-email PR sprint, rolling this out to a team, and why API quality now drives software choices.

chunks.heading: Cody's core shift: hand off the "middle work" to agents via Claude Code and APIs
chunks.text:
- Cody's framing: everything between an idea and the final polish is "middle work" he now hands to an agent. His job becomes curator: idea in, polish out.
- Setup takes about five minutes: make a folder on a local machine, run Claude Code inside it, add an environment file holding the API keys for the whole stack (Shopify, Google Search Console, Facebook ads, Google ads, Klaviyo and so on).
- He works conversationally with Super Whisper (a transcription app), "jockeying" about five agents in the background at once.
- Definition: "agent" = an employee with a small scope of work that does one specific thing. Once he sees a repeatable task, he ships it as an agent.
- Prompt the outcome, not the steps. Tell it "I'm trying to make this outcome," then "make a plan or ask me questions if you need more context." Prescriptive instructions are the biggest learning curve for newcomers.
- To find what to automate, audit what you did this week that matched last week, then ask Claude "can I make an agent out of this?"
- Over time the folder accumulates CLAUDE.md files, workflows, company descriptions and goals, so it becomes a knowledge base of how he thinks about the business. He can ask it "what am I not thinking about that I should be?" for blind-spot analysis.
- Timing claim: everything he describes happened in about six weeks. Eight weeks earlier he'd have said "agents are bullshit."

chunks.heading: The Facebook ads agent loop (and why it needs a data warehouse)
chunks.text:
- About a week from the interview he expected an agent to run his Facebook ads end to end:
  1. Research social for target-customer pain points and desired outcomes.
  2. Make creative: Nano Banana, plus writing React code and exporting it as a PNG.
  3. Upload the ads to Facebook.
  4. Analyze performance. Losers are turned off automatically; winners are promoted into their own ad sets with dedicated budget.
  5. Results feed the next round of creative, and the agent searches the internet for more context. "It's just a loop."
- Why agents fail when they hit APIs directly: rate limits, pagination (the agent thinks it sees everything but sees about 5%, so it decides wrongly), and context-window bloat from pulling in something like a million Shopify rows.
- His fix, and the reason his company Graph exists: build a data pipeline and warehouse, plus an AI data analyst agent callable over MCP from Claude Code.
- Of roughly 25 "we'll run your Facebook/Google ads automatically" tools he reviewed, he saw only one using a data warehouse. A client spending $180K/month on Facebook ads couldn't pull their data through the API in any useful way.
- The stack for an ecom founder: bulk creative generation (Veo 3, Sora 2, Nano Banana plus a brand style guide), then a Facebook Ads API key, then pipeline, warehouse and agent access to the data.
- Tip: create a developer-only Facebook app so you skip Facebook's authorization/credentialing process for internal use. Ask Claude to walk you through getting the marketing API key.
- Claim: you never need to touch the Facebook ads dashboard again.

chunks.heading: Boundaries beat instructions, and vocabulary is the superpower
chunks.text:
- Cody says it is easier to list "all the nos" than to say "agent, do this." The nos create the surface area where "yes" lives, and output improves. Companies find it hard to name their lines in the sand.
- Agents have moved from linear workflows to circular loops, which he compares to a cockroach: feel around, get stimulus, react. Do things, analyze what works, do more of it, repeat.
- Domain vocabulary is the leverage. "Write a blog post about X" gives mid content. Instead specify a persona ("top 1% direct response marketer who writes at the intersection of educational content and sales"), the product details, pain points and outcomes, and the customer persona, and the output is top tier.
- Same for ads: knowing Facebook terms lets him say "spin these up in a new ad set under the conversion campaign titled XYZ, this campaign ID, this conversion event."
- His expertise (seven years of go-to-market and growth) now lives in a GitHub repo that the team can query for context on why initiatives exist.
- Models are idiot savants: the language and deep technical knowledge you have becomes the most valuable asset.

chunks.heading: Cold email PR sprint: 2,000 podcasts, 35 booked calls
chunks.text:
- Workflow built entirely by Claude Code: researched 2,000 podcasts, scraped their emails, validated them with MillionVerifier, loaded them into Instantly AI, and cold emailed them.
- A reply agent's goal was to book an intro call with him.
- Results: 112 positive responses from about 2,000 outreach, 35 calls booked in a week. "I was like, 'Fuck, this worked too well.'"
- Problems found: the agent dropped the ball on 90 replies, people noticed it responded instantly and called it a bot, and it agreed to buy a guest two of his books so Cody could come on the show.
- Fixes: a response delay (pick a random time between 45 and 60 minutes), plus iteration as feedback comes in.
- His lesson: skip no-code. "Friends don't let friends use n8n." Code is more malleable when you build personal software and agents and need to adjust from real-world feedback. It is faster for him to modify an agent in code than in a no-code tool.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn content to lead gen agent workflow
chunks.text:
- During a company growth sprint, he posts how-tos (example: GTM engineering with Claude Code) and lets posts go viral before building the supporting Notion document.
- He got tired of writing Notion docs, so he gave Claude his Notion API key, built the tutorial doc structure together, then had it turned into a reusable skill.
- The flow now: here's the post, build the Notion doc, then hand it to another agent that comments back with the document, which becomes lead gen. He says this replaces work that would take multiple virtual assistants.

chunks.heading: How to roll this out to a team and incentivize adoption
chunks.text:
- Easiest first exercise for a team: brainstorm an email, write it, publish it as a draft in Klaviyo, all through Claude Code. Seeing it happen is the "holy shit" moment.
- Token quotas don't work: people just paste a spreadsheet into a column to hit the limit.
- What works: spotlight whoever builds something good. Example: Trevor builds a crazy workflow, gets a 30-minute fireside chat where he walks through it, and the boss amplifies it. Status in the community drives other people to adopt. Time off or more money are other levers.
- For employees: bring your own agent stack and personal software. A friend got poached partly because he had his own agent stack and could be productive on day one, which gave him salary leverage. "You're not hiring me, you're hiring me and all of the agents."
- His belief: he may never hire go-to-market people again, apart from an account executive who only hunts whales. Agency work like SEO at $35K/month can be done in about two hours with Claude Code, data access and publishing access to Shopify or another CMS.
- For freelancers: someone who learns this and approaches ecom brands could make $80K/month doing the work of hundreds, especially with repeatable processes like making, publishing and analyzing ads.

chunks.heading: Software buying: API depth beats UI, and switching costs collapse
chunks.text:
- His team picks software by how robust the API is. If an action works as a button click in the UI but not via API, "I'm not going to use that product. Full stop."
- This flips the old dynamic: Salesforce was clunky, so people chose HubSpot for its UI, but Salesforce's deep API is now an advantage.
- He and his team asked whether they should even build a front end for Graph, or build backend infrastructure as a tool for the customer's agent.
- Example: his brother, in healthcare, hated Mailchimp (about 120K list) and migrated everything (context, flows, campaign templates) to Klaviyo in a weekend, via APIs, with no downtime. The agent audited the account structure afterward and caught that the form wasn't connected to Klaviyo. Switching costs that once blocked such moves have collapsed, so the best software on API and capability wins.
- Prediction: go-to-market will be run by agents by the end of the year for the most sophisticated companies. The founder's job becomes building the right product.
- Cost-of-intelligence point: three months after Opus 4.6, an open-source Chinese model (he says it identified itself as Opus 4.6) shipped at a hundred-twentieth of the cost. He treats tokens as abundant and tries to "unbound" his constraints.

chunks.heading: Data analysis use cases and why ecom is positioned well
chunks.text:
- Example: a store with about 20,000 SKUs (wedding cups) could not see in Shopify which SKUs sell best or grow fastest. With data access, 10 of about 500 top SKUs drove 80% of revenue, half of them had no ad spend (organic only), and the agent was told to shift ad budget to them.
- SEO example: with a catalog of 10,000 items, ask which collection pages to build from product cross-sections, giving Claude Shopify, Search Console and Google Analytics access, and request an action plan. A two-hour deep dive into a 17% traffic drop surfaced about 100 hours of manual-equivalent analysis.
- Data-team bottleneck anecdote: a leader at a large brand whose SEO drove 20% of revenue waited 3 to 5 business days per data request. This was the origin of Graph. Data engineers cost roughly $180K to $250K, so small teams can't afford them.
- Postgres and servers: he uses Railway (strong API) to spin up servers and Postgres databases for agents and data analysis, and can harden servers for security.
- Why ecom fits: transparent unit economics make agent loops easy to measure. In software, "everyone is building things people don't want" because engineering used to be the constraint; ecom has physical constraints and knows how to sell what the market wants.
- Remaining question he flags: when every brand can do this, differentiation comes from each company's unique skills and product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains how Grafft runs 10,000-15,000 ads a month with agents acting as media buyers. He maps competitor messaging onto a pain-point matrix to find uncovered angles, runs ads in a tournament that kills losers in 2-3 days, and buys cheap impressions through TikTok real-phone farms.

chunks.heading: How Cody structures ad creative as a matrix and competitive map
chunks.text:
Cody's starting point is positioning. He asks what pain points and outcomes the target customer has, then builds a matrix to map them.
- Rows and columns are emotional triggers crossed with situations the customer could be in.
- Example trigger: "I took this restaurant over from my dad and I'm afraid I'm going to run it into the ground." Example situations: the Friday night rush, a weekend when the phone keeps ringing and the owner doesn't want to answer.
- Five emotional triggers times ten situations gives dozens of distinct ad concepts.
- He pulls every competitor's live creative and plots it on the same matrix. Usually only a few cells (he describes "the top left corner") are lit up because everyone talks about the product the same way.
- He then makes creative for the empty cells. The claim: ROAS rises and CPA falls because he is differentiating the message to the same customer rather than competing in a red ocean.
- Example: every beef tallow brand repeats the same three benefits. There may be seven other benefits, such as eczema relief or replacing Vaseline for slugging, that nobody is covering.

chunks.heading: Competitor angle over capital
chunks.text:
Cody frames smaller brands as competing with giants that have huge ad budgets.
- If a small brand runs the same thesis as a heavily funded brand, the big one wins "nine to 10 times out of 10" because it has more capital.
- The way to compete is "angle to angle," not capital to capital: zig when they zag and talk about completely different things.
- Rise Superfoods is his example of scale, with roughly 2,500 live ads and about 100 or more new ones deployed daily.

chunks.heading: Mining competitor ads and customer language with agents
chunks.text:
He describes this as software, not a person, and says Claude Code could build it.
- A daily cron job uses something like Apify to monitor competitor Facebook Ad Library entries and pull net new creative into a database of active ads.
- A vision model watches video ads and describes what happens second by second. Then aggregate across about 10 competitors to spot larger trends (his example: claymation ads going viral in women's health supplements), and recreate them with Seedance.
- An agent can run for about 12 hours reading Reddit to collect the situations people are in and the language they use. He maps persona by emotional trigger plus situation, using customers' own words that resonate with them.
- Historically, collecting this research would have been prohibitively expensive.

chunks.heading: The ad tournament system that replaces a media buyer
chunks.text:
Cody's agent-run media buying works as a tournament, running across his clients' ad accounts.
- Each day, for one company, he publishes about 5 new ad sets with 5 new ads in each.
- Ads within an ad set compete over a 2 to 3 day window. Losers are turned off automatically.
- Winners from each ad set go into a winners pool, and the pool competes for the available ad budget.
- Volume: he says they launch roughly 10,000 to 15,000 ads a month across all client companies, on Facebook, with a learning loop on top.
- His logic: a media buyer's job is an algorithm (publish new creative, look at what works, kill losers, double down on winners), which can be coded. It needs a data stream, an agent that thinks on top of that data, and the ability to make new creative.
- Andromeda view: Meta's ad delivery is effectively one-to-one, finding a single person each ad can reach, even at $30 for a lead, and creative is now cheap enough to feed it at volume.
- He expects the hard problem to shift to "if I'm publishing 10,000 ads a month, what the [ __ ] is working?"
- He predicts about six weeks until a plug-in ad machine produces cinematic, Pixar-style Seedance creative and uploads it to Facebook automatically.
- He says he is in B2B, so his tactics are different from e-commerce.

chunks.heading: Why he won't rely on Meta's built-in AI ads
chunks.text:
- He doesn't trust Meta to run ads for brands, comparing it to Google reps who just say "increase budget."
- Platform AI is trained to the average. He wants the outliers, because that is the better place to put limited time, money and mental energy.
- Meta's self-serve tools were designed for the "boost a post" SMB owner, and that may suit an HVAC or tree trimming business that just wants leads.
- To compete in the top 1% or 10%, strategy and context matter. Generic prompting gives bell-curve output ("go write me a blog post about X" gives vague average copy).
- His fix is a "walled garden": give the model source material (for example, 10 expert podcasts on hotel marketing in 2026) and it writes top-tier content. For ads, give direction: "You can go northwest, you can go northeast, I don't care, but you have to go north."

chunks.heading: TikTok phone farms for cheap impressions
chunks.text:
Cody uses real-device TikTok farms for brand awareness.
- Setup: real Android phones in a warehouse (his example is Brooklyn) with separate eSIMs and local IPs, scrolling like real users. His provider is Double Speed AI, which gives an API.
- Cost as he recalls it: about $100 per account per month; he runs 10 accounts for about $1,500 (he says "don't quote me" on the per-account figure).
- Math: at 500 to 1,000 views per video across 10 accounts, CPM comes to roughly $2 to $3, versus about $10 for TikTok ads to a general audience. The arbitrage is cheaper impressions.
- Content: slideshows made with Nano Banana, not video. Videos "doesn't work as effectively." The hard part is finding a format that already works.
- Finding formats: scroll TikTok in your category, or use a tool like Virlo (via API with Claude Code) to pull viral posts from the last 7 days.
- Example: a "day in the life of a corporate girly" slideshow that works the product in naturally (a supplement on slide three, taken with matcha). Accounts should look like normal people, not branded.
- He accepts that "the internet is fake" and says the goal is hunting impressions as cheaply as possible.
- Scaling the math: 10 accounts at 300,000 to 500,000 views a month, then 100 or 1,000 accounts. He says this is how new artists and brands appear from nowhere.
- Limits: it is brand-level, not bottom of funnel. It works for B2B only as category brand building, and for e-commerce it can feed the sales process. Attribution is hard, so judge it in aggregate (an average of about 1,000 views per slideshow hits the CPM target).
- Measuring it: look at branded search impressions and clicks in Google Search Console after a strong day. He says nobody has ever solved full ROAS attribution in his ten years.
- On brand: "branded search happens, we just don't know when," and impressions are how you influence word of mouth. His billboard analogy is that accident lawyers buy every billboard because it works.

chunks.heading: Creator seeding combined with the farm
chunks.text:
- A separate approach is creator marketing on payroll: scrape about 20,000 beauty creators, cold email them, and pay roughly $900 a month for a video per day across Reels, Shorts and TikTok. With 20 creators that is about 20 videos a day.
- Creators hunt for viral formats. When one hits, he rolls that format out to all creators and to the phone farm.
- Example math: if the average slideshow gets 1,000 views and the original hit 1 million, even 10,000 views on the farm is an outlier worth doubling down on.
- He separates this from influencer marketing, which is about reach and trust (his example is Meta Ray-Ban working with Kylie Jenner to elevate the brand).

chunks.heading: What agents can and can't do today, and his product
chunks.text:
- He says agents can do almost anything a human can do on a computer. The one boundary he has found is long-form video editing, such as a two-hour live stream. It needs word-by-word transcription and frame-by-frame vision, which is too expensive, so a Philippines editor at about $1,600 a month is cheaper. He expects it to be solved in roughly six months.
- Styleframe AI: he mentions it for motion graphics from key frames, citing an Apple-style watch animation.
- His company, Grafft, started as a data pipeline and warehouse tool. It now offers the infrastructure to deploy agents and artifacts (such as dashboards) onto live data (Facebook ads, Google Analytics, Shopify) in one place.
- Today he works only with B2B and sells outcomes (plan, engineer and run) because most clients "just want to buy the outcomes." He sees e-commerce as a longer-term fit.
- Open request: he is looking for companies working out a wholesale motion, such as getting into every boutique in the southeastern United States.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains what a real AI agent is (software running a repeatable job with a thinking loop), why agents need live revenue data, and how Graft deploys Facebook Ads, Google Ads, SEO and cold outbound agents. He also gives an adoption path for non-technical owners: co-work first, automate later, one workflow at a time.

chunks.heading: What an agent actually is
chunks.text:
- Cody defines an agent as "some job function or some job to be done" that runs on a repeated cycle, like a standard operating procedure. Under the hood it is "really just software" with a thinking loop.
- Chat tools need a human to push each step (find keywords, research page one, paste in, write the post). An agent runs that same chain itself, then publishes, reads live data on which posts bring customers, and refreshes the content.
- He says the category is full of "snake oil," e.g. tools claiming they will "entirely run your ad account." His rule: take the process a human does and have the agent repeat it.
- The human becomes a curator: deep domain knowledge, a clear explanation of what is wanted, and a measure of success (usually "make more money"), worked back into qualified leads and where target customers spend time.

chunks.heading: The four marketing roles Graft deploys most
chunks.text:
- Facebook ads management, Google ads management, SEO plus AI search (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity; he says Gemini referral traffic has been "exploding"), and cold email outbound.
- He says most business growth falls into three buckets: cold outbound, paid ads, and organic ranking.
- Other requests: social media management, influencer outreach and negotiation (contact 1,000 influencers, pick the 10 most underpriced), and Pinterest.
- Buyers include software companies that would rather work with Graft than hire a marketing team, and local businesses that say "I hate my agency." He also partners with agencies that run about 150 Google Ads accounts for appliance repair companies, with Graft as the white-label back end.
- Pricing for local businesses can be a flat fee while the agent optimizes in the background.

chunks.heading: The Facebook ads agent loop
chunks.text:
- Example client: an AI landscape design product that maps your backyard from your address and produces a material list for a local landscaper.
- Steps:
  - Scrape Reddit, YouTube and other social posts for customer pain points and desired outcomes (tools: Firecrawl or Exa AI, driven from Codex or Claude Code).
  - Generate 10 new static ad creatives daily with Nano Banana, given a brand style guide (fonts, colors, composition).
  - Upload automatically through the Facebook Ads API using a developer API key.
  - Optimize every ad for one conversion action, a form submission or qualified lead sent back to Facebook.
  - Turn off losers, promote winners to a winners campaign where they compete for budget.
  - Attach a vision model that studies what winners share and feeds those themes back to the creative agent.
- Result: cost per lead fell from $17 on average to $1.70 in three weeks, with first ads live in about three days.
- He says nothing here is tricky: "what are the top 1% of Facebook Ads marketers do right now": test a lot of creative, double down on winners, repeat.

chunks.heading: Agent architecture: data first
chunks.text:
- Graft's stack is three parts: a data pipeline, a data warehouse, and an agent harness. Pipeline sources might be Facebook ads, Google Analytics, a CRM such as Go High Level, and Stripe.
- Agents need live revenue data. His first attempt at a Google Ads agent hit API rate limits, truncation errors and hallucination, so the first product became a BI tool that solved the pipeline and warehouse. Agent infrastructure was added in the last 3 months.
- The early AI SDR/BDR tools did not fail at making leads. They made lots of low-quality ones because they lacked visibility into whether a lead was qualified or became revenue.
- Align on what a good customer looks like (sales wants "whales," marketing is measured on leads) and track it. The agent gets the same alignment a human team would.
- Harness: Hermes, running in the cloud on an always-on computer. He tried OpenClaw ("a digital human in a box") but found it brittle and not enterprise-ready; Hermes was far better, and he knows the founders. Claude Agent SDK is another option.
- Enterprise reliability matters: a $5,000 monthly ad budget should not turn into $50 thousand by accident.

chunks.heading: How a beginner should adopt agents
chunks.text:
- Don't start by building an agent that automates the whole business: "a tar pit that people fall into."
- Progression:
  - Co-work in Claude Code or Codex in another tab. He dictates with Super Whisper and delegates anything involving the mouse or keyboard ("the middle work"). The human explains the task and audits outputs.
  - List daily tasks you despise (writing, data analysis, lead-list cleaning) and turn each into a system.
  - Then automate it with Zapier or n8n, or a cloud Hermes agent. He mentions one-click Hermes on Hostinger at about $15 a month, controlled by text, Telegram, iMessage or Slack.
- Save brand style guides, goals and business context so the tool "turns into a co-founder."
- Cloud beats local for scheduled work ("every day at 9:00 a.m.") and for safety: a local agent has access to everything on your machine.
- Delegating costs "a tenth" or "a hundredth" of an employee.

chunks.heading: Content quality and human-in-the-loop
chunks.text:
- An agent asked cold to write about your industry produces average, unoriginal output. Give it 30 minutes of you talking about a specific topic as a transcript and ask for a thought leadership piece, and he says the output is "top 1%."
- Bad ads (looks like "Microsoft Paint") usually mean no brand style guide, color palette, or allowed and disallowed language.
- Give the agent boundaries. He found it works better to say what bad looks like and tell it to do anything else than to define "good."
- Human-in-the-loop is built for regulated industries like finance: the agent drafts, posts in Slack ("Todd, is this all right?"), takes edits, resends.

chunks.heading: Delivery timeline and Graft's model
chunks.text:
- Graft forward-deploys engineers into client companies. Clients come as repeat founders avoiding a marketing hire, or after getting "90% of the way there" and stalling on the last 10%. Some have failed three times.
- Pre-built agents are out in about 5 business days. Within the first 2 weeks, 2 to 3 agents are live; by 90 days about 10, of which about 3 are custom.
- Custom example: a "TikTok real farm" of about 100 cloud TikTok accounts with an API endpoint for bulk uploads, for a mobile AI photo-editing app. Each custom build becomes a playbook on the menu for similar companies.
- Marginal cost is low enough that he asks "why wouldn't we do everything" across channels.
- Success measure: the token cost to get a lead, replacing ad spend as the cost to watch. Anyone can make 1,000 ads now; knowing what works is the hard part, so feed agents the metric closest to revenue.
- He previously built "AI slop generators" (e.g. 1,000 blog posts that did produce leads), and learned scale without quality feedback fails.

chunks.heading: When agents don't fit, and rollout advice
chunks.text:
- Poor fits: early-stage companies without a clear target customer or positioning ("you can't build a system for a company that doesn't have a system"), and messy paper-trail businesses (real estate) where one employee holds all the knowledge.
- Test: if you can delegate a task to a team member to run on a cadence with a success measure, an agent can probably do it.
- Pick one workflow at a time, "eat the elephant piece by piece." He estimates about 40% of a business can realistically be automated, the parts that cause burnout.
- To drive team adoption, run a weekly lunch and learn where someone shows what they automated, and spotlight that person. Token quotas backfire (a friend at a payroll software company hits his by splitting columns).
- Resistance is real: a 50-employee company he spoke with was against adoption for fear of job loss.
- Learning: the free course at gtmengineeringcourse.com, plus YouTube and X, where new methods appear first, then YouTube, then LinkedIn, then Instagram. He says "everybody that's selling a course is selling old information."
- His closing principle: "What is the most boring thing I can do consistently? And that's what actually makes growth happen."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains how to build teams of specialized AI marketing agents with feedback loops, evals and safety guardrails rather than one generalist agent. He covers choosing businesses by search intent, why data ontology and good signals decide whether agents succeed, and why buyers want outcomes, not tools.

chunks.heading: Why Cody builds AI marketing agents, and what has to be true for them to work
chunks.text:
- Cody argues growth is engineering: "I have an outcome that I'm trying to get. I have limited resources of time, money, and mental energy," and the job is to distribute those resources most effectively. If it is a system, it can become a process, then software.
- He says the whole stack to have a company "market itself" already exists: the data, the intelligence, and the tooling. What remains is building the systems, operations, and quality standards around the agents.
- His startup pitch to clients is speed: "we can deploy an agent in like 40 hours," across channels, reusing the same playbooks that work for similar SaaS companies.
- He says buyers want outcomes, not self-serve tools. Companies "just want to pay for the outcome," and he is effectively building virtual employees for them at roughly 1/10th the cost of hiring 10 people.
- After adding an agent layer on top of Graphed (a data pipeline, warehouse and BI tool), users kept saying "cool, I have this insight, now I want to act on it." That feedback pushed Graphed into done-for-you, forward-deployed GTM engineering.
- He tested demand for that offer by posting it on Twitter and LinkedIn with a Tally form, and got over 100 inbound requests.

chunks.heading: Why AI SDRs failed, and how to avoid the same trap
chunks.text:
- Cody's postmortem of AI SDRs: the agent often performed "unbelievably well." It got leads, but the leads were terrible quality.
- The cause is optimizing for the wrong metric. He compares it to Google Ads ML self-optimizing into a cheaper sign-up event from the wrong subset of the audience.
- His framing: "it's not the agent's fault... it's optimizing for the wrong metric." If the wrong signal goes back to it, it does its job against that signal.
- The fix is to give the agent all the data and resources and tie it to revenue, not just the top-of-funnel event.
- He says the hardest remaining problem is human: deciding what the agent should optimize for. Pointing it at the wrong target is "pointing a nuclear weapon" at the wrong thing.
- He dismisses people who say agents can't work in marketing as "rookies" who don't see growth as a system.

chunks.heading: A multi-agent team: one narrow job per agent
chunks.text:
- Cody says "run Facebook ads" as a single prompt fails, like a human who has never done it. It is rare to find one person who can make creative, manage the account and analyze data, and the same limits apply to one agent.
- His approach is a team of agents, each in its own sandbox, each with a tightly scoped job:
  - Research agent: scours social media for target customers' pain points and desired outcomes and builds a corpus.
  - Script-writing agent: writes scripts from that research and uses the HeyGen API to generate raw video, then removes silence and adds captions, producing AI UGC ads.
  - Ad-account agent: uploads to Facebook Ads and follows explicit rules. If CPM hits $50, it stops that ad. If it sees a target CPA, it promotes the ad to its own ad set and allocates budget. After about 30 days, it turns off ads showing fatigue.
  - Analysis agent: finds what actually works and feeds that back to the others.
- He describes the structure as ICs, a manager above them, and an analytics layer over Facebook ads, Google ads, SEO and the whole organization, like "a board meeting with your agents."
- He says no single agent or human could hold all of this at once, so splitting by job is what makes it work.

chunks.heading: The SEO agent loop (built live)
chunks.text:
Cody built this on a livestream:
1. Keyword research.
2. Research what ranks on page one of Google.
3. Input a transcript of him talking about the topic (his example: how AI is changing Facebook Ads).
4. The agent writes and publishes the content.
5. It calls a web indexing API to get the page indexed.
6. A second agent reads live Google Search Console data and optimizes the article.
7. A third agent looks at which pages produce sign-ups and revenue, and feeds that into the next round of content.

- He says every good go-to-market system follows this loop: "I try things, I look at what works, I do less of what doesn't and more of what does, and I just repeat that growth loop."
- To grow fast, layer channels: do one, add a second, add a third, and "never stop what you're doing."
- He warns that "give it a keyword and it writes it" is why people say AI SEO doesn't rank. Under the hood, good content involves many steps.

chunks.heading: Vibe coding is not production: the last 20% is the work
chunks.text:
- Cody says vibe coding "from zero to 80% is pretty cool. 80 to production and live is a chasm."
- Examples of the hidden work: agent evals so output hits brand style guidelines, and an observer agent checking image outputs (he mentions Nano Banana via two API endpoints) against the guide before they move to the next step, such as upload.
- He says this is where companies underestimate: they want agents conceptually, but the build-out and implementation gap is huge.
- His example of speed when scope is clear: he gave Claude Code a plan, with "dangerous permissions," to build a medical-business directory site. The data-collection agents took time, but the product itself was done in about 45 minutes. It included location filters, login and paid placement for top listings.

chunks.heading: Data quality and agent evals
chunks.text:
- Cody warns that agents assume things about underlying data. Facebook Ads alone has 96 tables and hundreds of columns, so "link clicks" or "CPC over time" can be ambiguous, and the agent guesses from training.
- He says you have to teach the agent the ontology of the data: "when somebody says this they mean this." Then run an eval program so that when a user asks for something of that shape, the agent writes the right SQL on the first try instead of retrying five times.
- He says the worst outcome is making decisions on bad data. Many marketers hook Claude Code to the Facebook Ads API and assume the output is right.
- Failure modes he lists: rate limits that aren't flagged, truncation or pagination problems in MCPs that report "all the data" but return page one, and stuffing tabular data into the context window.
- He says evals are needed for both the data and the decisions the agent makes.

chunks.heading: Choosing tools in an agent world, and keeping agents safe
chunks.text:
- On CRMs: six months ago he'd pick HubSpot for its UI. Now the criterion is "what has the most API endpoints and can control the product at the largest scale via the API." He says he hasn't touched the HubSpot UI during live sales cycles and instead uses a Graphed agent with an API key to track deal flow and follow-ups.
- Graphed's product direction: rather than adding UI features like dropdown filters, give the agent a skill and an endpoint to create hosted artifacts. A user's agent can build custom dashboards, then slide decks with chart PNGs, for example a weekly client report sent every Monday.
- Safety practices Graphed uses for agents:
  - The agent never touches real API keys. Real secrets live in a local secrets file, the agent gets a "ghost key," and the real key is proxied in at call time.
  - Remove open web access. Give the agent Firecrawl only, and require approval for specific outbound actions, to reduce prompt injection from something like a random Reddit post.
- He says it is early and nobody knows the full safety surface yet.
- On cost: he notes Graphed ships a lot on MiniMax 2.5 because it is capable for the cost. His pattern: a frontier model ships, an open-source model follows about 3 months later at roughly 1/20th the cost, so he assumes intelligence cost trends toward zero.

chunks.heading: How Cody picks what to build, and his advice for marketers
chunks.text:
- Business selection: he asks whether it's a problem he faces or one with search intent. Example: the domain trackableqrcode.com (about 1,200 searches a month and growing quickly). Incumbents like Bitly aren't focused on it, and buyers include restaurants and consumer packaged goods companies putting QR codes on products. He bought it intending to have an agent build the product and market it autonomously.
- He sorts ideas into a fun side project (an example: a business making about $8k a month and a possible flip) versus one with "the biology" to be a large company.
- On too many options: "a business at its core is always the simplest thing": what the market wants to buy, and how to get in front of them. Customer demand tells you what to work on.
- Advice for people early in their career: become a marketing or go-to-market engineer. He says the title has widened from cold outbound to paid ads, cold email, SEO and nurture, and someone who can do all of it at scale with agents is "top 1%." He cites a friend hired as a GTM engineer at about $650k a year.
- He says the people who made impact usually combined two deep skills, and that a weekend of tutorials can now teach paid ads, cold email and SEO.
- Cody's prediction: companies will struggle to hire this talent internally, so they'll buy outcomes. He also says differentiation is an open problem once everyone runs the same playbooks.

chunks.heading: Cody's background and how his marketing instincts formed
chunks.text:
- He grew up in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, studied economics, and says he's started more companies than he's had jobs.
- Early on he taught himself Photoshop and Illustrator, bought a direct-to-garment printer, and mined Etsy's then-public best-seller data with a script. He remixed best sellers around their target keywords and reached about $10k a month in his early 20s, running it from his basement.
- He was banned from Etsy for scraping its data. The lesson he took: he was selling commodities and needed to build a brand alongside the product.
- He learned B2B marketing over four years with a boss who had been through Y Combinator and sold digital strategy to Fortune 500 companies. His first test was a bathtub and shower-base manufacturer: he proposed a Pinterest campaign built around an e-book on putting a shower in a van or RV, and was given a test budget.
- The job taught him long sales cycles and account-based marketing.
- At Rupa Health (he was around employee nine or ten), a friend sent him the growth curve: slow 3-4% compounding monthly growth, then a steep jump. The explanation was "I turned on ads." He said yes on a Sunday, had the call on Wednesday and the offer on Thursday, and moved to San Francisco the next Monday. His principle: act when you have real signal.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains how he automates go-to-market with Claude Code agents: a podcast-booking cold email agent, bulk Facebook ad generation, and a LinkedIn comment-to-lead loop. He also argues for owned media, solving the data pipeline before agents make decisions, and ideas plus polish as the only human work left.

chunks.heading: Cody's AI-agent GTM stack: how he booked podcasts with an agent
chunks.text:
- Cody ran a PR sprint after Graphed's pre-seed round (October) and three months of heads-down product work. He wanted to get booked on podcasts.
- His old manual process: pull shows and contact info from Refonic (a database of shows and contacts), scrape them, validate the emails with Million Verifier, load them into Instantly, pitch, then manage replies.
- The new process: connect all the APIs, load the leads into Instantly, and attach an Instantly agent whose job is to schedule a discovery call.
- Results from a 2,000-contact cohort: 112 positive responses, 35 calls scheduled, and the agent dropped the ball on 90 of the 112. He expected "maybe a handful" and mainly wanted data to improve the agent.
- His calendar ended up booked back-to-back, about 10 hours a day for a week.
- The mistakes were real. The agent replied within seconds, so people knew it was a bot. It agreed to buy two books from a host. Some people were "viscerally mad."
- His recovery: get on the call, acknowledge it, say it was a test, apologize for the poor experience, and explain that he needed data.
- He sees this as the same tension as with human PR. Hired PR people also pitch bad-fit shows. The difference is the iteration speed: the agent is code in a GitHub repo, so fixes shipped within 24 hours of feedback.
- He now asks what the boundary of PR is that agents roaming the web can handle.

chunks.heading: "Friends don't let friends do n8n": build agents in code with Claude Code
chunks.text:
- Cody says to go straight to code instead of workflow tools, because code is "so much more malleable." He can update the system prompt, tools, and behavior from live market feedback while Claude Code works in the background.
- Deployment: Claude Code builds the software and deploys it to Railway ("like a Heroku but it has a really robust API"), where the agent runs in perpetuity. Postgres databases on Railway are also easy to spin up. He says he "will never do a pivot table again."
- His definition of an agent: access to the things it needs (API keys), plus a system prompt with a goal. He builds a boundary by listing the "nos": "here's all the nos around the thing," which "creates a boundary for yes," and the agent works out the best path inside it.
- He treats an agent as a "malleable employee." When the meta shifts, he swaps tools or the conversion event in minutes. Example: UGC ads (HeyGen avatars with ElevenLabs voices) gave way to static ads with big text.
- Agent harness: he thinks the harness (model plus tools) is the product, and that is where differentiation and defensibility lie. He says Claude Code with the model beats raw claude.ai, and describes running 5-10 terminals on different Mac desktops, managing agents "like an agent jockey."
- Voice input: he uses Super Whisper to dictate instead of typing.
- Cost curve: he cites Opus 4.6 and then MiniMax 2.5 arriving about 3 months later at roughly 1/20th of the cost at similar intelligence (he says it appeared to be distilled from Claude via ~24,000 accounts). He sees three cycles of this, so hard work keeps getting cheaper.
- He calls the mindset "token abundance": unshackle yourself from old constraints.

chunks.heading: How to start building a GTM agent stack (the folder method)
chunks.text:
Cody's step-by-step for beginners:
1. Make a local folder (his is called "graph growth agents") and open it in Claude Code. Everything he does lives in that folder, essentially a code repo.
2. Create an environment file and add the API keys for your whole business stack.
3. Tell Claude what you want to do. Ask it to make a plan and interrogate you for more context.
4. Let context accumulate in the directory. It gets smarter as it accumulates knowledge about the business, the marketing process, and your challenges.
5. When a co-worked process lands on an output you like, tell Claude to save it as a skill for reuse.

- Example email workflow: Claude Code pulls a product-feature transcript from Notion, writes an email with a "top 1% direct response marketer" persona (educational, casting a vision), saves it as a draft in SendGrid via API, sends a test to his inbox, then sends it. He doesn't touch the SendGrid UI.
- He says the shift happened in the last ~6 weeks: it went from an assistant that "doesn't really do work" to doing real work.
- Audit method for small, high-touch businesses: audit the work you do daily, weekly, or monthly, find what repeats, and co-work with Claude to automate it. His example for a small agency: a weekly agent that sends 10 LinkedIn post drafts on Monday morning, then learns from impression data.
- He says GTM engineer is "the most desired role that exists" right now; he gets 10-20 messages a day asking how to hire one. A friend negotiated a much higher salary by saying he was bringing his whole stack of ~20 agents and personal software.
- He publishes a free tutorial series at gtmengineeringcourse.com, sponsored by Graphed.

chunks.heading: Automated Facebook ads loop
chunks.text:
Cody's pipeline, built in Claude Code:
1. Research pain points: scrape Reddit and Twitter for how people talk about what they hate about Looker Studio, and use that exact language in ads.
2. Generate creative: an on-brand template built as a React component, where only the title and paragraph change, with a before/after image below. Nano Banana can be used for images. He can make about 1,000 ad variations for essentially zero cost.
3. Upload through the Facebook Ads API.
4. Wait about a week, then use the Graphed MCP to find winners and losers.
5. Turn off the losers, promote the winners to their own ad set, and switch to a conversion (signup) campaign. He uses clicks only for testing.
6. Identify common threads among the winners and generate another creative round.

- He is about a week from turning this into a fully autonomous agent running Facebook ads.
- Why a data warehouse is needed: calling ad APIs directly runs into rate limits. An MCP over the API hits pagination and truncation. Stuffing data into context causes context bloat. Example: a client spending about $180K a month on Facebook ads could pull only about two hours of data through the API, so Claude hallucinates from partial data and the agent decides on bad information. His view is that the data pipeline and warehouse have to be solved first. This is the thesis behind Graphed.
- Graphed: an AI data analyst for growth teams. It connects and unifies data sources, manages the pipeline and warehouse, builds an ontology layer, and offers an MCP and a Slack integration (@graph in chat).

chunks.heading: LinkedIn "comment to get the doc" playbook
chunks.text:
- Cody posts content with an outcome and a Notion document that teaches it: "here's the seven things you're going to learn... Comment X to get the Notion document."
- Comments create a viral loop. A Claude Code skill using the Browser Use Chrome extension replies to the commenter (about 300 replies), which adds more reach. The asset is email-gated, so it becomes an email lead.
- He uses Phantom Buster to extract everyone who engaged on the post and gets their LinkedIn profiles. He enriches them with Apollo, validates the emails with Million Verifier, and loads them into an Instantly cold-email campaign. The system "just runs."
- Result: about 500,000 impressions on LinkedIn in 30 days. At an average LinkedIn CPM of about $23, he computes roughly $115,000 of free reach.
- Writing: he keeps markdown files with his writing style and examples of his best content by reach. LinkedIn and Twitter tone are different and are kept separate.
- Snowball technique: keep a repository of best-performing content and remix it from new angles ("everything is a remix").
- Graphed's acquisition has been all organic; the only ads he runs are remarketing. He publishes about 500 pieces of content a month and just re-enabled free trials about two weeks before the interview.
- Ideas he is exploring: Instagram persona accounts ("a day in the life of a corporate girly" slideshows with the product included, made with Nano Banana, scheduled and analyzed automatically), scaled to 10 accounts. He also thinks of podcasts and niche newsletters, such as one for automotive shop digital marketing, as content channels agents can run.

chunks.heading: Lead enrichment and rolling out AI inside a company
chunks.text:
- Lead enrichment: SDRs and AEs dislike doing it, and it doesn't make them money. An agent can research each lead about 30 minutes after it lands: org structure, how the lead fits in, a plan to sell into that structure, and what they need to get buy-in from their decision maker. APIs he names include LeadMagic, Apollo, and SalesQL.
- Agent for relationship building: he is building an agent that emails target customers with no intention to sell, asking about pain points and building a relationship at scale (one-to-one conversations with thousands of people). Later it can seed ideas or collect information. He compares it to a 13-month email thread with one person that an agent can run across many.
- Adoption incentives inside a company: he says time-off rewards, and token quotas or bonuses, both have problems. Example: a friend at a late-stage startup has a monthly token limit, so he splits and rejoins CSV files just to hit it.
- His preferred approach: give a crash-course, give people access, and let someone rise up ("Trevor") and do something striking. Then spotlight that person with a 20-30 minute fireside chat on the workflow. Status drives adoption: "everybody wants status."
- He doesn't expect to need growth employees. The main hires would be good salespeople who hunt whales, fed the best leads by a large brand. He doesn't think fully automated sales works yet: "people buy from people."

chunks.heading: Brand and owned media as the defense against rising CPCs
chunks.text:
- Cody has been "preaching" for five years that owned media is the future. He cites Andrew Chen's book *The Cold Start Problem* and his idea of the "law of shitty clickthroughs": as a market matures, more competitors bid and CPC rises, and the only counter is owned media that gives organic reach.
- At Rupa Health (a marketplace for specialty lab test ordering), they started with ads and then layered on a live class, a podcast, a big email list, and a big blog, so that customer acquisition cost stayed flat while paid costs rose.
- Graphed sits in a very competitive category (Tableau, Power BI, and others). Some VCs said it was the dumbest idea they'd seen; others said it was obvious. Cody's answer is brand and distribution real estate.
- Where your customers spend time includes physical places. At his old agency, a manufacturer found that physical pamphlets at gas stations in its geography outperformed every other channel, so it did that at every gas station.
- Goal: own mental real estate so that when someone thinks of a category, they think of your company.
- In the AI era, he says the only work left is "ideas and polish" (taste); everything in the middle is "how do I get an agent to do it?"
- On building product: code costs are near zero, so the hard part is knowing what people actually want to buy. He gives the example of a PM friend whose team builds prototypes and tries to merge features nobody wants. He thinks ecom has an advantage because physical constraints force a "does the market want this?" test.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains marketing engineering: using a coding agent like Claude Code to do the manual middle work of marketing. He lays out the infrastructure it needs (pipeline, warehouse, server, storage, crons, APIs) and demos ad creation, Facebook uploads, SEO, lead enrichment and dashboards. The video is sponsored by graph.com, his own product.

chunks.heading: Why marketing engineering matters and what it is
chunks.text:
- Cody defines marketing engineering as having a coding agent do "all of the middle work" a marketer used to do by hand. He says it works in any harness (Claude Code, Cursor, Hermes agent, Grok bot).
- Work it replaces: writing copy, making creative and graphic design, uploading blog posts, building landing pages, researching Google Ads keywords and target customers, finding emails and loading them into cold email software, building newsletters for webinars, and monitoring competitors' ad libraries on Facebook, Google and LinkedIn.
- He has done digital marketing for 15 years, and spent the last 4 working on getting AI to run marketing operations.
- Demand signal: marketing engineering searches and job listings are growing fast, with salaries of $150,000+ a year for marketers who learn the engineering side with coding agents. He says it tracks the same trajectory as GTM engineering.
- His pitch to marketers: learn this so you still have a job 2 years from now.

chunks.heading: The stack an agent needs to do marketing
chunks.text:
Cody's list of what a coding agent needs before it can act as a marketer:

- **Data pipeline plus data warehouse:** pull Facebook Ads, Google Ads, Google Analytics, Search Console, CRM (Attio or HubSpot) and Stripe data into one place the agent can query.
- **Cloud server:** an always-on computer in the cloud so scripts and agents run without your laptop being on.
- **Media storage:** an S3 bucket for images and videos (social posts, ads, AI avatars). He calls it super cheap.
- **Postgres databases:** the agent stores things like total addressable market maps for cold email, image/video queues organized by SKU, and the JSON sent to image or video models (he names ChatGPT Image 2.5 and Seedance). They should be creatable on a whim.
- **Cron jobs:** recurring tasks that run hourly, per minute or daily.
- **Artifact hosting:** shareable dashboards or pages (for example, all the ads you made, for approval). This brings in authentication so teammates can access them and the public can't.
- **Git manager:** makes the system multiplayer so several people can work on the same code without overwriting each other.
- **API gateway:** one access point for APIs that make images, find emails, make video, and scrape the web and social accounts.

His claim: once these barriers are removed, the agent "is the best marketer that exists on planet Earth."

Open-source or DIY mapping he gives: Airbyte (pipeline), ClickHouse (warehouse), Netlify (server), S3 (media), Railway (databases), a cron function on the server, Vercel (artifacts), a login database (auth), GitHub (Git), and subscriptions to roughly 40 APIs. He skips that route and uses the Graph (graph.com) marketing engineering cloud, which bundles all of it behind one CLI. The video is sponsored by Graph.

chunks.heading: Why you need a data pipeline and warehouse instead of calling APIs directly
chunks.text:
- Calling platform APIs directly causes three problems:
  - Rate limits. Hitting Facebook Ads too aggressively can break its terms of service and get the ad account banned.
  - Joins. Joining data across sources inside the agent is hard, and the agent hallucinates.
  - Context. Pulling something like 50 million Facebook Ads rows and 75 million Google Analytics rows blows past token limits.
- The pattern: sync every source into the warehouse, let the agent read from it with SQL (he says modern models are very good at SQL), and use platform APIs only to write (upload media, turn ads on and off, move ads between ad sets).
- Write actions flow back into the warehouse, creating a continuous loop.
- Why multiple sources: a single source like Facebook Ads can misrepresent what is happening. He says you must tie ads all the way down to what produces revenue, and sees people miss this constantly.
- He says a small single-channel account can run on raw APIs, but any real business at scale needs this structure. After 2 years he reports companies keep arriving saying they built locally and hit these problems.
- His summary: "All marketing, everything that we're doing is now code."

chunks.heading: Getting a Facebook Ads API token that never expires
chunks.text:
- Cody uses the Facebook Marketing API as the bridge for managing an account.
- Steps he walks through:
  1. In Business Settings, click Add (top right) to create a developer app and name it (for example "Graph Ads").
  2. Select the use cases: create and manage ads with the Marketing API and with Meta Ads Manager, and connect the business portfolio.
  3. Confirm the overview, create the app, and add a privacy policy.
  4. Add a system user, assign the assets it needs access to, and generate the token.
- Takes about 10 minutes and yields a token that never expires.
- Storage: he advises against keeping the token locally because it is a security vulnerability. Use a secrets manager (Graph does this automatically). He pastes the token into Claude Code and says "add this Facebook Ads API token to my secrets," then lists secrets via the CLI.
- His secrets list includes Facebook Ads, Google Ads, Instantly, and Strapi (his blog CMS).

chunks.heading: Making and managing Facebook ads from Claude Code
chunks.text:
- Making a static ad: he prompts "use the Graph CLI" to make a 1080x1080 static ad through the ChatGPT Image 2.5 endpoint, with the text "Marketing Engineering Crash Course," and has it check graph.com for the design style. The tool routes the call through a provider called Kai AI.
- Scaling creative: variations come at scale, and he can specify fonts, colors, and allowed or forbidden language (useful in regulated industries).
- Uploading: he pastes an ad set URL and says "upload the marketing engineering crash course ad to this ad set." The ad appeared in the ad set after a refresh.
- Managing: he turned off an ad in an ad set by title through a plain-language request, and it was off when he checked. Uploading, pausing and moving ads all work this way, for statics and video.
- Scale claim: 100 ads, plus 100 titles and 100 descriptions based on pain points and desired outcomes extracted from Reddit via the xAI API.
- His line: "I know I personally never want to touch a Facebook Ads Library again."
- Workflow habit: run several tasks in the background at once. Once a process works, deploy it to the cloud on a schedule so he doesn't have to babysit it.

chunks.heading: Conversational analytics and dashboards on live data
chunks.text:
- Because everything is in the warehouse, he asks questions across sources in one prompt. His example: how many sign-ups Facebook Ads and its pixel recorded, how much GA4 traffic has Facebook as referral, and whether branded searches (Search Console) are rising.
- The warehouse syncs hourly, which he calls real time. Agents can make decisions autonomously on top of it, and he builds dashboards for the team.
- He then asked for an artifact dashboard of the pulled data and edited it conversationally: switch charts to bar or line, show spend by month, add a date range picker.
- Artifacts get a shareable URL accessible to the team only, not public, and can be interactive software.

chunks.heading: Research, outbound and SEO workflows
chunks.text:
- **Reddit research for ad creative:** extract pain points, desired outcomes and objections from Reddit threads about why someone would buy a data pipeline and warehouse tool and give Claude Code access instead of using Looker Studio or Power BI. These get clustered for ad categories.
- **UGC scripts:** from those pain points he had it write 10 AI-avatar UGC ad scripts, with hooks like "Okay, this is kind of crazy" and "I wish I found this sooner." Example script opener: "Every Monday I used to spend like 3 hours pulling CSVs..." The scripts can be read by an AI avatar or a creator.
- **LinkedIn engager outbound:** take a LinkedIn post whose engagers would be target customers, extract the engagers, and run a get-leads endpoint to find emails. The post had 69 reactions and 316 comments, and likely duplicates. In his run, 5 emails were found and 44 people had none, which he calls a poor result ("We'd typically see about half").
- **Waterfall enrichment:** for people without emails, run the cheapest provider first and work down (Lead Magic, Apollo and others, paying only for credits used). Then guess emails from about 32 pattern variations and check them with Million Verifier. He says guessing plus verification is sometimes cheaper than any enrichment provider.
- **Keyword research:** used the DataForSEO API for "versus" keywords in the customer data platform space (HighTouch vs X, ClickHouse vs X). Got 765 results, then filtered to unique search intents by dropping X vs Y / Y vs X duplicates.
- **Page-two opportunities:** with Search Console plus the SEO data in the warehouse, he found 398 keywords in positions 11 to 20 with 100+ impressions in the last 90 days, and asked for a ranked top 10 to write content for.
- **Publishing a blog post:** with Graph's SEO plugin installed and wired to his CMS, he gave a target keyword. It researches what ranks on the first page of Google, writes the article with Claude Sonnet, uploads to the CMS, and returns the URL. He notes the plugin is modifiable.

chunks.heading: Pay-per-use tooling and how to start
chunks.text:
- Graph exposes about 250 tools through a unified API, added over time from workflows they identify. Examples he lists: scraping ads from TikTok, Google and Meta; finding and validating emails (Million Verifier, Get Leads); phone lookups; funding signals; news search; keyword research with DataForSEO; image creation; video creation with Seedance and HeyGen; LinkedIn profile extraction.
- Data sources: 800+ connectors (GoHighLevel, GA, Search Console, Instantly, Facebook Ads, Twilio and others).
- Pricing: pay as you go, usage-based for syncing and for API credits. He says you can start for free, and that $10 can pull roughly 1,000 emails.
- Setup: install an NPM package (the Graph CLI) by giving Claude Code the URL and telling it to install it. It bundles the pipeline, warehouse and tools.
- Plugins are installed by prompt, for example "Install the Graph SEO plugin. Help me set it up to my CMS."
- He is building a free course at gtmengineeringcourse.com, sponsored by Graph, and says he will post marketing engineering videos weekly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider defines GTM engineering as using Claude Code to do the hands-on work across marketing, sales and product. He shows the minimal setup (a folder, an env file, a CLAUDE.md), then runs keyword research, writes and publishes an SEO article, and tracks and improves it with Search Console data.

chunks.heading: What GTM engineering is and how Cody defines it
chunks.text:
- GTM (go-to-market) engineering originally meant the cold email and outreach process. Clay (clay.com) "solidified or owned" the term.
- Cody says it is quickly expanding to everything related to marketing: customer experience, product, paid ads, SEO, and anything in the go-to-market process where AI does the engineering, software development and build-outs.
- It is all the "middle work" that used to be hands-on keyboard and mouse. The person's role becomes having the ideas, handing the middle work to Claude Code, then acting as "the polish, the endpoint".
- Cody frames the person as a conductor and curator of what the agents do.
- He says this is actual work getting done, not a skill: keyword research, writing the blog post and publishing it; researching Facebook ad angles, making and publishing the ads, then analyzing low and high performers.
- Cody has done marketing for over 15 years and is co-founder of graph.com, an AI data analyst for go-to-market teams.

chunks.heading: Setting up Claude Code as a GTM workspace (folder, env file, CLAUDE.md)
chunks.text:
Cody says setup takes about 10 minutes:
1. Create a folder to work out of. His is "Graft Growth Agents"; for the demo he made a folder called "demo".
2. Open it in the Claude desktop app or the Claude terminal. Cody prefers the terminal so he can have multiple windows open and jockey between them.
3. In the terminal: `cd documents/demo`, then type `claude`.
4. Tell Claude to create an environment file (.env) in the directory and a CLAUDE.md file. The CLAUDE.md instructs: anytime he provides an API key, add it to the environment file so keys accumulate and can be reused in future.

- This is the foundation that lets Claude do the middle work for you.
- He dictates prompts with Super Whisper (transcription software), triggered with option + space.
- His real working folder already has all his stack's API keys stored, so Claude knows which APIs are available (for example Keywords Everywhere, Strapi, the Graph MCP).
- Cody's vision: open about five terminals at once and bounce between them, "jockeying the agents" while work gets done. During the demo he edited his video script while Claude worked in the background.

chunks.heading: Why Claude Code instead of Claude Cowork or n8n
chunks.text:
- Cody says he would send people "immediately to this instead of Claude Co-work or n8n" for GTM work.
- His reasoning: Claude Code can do the actual work end to end (call APIs, write, publish), and the work extends into building personal software and personal agents to get your job done.
- He says everyone in a growth role will be affected by this, and that anyone who thinks their job won't be augmented is "getting high on your own supply".

chunks.heading: Demo: keyword research to published blog post in about 5 minutes
chunks.text:
Workflow Cody runs in Claude Code:
1. **Keyword research:** "Use the Keywords Everywhere API and find all of the versus keywords you can" for the "Looker Studio vs Y" pattern (X vs Y keywords). Claude finds the API and returns the keyword list.
2. **Pick a target:** he chose "Looker Studio vs Metabase".
3. **Gather source material:** scrape what currently ranks on page one of Google for that keyword. His reasoning: Google is signaling "this is what we think a good search result looks like", so those pages are the model for what to write.
4. **Write:** prompt for a 1,500-word article based on that source material.
5. **Publish:** "Publish this article to our blog using the Strapi API." Graph uses Strapi as its CMS, but he says the same process works with Webflow, WordPress or anywhere content is published. The post went live on the site.
6. **Scale:** the same process can run for every keyword. He says to tell Claude to write and publish for each one.

chunks.heading: How to make AI-written content good, not slop
chunks.text:
- Cody disagrees that this produces "AI slop": "that is a skill issue. You can 100% get good content to come out of this. You are just not providing it guardrails of what good content looks like."
- The demo version (scraped page-one results as source) is "pretty good, and these will rank".
- His higher-quality version:
  1. Have an AI interview you for about 30 minutes about the topic.
  2. Take that transcript, which holds your perspective, opinions and point of view.
  3. Combine it with the scraped page-one source material, your tone of voice, and a style guide.
  4. Have the AI write from all of it. He says this gives "an unbelievable piece of content".
- He argues people who say AI SEO content doesn't work are usually not refreshing or improving the content at all.

chunks.heading: Tracking and improving content with Graph, Google Search Console and the MCP
chunks.text:
Cody's measure-and-improve loop:
1. **Dashboard:** in graph.com, connect the Google Search Console data source and ask it to make a dashboard for the "versus" campaign. It builds a line chart.
2. **Refine by prompting:** he asked for a scorecard of impressions for blog URLs containing "versus", then added clicks to the chart. Because clicks were far smaller than impressions, he said "Move clicks to the right side of the Y axis" (impressions left, clicks right).
3. **Share and filter:** the dashboard can be filtered daily, weekly or monthly and shared with the team via a link.
4. **Optimize from inside Claude Code via the Graph MCP:** prompt: "Use the Graph MCP and find the other versus articles in the blog... use the Google Search Console data connection and pull the top five versus pages. Find the keywords related to those pages and give me insights on how I can optimize them. Look at both the content and the data from Google Search Console."
5. Claude returns optimization recommendations based on his live data. Cody says he still can't get over it when this happens.

- This is how he says you can continuously improve marketing in parallel and handle reporting for all the go-to-market work.
- Graph offers a free 14-day trial with 10 seats for the team (this is Cody's own product).

chunks.heading: Cody's operating model: parallel agents and the middle-work handoff
chunks.text:
- Expand your thinking beyond one article: any repeatable growth task (keywords, ads, publishing, analysis, reporting) can be handed to an agent and run across every item.
- Run several terminals in parallel, one agent per task, and spend your own time on ideas, direction and final polish.
- Store all API keys in one .env via CLAUDE.md so every new agent in the folder inherits the whole stack.
- Pair the doing (Claude Code publishing through APIs) with the measuring (Graph and Google Search Console via MCP) so content is refreshed based on data, not left static.
- Cody points people to gtmengineeringcourse.com, a free course and newsletter of tutorials from him and Graph on this workflow.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody walks through the full stack for an agent that runs Facebook ads: conversion tracking, Reddit-sourced pain points, AI-generated statics and UGC video, API-based uploads, a test/winners campaign structure, and a data warehouse for analysis. Key ideas: creative is the targeting under Andromeda, move conversion events down-funnel, and qualify leads in real time with server-side events.

chunks.heading: Why Facebook ad agents work now (Andromeda)
chunks.text:
- Andromeda is Facebook's AI system for choosing which ad shows to which person. It rolled out from late 2025 and had a bigger impact in the first quarter of 2026.
- Targeting is no longer interest-based. Cody says "the ad creative itself is actually the targeting mechanism." The ad and the landing page are the signals Facebook uses to pick the person.
- So the job is to hit as many personas as possible with many different ads, giving Facebook the "firepower" to find the right person.
- Cody has managed Facebook ads almost entirely through Claude Code for four months, then built an agent that runs the account: researching, making and publishing ads, turning off losers, promoting winners.
- Example result: a company selling to financial advisors cut cost per lead from about $100 to $53 over four weeks.
- The loop: publish more ads, let Facebook prospect for winning formats, trim the losers ("survival of the fittest"), put maximum budget behind winners, then remix the winning formats and repeat.

chunks.heading: Conversion tracking and the analytics stack
chunks.text:
- Install Google Tag Manager once in the site head, then deploy all tracking pixels through it. Create custom events (form submit, signup, payment) pushed to the data layer, and send them back to Facebook as conversion events.
- Data sources to unify: Facebook ads, Google Analytics or PostHog, and the CRM or CMS (WordPress, Shopify). Cody likes PostHog because it shows multi-touch paths, e.g. a user came from a Facebook ad, left, then two days later googled the brand. Google Analytics would call that organic.
- Start the conversion event up-funnel and move down toward revenue as volume grows. Example from a content repurposing software company: signup, then "uploaded a recording," then payment.
- Why not start at payment: Facebook needs enough conversion volume to learn who becomes a paying customer.
- Don't track everything. Pick one or a few leading indicators; more than five is typically too much.
- Cody has treated everything on the call as work for a coding agent: Google Tag Manager has a robust API, so Claude Code or Codex can walk through and do much of the setup. He suggests giving the transcript to the agent.

chunks.heading: Real-time lead qualification with server-side events
chunks.text:
- The "lead quality was terrible" problem happens because the algorithm optimizes for the form submission, not for the right person submitting it.
- Fix: use the Facebook Conversions API to fire a server-side event only for qualified leads.
- Example: a manufacturer with roughly four-week deal cycles. Waiting for closed-won would delay feedback by four weeks, so the agent enriches the lead in real time instead. Apify's SimilarWeb endpoint is used to check site traffic as a proxy for business quality.
- Enrichment signals by business type:
  - Consumers: zip code of the address.
  - B2B: CRM used, headcount.
  - SMBs: number of Google reviews and review velocity.
- An agent scores the lead 1 to 10. Above a threshold (e.g. 6) it counts as a good lead and the event is sent back to Facebook. This works the same for Google and LinkedIn.
- To build the scoring "shape," take the best closed-won customers (the manufacturer supplied 2,900 best customers), study secondary signals such as website traffic and branded search volume, and score new leads against that profile. The yes/no score happens within seconds.
- Cody finds waiting on closed-won sync unreliable. Some friends swear by HubSpot deep-funnel optimization, but he prefers faster learning cycles.

chunks.heading: Researching pain points and making the creative
chunks.text:
- Source messaging from the language customers already use in public forums, not guesses. Prompt a research tool to scrape Reddit for pain points and desired outcomes. Example phrases found for an AI WordPress design product: "inconsistent page builders," "overwhelming themes and builders."
- Cody demoed this in Perplexity. In production he uses the xAI API (generous free tier) wired into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor.
- Statics: Google Nano Banana through Kai AI, a single API reseller for frontier image models (Nano Banana Pro, GPT Image 2, etc.). At his volume and price point Nano Banana is "more than capable."
- Solve the cold-start problem by mining competitor ads from the Facebook, Google and LinkedIn ad libraries. Send those images in the prompt along with your brand style guide (fonts, colors, logos).
- AI avatar UGC video: HeyGen avatars plus 11 Labs voices, which he finds much better than HeyGen's own voices. Use the public UGC avatars in HeyGen and pick a voice that matches the setting.
- Seedance is being tested for video but is more expensive.
