- Process: test with cheaper models, then use more advanced models once a winning format is found.
- Scripts: give Claude the product, the top hooks and the Reddit pain points, and ask for UGC scripts. These are sent to the HeyGen API. Because the scripts use customers' own complaint language, he finds them strong.

chunks.heading: Facebook Marketing API setup and safety
chunks.text:
- The Marketing API is the bridge for uploading creative and managing the account (turning off losers, moving ads between ad sets). Bulk uploads include creative, headlines and text.
- Don't make a public app and submit it to Facebook. Use a developer app with a token for your own account.
- Setup steps:
  - Go to business.facebook.com, open Apps in the left sidebar, and create a new app (upload policy and terms, publish it as a developer app only).
  - Create a system user.
  - Assign it the app, the Facebook page, the ad account and the Instagram account.
  - Generate the system user token, which does not expire, and give it to the agent.
- Don't use the API for analysis. Hitting it with many simultaneous calls risks violating the Marketing API terms of service and getting the business or ad account banned. He says "it's not because they're against a coding agent," it's API abuse.
- Agents pulling data through the API also hit hallucinations, truncation and pagination errors.
- The rule: the API is for writes only; all analysis queries the data warehouse. Cody says he has had no issues doing it this way and calls the "agent use will get you banned" rumor false.
- The Facebook MCP exposes only a handful of endpoints (as of about four weeks before) and can break at scale. The API covers everything the UI does. A Facebook CLI exists but he hasn't used it much.

chunks.heading: Campaign structure and the testing/winners loop
chunks.text:
- Testing campaign: multiple ad sets tested at once, with about five ads per ad set competing for budget.
- Facebook now identifies the winner itself and sends most budget to it. Winners can show in about two days to a week, depending on budget and cost per action. At $100/day and $5 per signup you learn far faster than at $100/day and $70 per action.
- Move winners into a winners campaign, where they compete against each other. Watch for ad fatigue (the audience has seen it so much it stops producing).
- Every ad has a shelf life, shorter under Andromeda and especially in B2B. Push budget until marginal returns diminish.
- Remix winning concepts into new variations and feed them back into testing, forming the learning loop.
- Optimization events can differ by campaign. Cody has prospected on signups and run the winners campaign on a deeper event like demo booked or payment. He has also run demo-booked and form-submit campaigns side by side with the same creative and saw no big quality gap, though demo bookers are higher intent. Lean toward demos for sales-driven motions, signups plus in-product action for product-led growth.
- Entropy problem: left alone, the agent keeps producing similar creative. Inject "new DNA" from competitor ad libraries and tools like Viralo AI (API for trending TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts).

chunks.heading: Data warehouse, deployment and budgets
chunks.text:
- Pipe Facebook Ads, Google Analytics, CRM and other sources into a warehouse through a data pipeline. The agent queries the warehouse (conversational analytics, live dashboards) and writes to Facebook through the API.
- Open-source option: Airbyte as the pipeline and ClickHouse as the warehouse.
- Why not Supabase: it is Postgres, not built for analytical queries. With 100 million rows a query could take minutes versus milliseconds in ClickHouse. You'd also have to handle rate limits and de-duplication of overlapping chunks. Facebook ads alone has about 42 tables with hundreds of columns.
- An agent is "just software with a thinking loop with some type of live data stream." Deploy it to a host like Railway on an hourly or daily cadence.
- DIY effort: roughly two weeks for a monkey-patched usable version, four to six weeks to be enterprise-ready. He found the open-source pipeline and warehouse "an absolute pain to manage." Many CTOs won't hand over Snowflake access either.
- Cody's company, Graph, deploys this agent in five business days (and agents for Google ads, SEO, AI search, social, cold email), and just launched self-service infrastructure.
- Budgets to get signal:
  - Cost per lead examples: about $30 for an SMB seller, about $80 per demo booked.
  - Local business: about $30/day, enough data in roughly two weeks.
  - National: about $100/day to get moving.
  - The goal at the start is just signal, then remix the winners.
- For small budgets, Cody still recommends setting up the API key with your local Claude or Codex so uploading creative (which he says is about four hours of work for 10 ads) isn't manual. Move to a cloud agent once it works, since the work is continuous.
- Attribution tools like Hyros audit each channel's claimed conversions. Cody calls attribution "an unsolvable thing" and says marketing is about building "digital gravity." He expects media management autonomy to come to every platform, but notes ad platforms' incentives are misaligned with advertisers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains how startups should use transactional channels (paid ads, cold email) for fast revenue, then invest in content, creators and SEO to build brand mass before arbitrage disappears and acquisition costs climb. He also covers AI search as a scrape of Google's top results, and automating only after a manual process is proven.

chunks.heading: Digital gravity: building brand mass instead of a linear funnel
chunks.text:
Cody's framing, discussed here with Jordan Mix of Late Checkout, is that buyers don't move down a linear funnel. They orbit a brand.

- Each asset (an ad, a video, a newsletter, a podcast) is another orbit ring, and each ring is a mini-funnel that adds mass.
- The more mass a brand has, the more people get pulled in, and the stickier it becomes in the buyer's head.
- Buyers don't sit at one point. Cody compares the orbits to ellipses: at different moments a buyer is closer to a purchase. The brand has to be in front of them constantly so it's there at the moment of readiness.
- He ties this to the law of seven (seeing a brand seven times before buying), and notes people are probably retargeted 20+ times before purchasing.
- The aim is to "make as much mass on the internet related to your brand in the niche that you are as possible" so you have maximum surface area during product discovery.
- Funnels still work, but they only give linear growth ("I put a dollar in and X comes out"). Nonlinear growth needs branded search and gravity.

chunks.heading: Transactional marketing vs. brand: the arbitrage seesaw
chunks.text:
- Early on, Cody looks for arbitrage with "tomorrow revenue", which he calls transactional marketing: paid ads, cold email, cold DMs, and sometimes influencer marketing depending on category. You act, and you get paid the next day.
- The "law of shitty clickthroughs": other people spot the same arbitrage, so the cost of acquiring a user rises over time across all transactional channels.
- His example: signups costing $1 became $5 twelve months later (5x).
- The hedge is a content-marketing flywheel that drives branded search and brand discovery. This lowers customer acquisition cost as the arbitrage fades. He describes it as a seesaw: arbitrage goes down, brand goes up.
- Sequencing advice to startups: don't invest in SEO pre-seed. "You don't even know if you're going to be here in two years," and SEO may not pay off for around 18 months. Start with transactional channels, then layer in content and brand.

chunks.heading: Where to start: test channels, then automate what works
chunks.text:
Cody's order of operations for a startup:

1. Find where the target customer spends time online.
2. Pick about three channels and test them.
3. Pour everything into the one or two that work best.
4. Only then automate the proven process with AI.

- Rule: "you need to operate it before you can automate it." Don't automate without a defined goal or knowing it works. This is "do things that don't scale", then automate.
- His Facebook ads example: scrape Reddit for pain points (e.g. why people hate Zendesk), generate around 100 static ads with the OpenAI image API, load them into a campaign, have an agent turn off the bottom 90% of performers and move winners to a conversion campaign, then look at what the winners have in common and repeat.
- There's no course for vibe marketing. The "course" is picking something you do a lot and working out how to automate it.

chunks.heading: Vibe marketing tactics and tooling
chunks.text:
- n8n is JSON-based, so Cody has Perplexity write the workflow JSON, which he pastes into n8n to skip the connectivity setup. Example prompt: scrape YouTube channel emails with an Apify actor from a keyword list, validate them with MillionVerifier, and send them to Instantly for a cold email campaign.
- He says this is early and not always perfect. He found the trick about two weeks before recording.
- A second pattern he saw from another marketer: n8n as the backend and Lovable as the front-end dashboard. The marketer used it to screenshot competitor ads daily, surface new ads and what competitors are testing, and view the insights in one place. Cody sees this as internal tooling a marketer would actually use instead of Retool or Metabase. Lovable pulls data via an n8n HTTP/REST endpoint.
- He is skeptical of most agents: they are "automation with embedded AI", often a human in the loop reviewing curated data. His definition: an agent is where a decision a human used to make is handed to AI inside a workflow.
- The only real agent-like use case he's seen: agents running LinkedIn or Twitter accounts. They research topics by scraping Reddit, write a controversial post (he prompts Claude 3.7 Sonnet for an "unhinged post that is controversial"), schedule it, then read impression data, deep-research the best performers, and loop.

chunks.heading: AI SEO: LLMs mostly scrape Google, so it's still the same game
chunks.text:
- Cody cites a conversation with Profound's co-founder: about 95% of searches on AI answer engines involve web scraping, and ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Perplexity largely return an aggregate of Google page one and two results.
- Reason: Google has 25 years of signal on which content best answers a query, and LLM companies will lean on it rather than index the whole web (maybe later, not now).
- He is skeptical of "AI SEO" agencies: many are just prompting ChatGPT to check whether you show up.
- Tools like Profound generate a synthetic corpus of question variations (AI search is question-based more than keyword-based), then score your surface area, show gaps, and recommend content. The action is to make content for the gaps.
- Bottom-of-funnel software keywords drive signups: "X vs Y", "X alternative", "how to [product]", "best X for Y". Mention your own brand inside those articles (e.g. a tool that integrates with Rippling inside a "Rippling vs Deel" post). Ranking on page one or two raises the chance of appearing in AI answers.
- Habit SEO (his SaaS SEO service) does keyword research, writing, publishing and optimizing of these bottom-of-funnel articles.

chunks.heading: Creator flywheels and YouTube-led discovery
chunks.text:
- Match the content channel to where people discover the product. For an AI video editor, YouTube first; LinkedIn is probably the wrong place, but Instagram Reels might work.
- Then ask how to automate production to maximize volume in that channel.
- Creators chase outliers. If you make an outlier video, others copy and remix it, producing a cascade of videos you didn't pay for (e.g. a startup-ideas podcast spotlighting a tool, then about 40 videos on it two weeks later).
- His founder example: a Jungle Scout-for-Etsy tool whose entire growth strategy is YouTube. About 100 creators in an affiliate program, each doing a video a month, produced roughly a thousand videos about the product, which he says the founder "couldn't afford that ever".
- The game for a founder is to find a repeatable process for outlier-style content, then let the knock-on effect happen.
- Companies increasingly hire in-house creators as a job title (Vio is cited as doing this early). The risk is that the creator becomes popular and leaves, as with Triple Whale and Tommy Clark.
- Hedge by combining in-house creators and contracted creators with other strategies. You own the IP, but the face of the brand can walk.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues AI automation agencies are a bad business (one-time project revenue, hard sales, 12-18 month lifespan) and that productized monthly services delivered with AI tooling are better. He walks through six niches (med spas, beauty e-commerce ads, nutrition coach social, webinar lead magnets, data analytics, voice agents) with delivery stack, pricing and acquisition plays.

chunks.heading: Why productized AI services beat AI automation agencies
chunks.text:
- Cody says he has watched many friends start AI automation agencies. In his telling, they last 12 to 18 months and then pivot hard into a productized service.
- He thinks the business model is weak:
  - You need strong top-of-funnel lead generation.
  - You need strong sales skills, because the tickets are fairly high and the sale is traditional.
  - Revenue is one-time and project-based, not recurring. It is "a hard business to build and scale."
- His alternative is a productized service with a fixed monthly deliverable, produced with AI tooling. It gives recurring revenue, can run remotely, and removes the constant scramble for lead volume to cover payroll.
- He says a solo operator can plausibly reach $40K to $80K a month within about 6 months with this model.
- Every idea he gives follows the same pattern:
  - a niche with high customer value
  - an AI-automated deliverable on a monthly cadence
  - public case-study content for acquisition
  - reporting tied as close to revenue (usually leads) as possible

chunks.heading: Idea 1: Med spa marketing ($2K-3K/month)
chunks.text:
- Med spas average roughly $1.4M to $2M in revenue per location. Customer lifetime value is about $6,000, so clients can afford a retainer.
- Purchase decisions come mostly from paid social (Instagram, Facebook, maybe TikTok) and local SEO, so the service covers two things: Facebook ads and Google Maps optimization.
- **Ad creative (about 10 new pieces a month):**
  - Static images come from the ChatGPT API.
  - Video comes from HeyGen or Arc Ads.
  - Research comes from Perplexity, scraping Reddit and social for the problems, benefits and language around each med spa treatment.
  - Scripts and descriptions are written by AI.
  - Nothing here needs a graphic designer or video editor.
- **Google Maps:**
  - Searching "med spa" in any location shows a map pack, so ranking in the top three matters.
  - Optimize the profile for reviews, keywords in the listing, and images of the physical location.
  - Add directory/citation listings (name, address, phone) on sites like Foursquare. Cody mentions local rank.so for one-click submission to all of them.
- **Reporting:** report on leads and new revenue. This is how you justify the fee. He suggests Looker Studio or Graph, a "chat with data" dashboard tool his team launched that week.
- **Acquisition:**
  - Med spa contact details are public, so you can cold-reach them.
  - Run Facebook ads targeting people who work at med spas, with case studies and a lead magnet PDF that walks through your exact process. Readers see it is painful to do themselves and hire you.
  - Post YouTube case studies with titles like "I grew this med spa by X revenue from Facebook ads" or "I got 100 leads from Google Maps for this med spa." He says "just talk your book."

chunks.heading: Idea 2: Facebook ad creative for beauty e-commerce brands ($3K-5K/month)
chunks.text:
- Beauty brands burn through creative fast, because audiences see the same ad too many times. Fresh creative is business-critical, and e-commerce ad agencies are a fast-growing category.
- **AI workflow:**
  - Use a research agent (many n8n-style builds exist on YouTube) to scrape product reviews, extract pain points, find hooks and run competitor analysis.
  - Make the videos with MakeUGC.ai. Its differentiator is that the on-screen person can hold the actual product, which beauty brands need.
  - Deliver something like 20 ads a month, plus analysis of top performers and remixes of them.
- **Where the hooks come from:**
  - Scraping competitors' ad libraries makes everyone's ads look the same.
  - Cody prefers mining Reddit for odd phrasing, for example how someone describes an acne cream. Use Claude to extract the quote and turn it into the hook.
  - Copy competitors' formats (selfie video, static) but not their language, to get pattern disruption in the feed.
- **Pricing context:** traditional human UGC agencies charge about $6,000 for five videos, so an AI offer with more volume at a lower price wins.
- **Strategy:** more creative variations, tested faster, with broad targeting on Facebook, TikTok or Twitter ads. He argues the platform algorithms find buyers better than manual targeting does, so your job is the creative production process.
- **Acquisition:**
  - Publish YouTube breakdowns of how you use the research agent.
  - Post LinkedIn and Twitter breakdowns of ad types and formulas, with a discovery-call CTA.
  - He also endorses "comment to get the asset" posts, such as "I scraped 100 beauty ads, comment 'ads' for the library." It can be a plain digital download or a Google Drive link after an email capture.

chunks.heading: Idea 3: Organic social media management for nutrition coaches (about $2K/month)
chunks.text:
- Cody is "obsessed" with nutrition and health coaches. He believes any coaching business is disruptable by AI.
- Coaches serve about 100 clients a month, but lifetime value per client is small (about $1,000). That means they need an organic strategy, because paid ads are hard to justify at that value.
- Searches for "nutrition coach" have grown steadily over the last couple of years.
- **Deliverable:**
  - One post a day.
  - AI-generated food/recipe images (the Pinterest-style approach) combined with client stories.
  - A lead magnet such as a 100-day recipe ebook, which captures emails into a drip nurture.
  - Success is measured in impressions and leads.
- **Tooling:** Assembly (assembly.com) lets you connect many social accounts in one portal. Clients approve each post in a client-facing view, so a solo operator could run the whole business on it. Cody thinks one person can manage 10 accounts.
- **Acquisition:**
  - Cold DMs to nutrition coaches on Instagram, where he sees the ecosystem living.
  - Facebook ads targeting nutrition coaches.
  - An email-gated educational YouTube video.
  - YouTube case studies ("how I grew a client's social account and the leads we got").

chunks.heading: Idea 4: Lead magnets from webinars
chunks.text:
- Over half of B2B marketers hosted a webinar in the last year. Their pain points are:
  - getting people to register
  - getting people to show up
  - doing something with the recording afterward
- **The service:** turn a company's back catalog of webinars into ebooks, white papers and other lead magnets, delivered as a monthly quota (for example 4 or 8 a month). Cody describes it as turning "rotting fruit" into juice.
- **Production:** transcribe the webinars with AI tools, turn the transcripts into bolded lists, and format them into branded PDFs.
- **Acquisition:**
  - Do the work first. Reach out to companies running webinars with an ebook you already made from their webinar, then offer the service on a discovery call. You "show your work before you're even working with" them.
  - On LinkedIn, post a "comment to get my webinar marketing guide" lead magnet, since their measure of success is attendance.
- **Why webinars work:**
  - Free educational content builds trust, especially for high-ticket sales.
  - Short-form video will never sell a $3K to $10K+ per month service. Use it to feed top of funnel into long-form content. Webinars can be the bridge.
  - Cody's example is Rupa Health. They grew an email newsletter on the back of the podcast, then promoted weekly webinars through it. About 6,000 people registered and about 1,000 attended each time. The webinar was basically a demo of how to use the product (how to do a lab test the product offers).

chunks.heading: Idea 5: Data analytics as a service for SMBs
chunks.text:
- Businesses sit on large amounts of data they cannot interpret, and more founders want to make data-driven decisions but lack the skills.
- **Offer:** "unlimited data analytics" for SMBs at a flat monthly fee.
  - The client asks questions in a Slack channel or message thread, and you answer as fast as possible.
  - You build dashboards and a weekly KPI report.
  - Data sources include the CRM, QuickBooks (cash flow, P&L), customer counts and Google Analytics.
- **Tooling:**
  - Claude or ChatGPT connected to data through MCPs.
  - Looker Studio, Tableau or Power BI (aggressive learning curves, but tutorials are on YouTube).
  - Graph, which he says turns a connected data source or CSV into dashboards and insights.
- **Example customer:** a local operator running 10 children's swimming locations who wants to know cash flow and P&L.

chunks.heading: Cross-cutting content and distribution lessons
chunks.text:
- **Faceless video works.** Cody's winery-industry friends run faceless ads: a voiceover monologue over social footage of the tasting room and vineyards. It feels like organic content and performs "absolutely ripping."
- **Static image plus audio works.** One of his Instagram posts, a static image of a tweet with audio, got 195,000 likes. He says the content has to be outstanding for any of these formats to work.
- **Staying current is part of the value.** Formats from six months ago stop working. Part of what clients pay for is that you keep a pulse on what currently works and refresh the content, because you see many clients at once.
- **Case-study content is the main acquisition engine.** Show the work publicly on YouTube (with numbers in the title), then LinkedIn and Twitter, with a discovery call or lead magnet as the CTA.
- **"Comment to get it" posts** on LinkedIn create an engagement flywheel that generates leads.
- **Prove value close to revenue.** The closer your reporting is to leads or revenue, the easier it is to show the work is worth the money.

chunks.heading: Voice agents and agentic browsing
chunks.text:
- Cody is most excited about agents that actually finish tasks "to the last mile," after a lot of vaporware. He has been testing which agent platforms really get there.
- He likes Perplexity Comet because it lets you do recurring browser tasks without an automation tool. His example is accepting LinkedIn connection requests every morning and sending a set message.
- He increasingly wants to talk to websites and companies (he uses Superwhisper for most communication) and wonders whether apps become a conversational layer over information.
- **Voice-agent example, medical:**
  - His brother's company in the medical space built a large knowledge document and a voice agent that anyone can phone.
  - It answers every buyer question and is trained to educate rather than sell. Callers stay on for about 20 minutes, then transfer to a human call center to book.
  - A human could never learn that much specific information.
- **Voice-agent example, restaurants:**
  - A friend's company builds voice agents that take restaurant orders, send payment links and enter orders into the POS (such as Toast). It is growing fast.
  - Customers want the agent to sound like the brand. A New York bagel shop wanted the original owner's thick accent, and a New Jersey pizzeria wanted an in-store feel.
- **Business idea:** help companies become voice-first by building branded voice agents with characters, lore and origin stories, using platforms like Vapi.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues the marketing funnel is the wrong model and proposes "digital gravity": build mass through continuous content and ads everywhere your customer is, so people orbit and eventually convert. He walks through a B2B stack (scraped lists, custom-match ads, cold email, podcast as media business) and a consumer stack (UGC ads, influencer arbitrage, programmatic SEO).

chunks.heading: Digital gravity: why Cody replaces the marketing funnel
chunks.text:
- Cody argues the funnel is "the entirely wrong way to think about marketing." People don't enter at the top and exit as buyers. They interact with a brand, drift away, get pulled back, do "three rotations," then touch down and buy.
- His replacement is "digital gravity": building mass on the internet through content and marketing everywhere the customer shows up. More mass means more influence in the niche, and more passers-by get pulled into orbit.
- Touchdowns turn into revenue. Revenue is reinvested into more mass, which creates a growth flywheel.
- He says he used the same approach for a musician (helping get him signed to Sony) and at Rupa Health (Employee 6, multi-hundred-million-dollar exit).
- Long purchase cycles make the funnel picture worse. When he did marketing for doors and windows, a hotel group buying 2,000 shower bases decided over about five years.
- He says "campaign" is a World War II hangover: a campaign starts and ends. His view is "you're not doing marketing, you're marketing," continuously, like an app or website that is never "done."
- Email is the one channel that can't be taken back after sending. His team's rule: three people must proof the copy before any send.

chunks.heading: Resources by stage: where to market
chunks.text:
- Funded companies have time, money and resources, so the answer to "where should I market?" is "everywhere."
- Bootstrapped founders usually have time and mental energy but no money. Their resources shift as the company scales.
- Cody's volume rule: marketing is a surface-area game. He cites a TikTok Shop agency owner whose best affiliates post about 10x more videos than low performers.
- His batting-average analogy: a .300 hitter who swings once rarely touches the ball, but swinging 10 times gets them on base.
- He calls "one Instagram account" and "a blog post a week" old-school thinking.
- For founders who have raised money, he says making yourself famous is "the game you're playing." It makes the next round easier. At Rupa, growing the CEO's and the company's Instagram brought healthtech investors inbounding to ask how they did it.

chunks.heading: B2B playbook, layer 1: scraped list, matched ads, cold email
chunks.text:
- Start with a small target audience, often around 50,000 people. Scrape every email. Apollo.io is about $99/month for roughly 10,000 emails, with industry filters. LinkedIn also works.
- Upload the list as a custom match audience to Google Ads, Facebook Ads, LinkedIn Ads and wherever else they spend time. On Facebook he expects about 30 to 40% of emails to match. Ads then run indefinitely in the background.
- Ad format: UGC-style AI avatar ads aimed at the pain points. Tools: HeyGen for the avatar and ElevenLabs for the voice. The founder makes a digital clone of themselves, because "people buy from people, not brands."
- The ad story is a hero's journey: "I had this problem, I went on a discovery journey, and I ended up here, better."
- Test about 100 variations (hooks, settings, backgrounds, pain points). Put 80% of spend on the best performer by lowest CPC and keep 20% always testing. Promote any new winner into the 80% campaign.
- Cold email the same list at the same time, using the same problem-solution angle as the ads.
- Infrastructure he describes:
  - Mailreef, a server for managing sending inboxes, about $400/month for 50,000 cold emails.
  - Smartlead or Instantly, about $89/month, as the sending software.
  - Around 30 domains with 5 inboxes each, all sending under the same name in variations.
- He separates three email types and keeps them on separate domains:
  - Transactional: send from the core app domain.
  - Newsletter: send from its own domain.
  - Cold: send from throwaway domains. Founders often cold email from the core domain, then land transactional mail like password resets in spam.
- Both channels reinforce each other. Prospects often see the ads months later and search their inbox for the original cold email, then come back as a lead.
- He rejects the fear of "burning the audience": "they don't care about you at all," and "cold email doesn't work" is wrong when messaging is specific. Example: dock management software for shipping yards. The message named a daily pain (dock check-in) and one in five recipients said yes.

chunks.heading: B2B playbook, layer 2: build a media arm
chunks.text:
- His core idea is to layer growth curves. After ads and cold email, add a podcast and newsletter to the same list, then clip the podcast into shorts for LinkedIn and Instagram.
- Content source: record customer conversations in a slightly more formal setting. They already contain the industry's pain points.
- Newsletter format: import about 200 contacts a day. Subject line is "podcast + episode name." Body is "Hey [name], the newest episode of X is live," then a one-paragraph summary and five key takeaways.
- Tools he names: MailerLite and Beehiiv (he has also used others). Because the content is industry-specific, it reads as educational and is "way more approachable" than a transactional cold email.
- Rupa Health results:
  - Podcast reached 180,000 downloads/month after 6 months and ranked top 20 in US medical podcasts.
  - Big labs that would not take their calls started inbounding. Cody used the media placements as leverage to negotiate down the fee percentages Rupa paid.
  - They sold ad placements in the podcast and newsletter to health brands. Athletic Greens subsidized the entire growth team's cost. He calls this "negative CAC," turning a cost center into a profit center.
- He says every B2B company should build a media business. Examples he gives: Arrow Electronics (about $6 billion market cap, with a large media arm), Red Bull, and Y Combinator, which he describes as a media company selling venture capital.
- Repurposing: his product Swell AI takes the long recording and produces clips, show notes, blog posts and white papers, which are then scheduled across every platform. This replaces what used to take a team of five.
- A newsletter case: an 18-month client in life sciences has a 130,000-person list. Each send drives about 10,000 clicks, sent twice a week, so roughly 80,000 clicks a month (rounded to 100,000), at about $450. He says that audience pays about $5 a click elsewhere.
- A podcast lead from a Fortune 500 company led to a $2.2M proposal, which they accepted.
- The first 90 days of a podcast show little, and "you're just trusting the process."

chunks.heading: Social and Instagram follower ads
chunks.text:
- Short-form content from TikTok or Reels posted on LinkedIn can go viral right now.
- Instagram-only follower ads: run for Impressions, with a call to action in the caption to follow the account for more content like this. Cody says this grew a musician's Instagram at around $0.30 per follower, and grew Rupa's account to 100,000 followers using the same method.
- Reason: the closer an ad is to native content, the less you pay for it. That is why he tests 100 variations, to find content that doesn't feel like an ad but still produces revenue.
- Larger accounts also earn free impressions.
- Categories are mental real estate. People hold only two or three brands per category. HubSpot's "inbound marketing" is his example. He advises attaching to an idea people already hold and evolving it, because creating a new category costs too much.

chunks.heading: Consumer playbook: huge TAM and impulse pricing
chunks.text:
- Cody's warning: don't start in consumer. "You have to be unbelievable at marketing to win," it's far more competitive, but winning there is the best outcome.
- It requires a huge total addressable market, because content has to be broad enough to reach a large share of the population. His example is a women's health app where about one in three women have the problem. Ebook downloads there cost about $0.40, then he upsells into the product. Ebooks can be written with AI and published with Gamma.
- Pricing tactic: charge $7.99 a week (about $29 a month). It sells as an impulse purchase and turns into roughly three months of revenue. A $10 CAC then yields a roughly 10x payout over the customer lifetime.
- Paid acquisition: Facebook and TikTok ads optimized for the signup or paid action via deep link. Run many variations.
- UGC creators: about $1,000/month per creator for a video a day, cross-posted across their accounts. They act as a test bed for what goes viral. Format: hook, pain point, then the product as hero. The goal is an ad that feels like entertainment plus education.
- Remix the winners: spin up about 10 TikTok accounts, use ChatGPT to rewrite scripts, HeyGen for the avatar, ElevenLabs for audio, and CapCut to remove the green-screen background and put the app behind the avatar.
- Pick a unique name nobody else uses so you don't compete with similarly named companies on Google. Many viewers Google the product after seeing a video.
- Pixel every site visitor (Facebook, TikTok, Google) to retarget indefinitely, add an email capture for a nurture sequence, and use customer-match lists.

chunks.heading: Influencer arbitrage and programmatic SEO
chunks.text:
- Influencer outreach at scale:
  - Search YouTube by category keyword, scrape creator emails from their bios, and cold email them for pricing. Do the same on Instagram with a tool called IG leads, plus TikTok.
  - Roughly 10 to 20% reply with pricing. Build a table of price versus average views to find mispriced creators, since it is an imperfect market.
  - Deal structure that works for him: a 3-video package (for example $1,500) plus an affiliate commission, with about 30% mentioned and recurring payouts. Three videos build enough trust, and the recurring commission creates a moat, since competitors would have to buy creators out of the contract.
- Benchmark: Cal AI and Rizz GPT founders told him they pay about $5 CPM, versus roughly $10 average TikTok CPM when buying through ads.
- Programmatic SEO (Cal AI example: diet plans, nutrition plans, weight loss, calorie counts):
  - It works once the site has domain authority around 40 or higher, built from backlinks, so you can rank for low-difficulty long-tail keywords.
  - Process: scrape what ranks on page one for the target keyword, feed it into a context window, create an outline, then write the post section by section (he finds this gives the best quality and readability).
  - Publish at scale (he mentions 10,000 articles). When a page gets its first session, a human edits it. His team has an SEO/content specialist whose job is rewriting anything humans have seen.
  - Conversion: a CTA after the first paragraph, one call-out in every scroll frame, and a full-screen popup at 25 to 50% scroll, plus pixel everyone for retargeting.
- He also mentions a sober-tracking app, Sunflower Sober (with an AI "sponsor"), growing quickly through Facebook ads at a sensible price.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains why For You page algorithms make creators with no followers cheaper and more effective than influencers. He covers the CPM math, how to find and manage creators, the tool stack, which products fit, and how it lifts branded search.

chunks.heading: Why creators beat influencers: the cost-per-view arbitrage
chunks.text:
Cody argues that social has shifted from a "who you follow" social graph to "what you're interested in" For You page algorithms (TikTok changed this; Instagram Reels, Twitter, LinkedIn and YouTube now work the same way). Platforms do this because it keeps people on-platform longer, and attention is what they sell. For brands, the value is in "somebody that understands your niche and how to get views and traction within the category", not in follower counts.

His worked example (illustrative numbers):
- **Influencer:** about 100,000 followers (the table he reads out says 10,000), charges $2,000 for one post. Only about 1 in 10 posts goes viral, so one post might get around 30,000 views.
- **Creator:** starts with zero followers, paid $900 a month for one post per day (about 30 posts) across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts. About 10% of posts outperform, so more chances to hit an outlier.
- Cody's claim: people don't make purchase decisions largely off influencers. They buy from creators who consistently talk about a topic. Influencers only work at massive scale (a Kim Kardashian), and those people make their own products because they know their audience is valuable.
- Because For You page content is shown to whoever the algorithm thinks will stay, a creator with zero followers can reach people they never could before.

chunks.heading: The CPM math versus paid ads
chunks.text:
- Average Facebook CPM is "about $6 depending on which category you're in". $900 of Facebook spend buys about 150,000 impressions.
- If a creator gets about 500,000 aggregate impressions for $900, the CPM is roughly $2 (he states the figure loosely), which is cheaper than Facebook.
- His TikTok illustration: an $8 TikTok ad CPM versus about $2 via creator marketing. "That's a better allocation of the limited resources that I have."
- Core framing: this is marketing arbitrage, the same game as in his other videos. Find a channel where attention costs less than the market rate.
- Organic content converts better than paid because people prefer buying from content that feels organic. His analogy: Meta ads are a billboard in a busy town square, while this is handing out value-add flyers (like the top 10 restaurants in the area, one of which is yours).

chunks.heading: The compounding flywheel across 5-10 creators
chunks.text:
- Don't hire one creator. Work with 5 to 10, each posting one video a day.
- With 10 videos dropping daily, about one will be an outlier, "based on the math". Share that learning with every other creator so they remix the winning format.
- More creators means more surface area for learning which content types produce reach for the product.
- Promote winners to paid: "If they work organically, they're also going to work in a paid setting." This turns the program into a UGC content engine for ads.
- Keep top performers on retainer, drop the worst, then restart the cycle with new creators.
- Example: his friend's company Focus Tree (a phone-free study/productivity app) uses exactly this strategy across hundreds of TikTok accounts. Cody says it grew to around two million users, but he's unsure of the current figure.
- Format tip: make ads look native, as if recorded on an iPhone and edited in CapCut or in the Instagram app. Brands find this uncomfortable because they want polished, "red camera" production, but a 20-year-old creator paying for school is the model. Creators typically hold deals with several brands (for example five brands at about $1,000 each) and post multiple videos a day.

chunks.heading: The playbook: finding, hiring and managing creators
chunks.text:
1. **Find creators already in your category.** Scroll TikTok and watch niche videos until the algorithm silos you into the space, then note the recurring faces. Larger categories (like real estate investing) have more creators than smaller ones (like vibe coding).
2. **Reach out** by DM or the email in their bio: "I want to hire you on a cost per video basis, a video per day for $900."
3. **Creator starts a fresh account** from zero followers, posting in your category.
4. **Keep winners, cut losers** and repeat the cycle.
- Lovable as an example: Cody points to a "coding_dev.app" style account as a likely test of this approach, though it may be run by an in-house team or a clipper. He is skeptical of the "clipper" model: "I think all the data is fake."
- Management is the main pain point. Common fix: make your best performer a manager of the other creators, paid more to ensure the team delivers daily and to share outlier videos with the group.
- Many teams manage creators in a Discord server or WhatsApp group.
- Hiring someone who understands this is hard. The people involved are often flaky 22-year-olds, so expect friction.

chunks.heading: The tool stack
chunks.text:
- **Stormy AI:** finds creators by category on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, DMs them, and negotiates pricing, which removes the biggest time sink.
- **Shortimize and viral.app:** creators submit videos and the tools track views and engagement to measure campaign success.
- **Virlo (pronunciation unsure) and Sandcastles AI:** scrape and aggregate TikToks, Shorts and Reels so you can search for outlier videos in your category, then hand them to creators to remix for your brand.
- Management layer: Discord or WhatsApp group.

chunks.heading: Which products this works for (and which it doesn't)
chunks.text:
- **Best fit:** B2C and mobile apps, and products with one killer feature (his example: Incogni, which blocks data brokers from selling your data).
- **Requirement:** an impulse purchase that can happen on a phone, with no learning curve. The viewer can search, install and understand the value instantly.
- **E-commerce:** works at price points around $29. For TikTok Shop, find shop creators, pay per video, and add an affiliate commission on what they drive.
- **Poor fit:** products with a learning curve that need long-form education to use.

chunks.heading: Layering it into B2B and web apps: brand search and "digital gravity"
chunks.text:
- Cody's friend's API company uses this approach and it works. It builds top-of-funnel branded search and a discovery flywheel.
- His concept of "digital gravity": create as much surface area for your brand within your category as possible and layer strategies on top of each other.
- TikTok and Instagram reach so many daily active users in the US that some share of your target customers will see the content, which builds mental real estate in your category and lifts branded search.
- Measure it in Google Search Console by filtering queries that contain your brand name. E-commerce brands see branded search on Amazon spike after a TikTok goes viral.
- The ROI is hard to quantify, but it works if the goal is "have an entire industry know that I exist".
- Suggested sequencing: start with the YouTube creator strategy (top of funnel awareness and bottom of funnel conversion), then layer the short-form creator strategy on top.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider walks through a step-by-step playbook: scrape emails of YouTube creators in your niche, cold-email them for a 3-video package plus affiliate commission, find the underpriced ones, and put the winners on retainer. It works because creator attention is mispriced and affiliate links make ROI trackable.

chunks.heading: Why YouTube creators plus affiliate commissions work for early customers
chunks.text:
- Cody calls YouTube creators plus affiliate marketing "one of the best ways to go about getting your first customers", especially for SMB products or tools with one killer feature.
- The reason: it is "basically a product demo that's in disguise." He reaches out to creators, has them make videos about the product, pays a flat fee per video, and adds an affiliate commission on the traffic they drive.
- He calls it an inefficient market. Creators sold through aggregators, networks or agencies know their value. Independent creators, especially smaller ones with 10,000 to 50,000 subscribers, "don't know how to price themselves."
- Example math: contact 100 creators, about 50 respond, and around 10 underprice themselves so much that they are "basically a marketing arbitrage." He then finds the winners among those 10 and puts them on retainer.
- ROI is trackable, unlike short-form (TikTok, Reels, Shorts), where viewers see a video and then search Google. With a 10-minute YouTube video and an affiliate link in the description, he can see the exact dollars each creator drives.
- Scale claim: a friend (Cody McGuffy, Everbe) went from zero to 6 million ARR in 18 months, bootstrapped, using only this strategy. Cody's framing: with 100 creators posting about your product monthly, "you're going to be everywhere overnight."

chunks.heading: Finding creators and getting their emails
chunks.text:
- Start by searching YouTube for videos in the product's category (his example: Google Ads tutorials for a tool sold to people who run Google Ads). Filter to videos of 4 to 20 minutes from the current month. Every creator making that content is a prospect.
- Creator emails are visible via "view email" on the channel profile, but it sits behind a captcha and YouTube limits it to roughly 8 opens per 24-hour rolling window.
- Ways around the limit:
  - Do it manually: about 8 a day, roughly 50 a week, so about 100 creators contacted in two weeks.
  - Hire someone on Fiverr. He paid one person $125 to scrape 10,000 emails in a category.
  - Use a YouTube channel email scraper endpoint on RapidAPI, which he believes uses offshore human captcha-solving. He has used it before.
- For automation: scrape via RapidAPI, load the contacts into Instantly, and send the cold email from there.
- Stormy AI (founder Robert) is a tool he recommends. It searches for creators who have already made videos on a topic (e.g. Claude Code), finds their emails, drafts the outreach, and negotiates pricing with an AI agent before bringing in the human to confirm. He describes it as early stage and useful for a one-person team.

chunks.heading: The outreach email and follow-up cadence
chunks.text:
- Subject line: "paid collaboration", all lowercase. He says they have tested everything and this performs best.
- Body, in his words: a short note like "hey [name], I love the content you're posting on YouTube. Can I get a cost breakdown for a three video package and I'll give you an affiliate commission of 30%." He dictated it with Superwhisper.
- Send about 10 follow-ups in different phrasings. Creators are "constantly getting blasted", so persistent follow-up is required, even though it is "a pain in the ass."
- Ask them for their price first rather than naming one.

chunks.heading: Why ask for a three-video package plus an affiliate commission
chunks.text:
- Three videos beat one. A single video is "a flash in the pan" for the audience. Three videos at different angles, spread across six to eight weeks and mixed in with their other content, signal that the creator actually uses the tool.
- The affiliate commission does two jobs:
  - It lets him track the ROI each creator produces.
  - It creates lock-in. A creator earning, say, 10 grand a month in commissions is uncomfortable raising rates or taking an exclusivity deal from a competitor, because it would hurt the relationship. Good creators naturally grow and raise prices with other brands, so this keeps his pricing from rising.
- For tracking affiliates he suggests Rewardful as one of the best-priced options for a small or vibe-coded tool, and says most tools work in a similar way.

chunks.heading: Spotting underpriced creators and negotiating
chunks.text:
- Put every creator's quote for the three-video package in a spreadsheet next to their subscriber count. Divide cost by subscribers to see what he pays to reach each audience, then rank to find the cheapest per audience.
- Better still is a composite of subscribers and average views per video; he typically uses both.
- Negotiation tips:
  - Counter low. "I would cut that in half and work your way up from there."
  - Often ask "what can you afford / what can you pay," since many creators don't know their price.
  - Or say "creators of your size we typically pay X per video." If they come back higher, it turns into a negotiation.
- Example of the underpricing he looks for: a creator who says "Hell yeah, I'll do it for $200 a video" when they should be charging around a grand.
- On CPMs: he doesn't focus on them. He cares more about whether the creator already makes content in the category, because they understand the audience and how to talk to it. A smaller but highly engaged audience that trusts the creator converts very well.
- He treats such a video as an asynchronous, evergreen video sales letter, product demo or webinar that "lives forever."

chunks.heading: Turning winners into retainers and scaling the cycle
chunks.text:
- After the first cohort, check the affiliate data. Of roughly 10 creators worked with, he expects two to three to drive about 80% of the revenue.
- Go back to those winners and propose a retainer of one video per month. He says they will "100% say yes" because creators want recurring money.
- Then repeat: contact another 100, find the 10 who underprice themselves, work with them, pick the two winners, and add them to the retainer list. Over time this grows to about 100 creators on retainer, each one a known ROI-positive source, with 100 videos a month dropping in the niche.
- He describes this as astroturfing the category with content. A knock-on effect: when one video goes viral, around 10 other creators make videos reacting to it, and many join the affiliate program, creating a "spiderweb effect."
- Operating at scale gets hard because he must verify that videos actually dropped. Tactics: a form submission when a video goes live, which feeds a Make automation, plus a spreadsheet pulling in each video's views and graphing the impact.

chunks.heading: Mispriced attention and why timing matters
chunks.text:
- He frames the whole play as finding "mispriced attention": high-quality attention that is relatively cheap. The pattern he cites is "find misaligned things that don't make sense and then exploit it as aggressively as they can."
- Examples he gives of businesses built on mispriced attention: Wish.com became a billion-dollar company in about 18 months on Facebook ads, when 1 cent link clicks were available and nobody else advertised cheap imported goods. Zynga is cited as the same strategy.
- Caution on competition: "by the time you're hearing about it, it's already cooked." Do not buy a course on this; "they're just reselling their used clothes."
- Where it works best: a niche with a specific pain point (his example: depot resellers). Highly competitive categories like dropshipping will be very expensive.
- Even in competitive spaces there is room (he compares it to real estate in 2008). You just need a process to contact thousands of creators, for instance 1,000 or 10,000, to find the underpriced ones.
- He says it is currently "medium rare" rather than fully cooked.

chunks.heading: Work with creators who already have success
chunks.text:
- His view is that people now discover products passively, through For You-style feeds, rather than actively searching.
- A creator has to balance getting distribution on the platform with giving enough entertainment and value to earn reach.
- His advice: "don't hire somebody for this, find somebody that's already doing this and work with them." They have already figured out the algorithm for that category, and it is much harder to train someone to understand the YouTube algorithm than to give an already-successful creator resources to include your product.
- Do not start from ground zero.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider walks through several one-person business ideas: an AI avatar UGC ad agency for supplement brands, webinar-to-ebook lead magnets, and city-specific flight deal newsletters. The common thread is mining real customer pain points, niching down, and selling to buyers who already spend money on the problem.

chunks.heading: AI avatar UGC ad agency for supplement brands
chunks.text:
- Old UGC process: Cody paid creators about $100 per video and mailed them the product. He got one script read once, with no hook variations. Ten ad variations cost about $1,000, and one in ten hit.
- The new unlock: AI avatar tools (he names make UGC.ai) now let an avatar hold a physical product. You pick an avatar, upload product photos, and the tool composites them. Cody says this wasn't possible until recently.
- He now generates "a thousand different pieces of creative" across ~10 avatars, ~100 hooks and ~100 scripts, with no product shipped.
- Search interest in this category went from 1,600 to 4,300 searches a month over a year.
- Niche: supplement and consumable e-commerce brands, which need someone holding the product. They are high-margin, recurring, and spend a double-digit percentage of revenue on ads.
- Why it fits: the best brands now run broad Facebook targeting with a conversion event and compete on ad creative, testing a hundred pieces a month.
- Offer: about 25 videos a week. You do the hook research, generation and editing, and deliver them with a dashboard of what's working. You don't run the ads, so you don't compete with their ads agency.
- Each week's next batch is built from the prior winners. Once a format wins, the brand can have a human creator remake it better.
- Pricing and scale: about $5K/month per client. 16 clients is roughly $80K/month, or a million a year. Cody says 25 ads take about two hours, so ~32 hours a week for 16 clients. He knows agencies charging about $8K/month for 10 videos.
- The human job is curator: generate 50, deliver the best 25, and add ~5 free extras as a kickback.
- Prospecting: find supplement brands doing ~$10M a year with ~5 people and email all five. Include a Google Drive folder with five example ads already made, built from researched pain points.
- Principle: sell to people "addicted to ads" who already know ads work, not people you must convince to start.
- Niche down further, e.g. creatine gummies for women long-distance runners. Scrape Reddit quotes on their pain points, then write hooks and scripts from those quotes.

chunks.heading: Finding pain points from Reddit and turning them into businesses
chunks.text:
- Process: prompt Perplexity with something like "what are the main pain points med spas have in growing the business Reddit". Adding the word "Reddit" is enough, and deep research modes work too.
- Example output for med spas: client acquisition and retention, staffing turnover, over-reliance on discount platforms like Groupon, reputation, facility standards.
- Each pain point maps to a possible business: lead gen, a staffing pipeline, social media management, cleaning.
- He rules out spaces he doesn't want to touch (financing, staffing).
- Math check: med spa customers visit roughly four to eight times a year, and he puts lifetime value around $5K. A paying customer acquired for ~$1,000 is about a 5x return, so you can charge a lot for leads.
- Principle: "A business is two things at its core. You have something people want to buy and you can sell it." Once you find something people hate doing, you do it for pay.
- Online businesses deserve the same mindset as local ones. Tier-one US cities have 80+ window washing companies that all make money at different levels. Likewise there can be a thousand Redfin scrapers. A small, automated product doing a couple grand a month with no staff and Stripe revenue is a real business.

chunks.heading: Med spa lead gen: targeting and local SEO
chunks.text:
- Targeting: women ~30 to 50 in roughly the top 5% of income, via Facebook ads promoting individual services.
- Pick the richest neighborhoods in the town and improve Google Maps listings there.
- Local SEO steps:
  - Put keywords in the listing name and description.
  - List the service offerings.
  - Add photos of the interior so it looks great.
  - Submit directory listings with identical name, address and phone to MapQuest, Foursquare, Yelp and similar sites.
- Matching citations help the business rank higher in the Google Maps pack for "med spa near me". The top three organic Maps results get most of the clicks.
- Add-ons: encourage word of mouth with discounts for customers who post on social, and run referral incentives.

chunks.heading: Webinars turned into lead-magnet ebooks
chunks.text:
- Market: Cody says over 60% of B2B businesses run a webinar every month. So almost every company hosts one at least yearly, and you can email any marketer.
- Offer: turn each webinar into a written lead magnet (ebook/PDF). The client posts the insights on LinkedIn ("comment for the free guide"), people hand over their email, and the list is used to promote the next webinar. He calls it a flywheel.
- Capturing commenters: a tool like Phantom Buster, or VAs, or a sales rep watching comments. Commenters are buyer signals, and for high-ticket offers they're worth manual outreach.
- Finding leads: on YouTube, search "webinar", filter to this week and over 20 minutes. Don't be put off by videos with ~600 views.
- Outreach: find the company on Apollo, email its marketers, and DM them on LinkedIn: "I saw you posted this webinar last week. I turned it into an ebook lead magnet for you. Here it is for free." Pitch an ongoing service.
- Production: take the transcript, drop it into Claude, ask for an ebook with key insights and takeaways, and finish in Canva.
- Pricing: about $1,000 per webinar (four webinars a month is $4K), or an unlimited plan around $8K/month that also covers the back catalog.
- Proof: at Rupa Health he ran a weekly Wednesday live course series, built from social and an email newsletter. It grew from nothing to 4,000 people per webinar.
- Niche down: pick one industry (biotech, cybersecurity). Cold outreach then name-drops companies the prospect knows, as in "SEO for e-commerce beauty brands".

chunks.heading: City-specific cheap flight deals newsletter
chunks.text:
- Critique: Scott's Cheap Flights (now going.com) finds flights that are just cheap, but people want cheap flights from where they live. So unbundle it by city.
- Build: set up Google Flights price tracking with "any dates" on a dedicated Google account, e.g. Dallas to London, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Tokyo. Alerts arrive in an inbox, then an automation rewrites each into your newsletter format with AI and links to the flight.
- Acquire with Facebook ads to a signup form (a Beehiiv newsletter works). Launch in Dallas, get the playbook, then copy it to every major city.
- Monetize: a subscription, kickbacks from partners, and ad slots sold across the whole network. A million travelers across all the city lists is a sellable audience for a hotel chain's promotion.
- Scale reference: Scott's Cheap Flights reported about $3.8M in 2020. Going.com does about $35M a year now.
- He says it can be set up in a weekend and automated end to end. A $20M/year company would take time and some capital.
- He's written about half the script for it but lacks time.

chunks.heading: Nextdoor marketing for a lawn care business
chunks.text:
- Tactic from an 18-year-old running a lawn care business entirely on organic Nextdoor posts.
- Mow a lawn, then post before and after photos: "I just did [address] in your neighborhood. If you want this, message me."
- Social proof is built in. A real neighbor lives at that address, the photos match what the house looks like, and neighbors see the result.
- Cody says it generates a ridiculous amount of inbound.
- He says to speed it up by knocking on doors and offering to do a lawn free. Someone will say yes, and the post is the marketing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider recounts scaling Rupa Health by layering growth channels, then explains how to find underpriced distribution (paid creative testing, creator posts, programmatic TV) and why early startups should do transactional marketing first. He also pitches Graph, an AI marketing analytics agent.

chunks.heading: Growth flywheels: layer channels in sequence
chunks.text:
- Cody's growth model at Rupa Health (a three-sided marketplace of specialty labs, practitioners and patients) was layering flywheels. Find a channel, test about five things in it, and put all mental energy, money and resources behind the one that shows traction.
- When the growth curve hits its inflection point (the S-curve ceiling), he layers on the next channel. That is how he gets "this compounding, hockey stick style thing."
- Results at Rupa as first growth hire:
  - Signups went from about 30 a month to 280 in five months.
  - A podcast went from zero to a top 20 medical podcast in six months.
  - An email list went from zero to 400,000 subscribers in about a year.
  - A weekly Wednesday webinar drew about 5,000 viewers.
- Physicians are constantly sold to, and inventory to reach wealthier audiences is expensive. So Cody made content from day one. He found physicians care about patient outcomes, not business, and built content around that.

chunks.heading: Early-stage rule: transactional marketing first, long-term bets later
chunks.text:
- Early on, Cody focuses on marketing that makes an action happen tomorrow: revenue tomorrow, not six months from now.
- He sees first-time founders start SEO and other long-term investments in month one. His view is that this is a mistake if you might not be around when the payoff arrives.
- His early channels are paid ads, cold DMs and cold email. Lock in all three, and one will show more traction.
- Portfolio analogy: a young person spends about 80% of income on surviving and 20% investing; as they mature the split swaps. A company does the same. Only shift to the longer-term portfolio once short-term channels cover the next 12 months.

chunks.heading: Validate before building: landing page plus ads
chunks.text:
- Cody tells young founders deciding between ideas: "don't build anything."
- Stand up a landing page (he suggests building it with Claude Code), run ads to it, and see which idea gets the cheapest signups.
- The strongest signal is someone who goes through the flow, starts a free trial, or gives a credit card with no product, only screenshots of what it could be. That is instant validation.

chunks.heading: Facebook ads for B2B: how it worked and how it works in 2025
chunks.text:
- **Older approach (Rupa):**
  - Scrape the entire target audience's contact data: directories and all of Google Maps.
  - Use tools like Hunter.io, or bulk data sellers like Targetatron, to buy lists (for example every nurse practitioner in the US).
  - Build a crawler to scrape practitioners' websites for emails, since many used Gmail addresses.
  - Upload the emails as a Facebook customer match list. Only about 30% matched because they were business emails.
  - Use that seed to build lookalike audiences and an exact target cohort.
- **Current approach (as of August 2025):** targeting has improved, so creative is now the filter for finding the audience.
  - Make creative that speaks directly to the segment (for example local business owners) and target all of Facebook.
  - Set conversion events (signup, then payment) and send both back to Facebook.
  - Build about 100 pieces of creative. Run them as CPC campaigns to find the cheapest clicks. Spin the winners (for example five) into a conversion campaign.
  - Typically one to two of the five outperform on the payment event.
- Cody notes people don't use Facebook for B2B and says "please continue not using it," because it leaves him more inventory. He says it "especially right now just prints money."

chunks.heading: Unit economics: it's fine to lose money on the first month
chunks.text:
- Back into the numbers: "every dollar that we spend turns into $5 of customer lifetime value," with a payback period of about three months. Then set spend to hit a revenue target.
- Real example from a past company:
  - CAC about $89.
  - Average revenue per customer about $39 a month, so payback about two months.
  - Customer lifetime value about $600.
- First-time founders must accept that they lose money on the first transaction. Lifetime value is what matters.
- He cites the "law of shitty clickthroughs" (Andrew Chen, *The Cold Start Problem*): early on CPCs are cheap, and as competitors and incumbents enter, the arbitrage disappears and CAC rises. Product improvement raises LTV over time.
- Some categories won't work for ads. He says Graph will find it hard to do ads, so it needs unusual marketing strategies.

chunks.heading: Underpriced attention: find the arbitrage
chunks.text:
- Channel-product fit: for any product at any moment there is a channel with an unexploited arbitrage. Find where people spend time online that is not yet saturated with advertisers, or is hard to market in.
- Early Facebook gave one-cent CPC clicks because of abundant inventory. He says this is how Wish.com became a billion-dollar company: it abused new, underpriced media.
- **Local TV streaming ads (programmatic):**
  - A friend from out-of-home advertising works in this space. Cody has seen data of about 80 cent CPMs on local TV.
  - You can target from a customer match list.
  - Attribution is direct: someone watches a Hulu ad, then searches on the same IP and buys, and it ties back to the household.
- Cumbersome entry processes are a plus. He thinks of them as "illiquid markets."

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing in illiquid markets
chunks.text:
- Cody avoids marketplace hubs with posted per-post prices. He wants illiquid markets and negotiates directly.
- Process:
  - Pay roughly $800 to $1,000 per creator, around $900 for 30 posts in one example, and run about five creators at once.
  - Roughly every 10 to 20 posts, an outlier format appears. Hand that format to the other creators to iterate on. This creates a flywheel.
  - Scale up or down with 5, 10 or 20 creators.
  - Cut underperformers aggressively and judge on CPM.
- The arbitrage: average platform CPMs are about $7 on TikTok and about $5.50 on Facebook (as platforms report them). Getting creator CPMs under that, for example around $2 per thousand views, beats paid ads.
- This works because about 10% of posts generate about 80 to 90% of an account's views. You are betting on the outlier, and that is how you get the discounted CPM.

chunks.heading: Building Graph.com: an AI agent for marketing analytics
chunks.text:
- Graph aims to replace the data scientist you would hire. A friend hired an ex-Uber data scientist at $200k to answer data questions.
- The problem: getting insight requires a data pipeline, a data warehouse and fluency in tools like Tableau, Looker Studio or Power BI. He says learning those takes months and "you literally have to use the software to get the insight."
- The product:
  - One-click setup for data connectors.
  - Graph manages and continuously optimizes the data warehouse.
  - Chat on the side and a dashboard in the center, for example "build a stacked bar chart showing new users versus total users over time" with a line of best fit, week over week.
- The data warehouse is the hard part. A client had about 25 million rows of Facebook data alone, which hits rate limits if plugged into a generic AI solution.
- The vision: first augment the data person, then replace them. Graph watches your data constantly, researches online, and Slacks you insights and opportunities.
- Finance stack: Stripe Atlas ($500, Delaware C-corp, with perks like instant Carta and Mercury setup) and Fondo for accounting, so 90% of energy goes to building product and selling.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains his "digital gravity" view of marketing: pick repeatable channels (X, email nurture, newsletters, podcasts, short-form clips), publish at high volume, read the data, and double down on winners. He covers recycling top tweets, growing newsletters from social, pairing podcasts with newsletters for trust, and setting a North Star metric per channel.

chunks.heading: Digital gravity: the core marketing worldview
chunks.text:
- Cody's central idea for marketing is "digital gravity". He says "you're trying to build digital mass on the internet so that you have more digital gravity within your sphere" (your niche).
- Digital mass comes from content. More content creates more gravity, which creates a larger inbound that "naturally happens over time".
- He rejects the traditional funnel as "a very old way to think about it". His model: a human is like a comet flying by that gets pulled into orbit, and at different points in the orbit they are closer to touching down and purchasing.
- He frames marketing as "building relationships at scale". A brand is a one-to-many relationship happening simultaneously.
- His answer to "what marketing should I do?" is "everything". His background is early-stage startups: you have a product and an audience that wants it, and the job is building distribution that takes a brand "from zero to one" until the whole industry knows it exists.

chunks.heading: Make marketing a lifestyle, not a campaign
chunks.text:
- Campaigns start and stop. Cody wants marketing activities you can do "indefinitely into the future", chosen as a lifestyle for the next five years or so, at a weekly, daily or monthly cadence.
- Sustainable and repeatable beats scrappy one-offs. His example of the wrong approach: a Reddit post that produced leads once, which "was once a quarter" and can't be repeated.
- Doing two TikToks a week for 12 months beats a video a week for only 30 days. The longer you sustain something the more it compounds, and sustainability also reduces burnout.
- His filter for any activity: don't do it if it can't be automated or delegated. Automate as much as possible, then delegate the rest.
- Cadences he says work:
  - Twitter: 70 tweets a week.
  - Short-form social: a post a day.
  - Podcast: one interview a week, paired with a weekly newsletter about the episode.
- Using the podcast-plus-newsletter tactic alone, he says he has taken shows to the top 20 of the US medical, marketing and lifestyle podcast charts.
- A new channel is ugly at first. For client podcasts, the first four episodes are rough and slow, then it gets into a rhythm around day 60, cruises by day 90, is a no-brainer by month six, and by month nine "my whole industry knows I exist".

chunks.heading: Twitter system: volume, data, and remixing top performers
chunks.text:
- Cody's view is that For You page content has changed everything. TikTok invented it and LinkedIn, Twitter, YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels all adopted it. Platforms serve content based on taste, to keep you on platform, not based on who you follow.
- Because platforms decide what is good content (whatever keeps audiences watching), he treats it as a volume game, "at bats". Five clips a day gives 150 data points a month versus 30, so conclusions are more reliable.
- His weekly routine:
  - Every Sunday he writes 70 tweets and schedules them from 7am to 5am.
  - Weekly he reviews the data for top performers and remixes them.
  - He no longer writes new tweets. He recycles top performers every six weeks to two months, because "people have short attention spans so you can say the same things over and over again".
  - Some of his tweets reliably get 250,000 to 300,000 impressions each time they run. He calls it "playing your greatest hits over and over again", with new material peppered in to add "new DNA to the gene pool".
- Roughly 8,000 tweets have gone out over about 18 months.
- Data workflow: X removed the CSV export from analytics, so he built a custom Python script that calls the API and writes a CSV, then analyzes it in a Google Sheet.
- Results (as of August 2024):
  - About 27,000 followers, 24,000 of them gained in the last year.
  - About 5,000 new followers a month, growing about 7% month over month, compounding.
  - About 2.5 million impressions a month on Twitter.
- General rule: "do a bunch of stuff, look at the data to see what works, do more of what's working and less of what isn't" to build a growth flywheel. The same approach applies to shorts, emails and podcasts.

chunks.heading: Turning social reach into an owned newsletter
chunks.text:
- Every tweet gets an automated call to action about five minutes after it posts, pointing to his newsletter on "growth tactics and startup ideas". He calls these "junk food for entrepreneurs" and "the honey pot".
- The same CTA runs on LinkedIn, YouTube and other channels.
- Organically this adds about 2,000 to 2,500 subscribers a month.
- He layers "gray tactics" on top: sequencing people he knows are interested in the content into the list daily. That brings growth to about 5,000 subscribers a month.
- Past about 20,000 subscribers, he says lists can grow about 30% a month compounding with these tactics, which means going from zero to 100,000 subscribers in a year for clients and for himself.
- Owned-audience stats double as outreach leverage. When pitching himself for podcasts he cites a newsletter (he says 50,000 subscribers) plus monthly Twitter and LinkedIn impressions, and says about 20% of the people he reaches out to reply.

chunks.heading: Email is the answer: cold email, nurture, and newsletters
chunks.text:
- His tweet: "what marketing should I do? email. cold email, nurture, newsletters". He says email is his favorite channel and he could talk about it for days.
- Case: a friend's SaaS for interior designers (turning 2D designs into photorealistic interiors) had lots of top-of-funnel leads but poor activation and no email nurture at all. Cody's fix was a nurture sequence, which he handed over as a template.
- His claim: he has seen companies reach a million in revenue with just cold email, email nurture, and a newsletter to those same people carrying product updates and industry news.
- He says email looks unsexy because it's old, but the depth is technical: deliverability, open-rate management, A/B testing.
- His team builds custom software behind the newsletters they run, and uses AI more and more.
- On cold email resilience, he has done it about six years and gone through roughly 15 cycles where "it's dead, game over", and each time you adjust to the new stimuli.
- Example of newsletter content as outbound: for a winemaker friend on the California Central Coast, they scrape local business owners, sequence them into a twice-monthly newsletter, and write it from a 30-minute Zoom chat ("story time with my friend Chad from the ranch"). Cold recipients email back saying they love it.
- On sharing your process, one of his most viral tweets is just how his team's cold email infrastructure works. He reposts it about every six months and wins new clients each time. "People like sausage making", i.e. behind the scenes.

chunks.heading: Pillar content (podcast + newsletter) and repurposing
chunks.text:
- He calls pillar content "the biggest arbitrage right now for B2B". His reasoning: a weekly podcast means people sit and listen to you for 45 minutes, which builds far more trust than anything else, "basically a church leader" with a congregation.
- Podcast plus newsletter together builds deep trust, so by the time prospects reach sales they are "buy ready", having binged the back catalog, and say "here's the check, let's go".
- It also warms outbound: when the sales team reaches out to people on the list, they aren't cold ("I listened to your show").
- Clips drive impulse purchases but not high-ticket sales, so match the content type to the business. Long-form builds trust for high ticket.
- One anchor piece becomes everything else. In roughly an hour and a half of founder time, one conversation is handed to an editor/team who produce clips, social posts, blog posts, newsletters, white papers and ebooks. Cody is building Swell AI around this idea (content repurposing powered by AI, evolving into "your AI content team").
- He says founders' scarcest resources are mental bandwidth, money and time, with mental bandwidth the hardest.

chunks.heading: Content strategy and clip-farming at scale
chunks.text:
- What goes wrong in content: people focus only on sales. His ideal is the intersection of sales, entertainment, and your product as the solution to a problem.
- Example (a friend's company, Reveal AI, a qualitative analytics tool that scrapes TikTok comments for market researchers): content analyzes a known brand's TikTok comments, shows the tool used, and shows the outcome. It attaches to something the public already knows, adds a novel thought, and the product is the solution. That arc "creates a hook, creates a what-if, then gives them a solution".
- The other half of content is volume, which he treats as at-bats (batting average logic).
- Experiment he is running: a proxy network with virtual machines to create many TikTok accounts. He calls the planned product ClipWave. It takes a podcaster's or musician's back catalog, chops it into clips, and schedules them across many accounts.
- Math he cites: 100 accounts each doing 30,000 views a month is three million views a month, and he asks what happens at 1,000 or 100,000 accounts. He notes this is lower quality than fully human-run networks, such as the agency model he says is reported to charge about $35,000 a month.
- He expects platforms to eventually crack down on such networks and on AI-generated garbage via shadow-banning, and says there is an arbitrage during the window before they adjust.
- Platform feedback is free data. YouTube shorts and TikTok show viewed vs swiped away and retention, so you can see within an hour whether a clip is a dud. His method: find the outlier, then work out why it was an outlier and repeat it.

chunks.heading: Ops, hiring, and agency design
chunks.text:
- Define a single North Star metric per offer up front and get everyone to agree on it. Examples:
  - Programmatic SEO: impressions, clicks, signups (signups matter most; impressions and clicks are leading indicators).
  - Newsletter growth: subscribers.
- Internal selling tip: get your boss to agree "this is what I'm measured to" and show a dashboard; then everyone optimizes toward it.
- His agency sells productized services per channel: cold email, email newsletter growth ("sub growth as a service"), full-service podcasting, unlimited Google/Facebook ads, programmatic SEO. Team members don't cross over between channels, each has a finite scope of work, documentation and training.
- Hiring approach depends on company type. For venture-backed early-stage growth, hire autonomous people who decide, act and then report, not people who ask permission or pitch internally. For cash-flowing businesses, build processes and systems where people are nodes with finite scope.
- He believes an "AI automations engineer" will be one of the most valuable team members by early 2025, since they save cost and also raise revenue through throughput. Example he cites from a friend: cutting real estate teams' time costs by about 60% in four weeks.
- Many industries still run on paper intake forms, so connecting a PDF reader to a CRM through tools like Airtable and Zapier can have an overnight business impact.
- He notes search volume for "AI automation agency" is rising vertically.
- On saturation: there is plenty of market, like hundreds of window-washing companies in Denver that each feed an owner. "We're just building window washing companies on the internet."
