- He sees growth as spurts rather than a line: zoomed in it is spiky, zoomed out it looks smooth. He expects fine-tuned, use-case-specific models (for example clip making or SEO writing) to arrive within a couple of quarters and beat humans at their tasks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody lays out several AI-era arbitrage plays: mass-testing AI avatar ad variations, bottom-of-funnel programmatic SEO with early CTAs, and tiny-scope apps or exact-match-domain tools that undercut high-ticket services. He also explains why he prefers B2B over B2C and how he spins killer features into standalone products.

chunks.heading: AI UGC ad and organic social content as an agency opportunity
chunks.text:
- Cody calls AI content the biggest money opportunity right now and says "you could get an agency to like 40K a month in like 90 days doing this."
- Traditional UGC ads for Meta/social cost about $80-$120 per video from a human creator (e.g. on Billo). Testing 100 scripts that way is about $8K, which is why it was never economic.
- His method: write many hooks, bodies and calls to action for one value prop, then render them with HeyGen's built-in UGC avatars and ElevenLabs' voice library.
- Example: a test for an AI audio-journaling app (Record Book AI, co-built with Casper Studios) used a "New Year's resolution to journal more, but writing is hard" script. He reports about 15 cent CPCs with US targeting and roughly $2.50 leads, with a goal of getting leads to around $1.
- Playbook: generate about 100 AI variations, find the winners, then give the winning scripts to a real human creator to do their own version. He expects CPC to fall further once a human delivers them.
- Agency packaging he suggests: about $3K/month to run Facebook ads plus unlimited AI UGC avatar creation and constant testing of around 100 creatives.
- Imperfect avatars still work: "it doesn't have to be perfect... it just has to work." The best avatar he used even had visible acne.
- Organic version: build about 20 TikTok accounts, write 1,000 scripts, have avatars speak them, and schedule the shorts across the accounts. Even at 1,000 views each, he puts the effective CPM near $1.
- Pricing for organic: $3-5K/month for X accounts and X pieces of creative. DTC ecom brands are looking to buy this.
- Story format: a simple narrative where the product is the hero ("I had this problem, found this thing, it helped"), often with no hard call to action.
- LinkedIn video: he gets inbound from founders and brands wanting it. He suggests about $5K/month for 30 videos scheduled to a business or founder profile.
- Mindset: "it's about I test the variations at a scale that I couldn't previously."

chunks.heading: SEO as TikTok and Instagram search, plus ecom bottom-of-funnel SEO
chunks.text:
- Cody is testing social as the next search engine, since Gen Z goes straight to TikTok or Instagram for queries like "cool bars near me."
- Experiment with a friend who runs TikTok meme pages: use AI avatars across multiple accounts, each speaking different scripts aimed at one target keyword (e.g. "AI essay writer"), to own the front page for that term.
- Open questions he flags (still early): whether volume is what matters, and putting the keyword in the title and the first ~10 seconds of the video.
- Listicle videos work well, e.g. "top five bars in Echo Park this month," with the client placed at number one.
- Freshness matters: he has seen pages hold page-one for about 30-45 days then drop off, so content must be refreshed. He notes this makes a good low-churn agency business.
- Ecom SEO: he says there is more bottom-of-funnel SEO opportunity than ever. His new company, LandingCAD (landingcad.com), ingests a product catalog, finds every long-tail keyword related to the brand, and builds collection pages and blog posts programmatically.
- Typical ecom agencies charge about $45K over six months for roughly eight blog posts that do nothing, so brands are jaded. His pitch is being ROI positive within 30 days.
- For small catalogs (1-10 SKUs), he does "best product for X / for Y / for Z" variations, with dashboards showing revenue impact and Klaviyo pipeline from those pages.

chunks.heading: Programmatic SEO workflow, topical relevance and conversion tactics
chunks.text:
- On the HubSpot traffic drop, he argues the pages hit were generic business terms not core to its product. Real companies ranking for relevant topics is what holds.
- For SaaS, integration pages work well. Example: "how to X with HubSpot" tutorials if your software integrates with HubSpot are a natural vehicle for signups. For ecom, "best collagen for X" works for a collagen brand because it is topical.
- Content workflow: find long-tail keywords related to the company, scrape what ranks on page one, put that in the context window, and use the strongest model to draft the article.
- Optionally use an NLP model to pull the keywords that should be included, to get a strong Surfer SEO or Phrase score.
- After it ranks, have a human polish it. He frames two audiences: the Google robots, and human dwell time on the page.
- Comparison and alternative pages: do "X vs Y" and alternatives pages programmatically. Comparison intent is "the perfect search intent for your software."
- Conversion layout for blog posts: a call to action after the first paragraph and every other screen, plus a popup at 20% scroll rate. He says clients see "five to 10% signup rates" when the offer is self-service.
- Why founders say SEO doesn't work: they rank for unrelated terms, and the call to action sits at the bottom of a 2,000-word article where only about 1% of readers scroll. Fixing both produced signups "overnight."

chunks.heading: Directories built with AI scraping
chunks.text:
- Cody is "obsessed" with YouTuber Frey Chu's directory case study (a dog park directory).
- His insight: directories used to be hard because of data organization. With AI agents and scraping, unstructured data can be turned into structured data at a scale that wasn't previously possible.
- Example method: scrape Google Maps data, use reviews as source text, add yes/no columns (does it have benches, shade, etc.), and query the review data to fill them.
- He is considering spinning out a directory arm at his agency. He notes link building for niche directories is easy and they can rank quickly.

chunks.heading: Podcast SEO and the AI podcast flywheel
chunks.text:
- He says he could make any B2B founder "famous" to their audience with a podcast.
- Podcast SEO is simple, with four factors: keywords in the show title, in the show description, in the show notes, and getting downloads.
- Method: name the show with a broad long-tail B2B phrase (e.g. "B2B Marketing Podcast"). He ranks for "growth" on Apple and Spotify by keyword stuffing and getting downloads.
- A content shortcut he describes (idea he shared but doesn't plan to run): use Google's deep research agent to gather everything on a topic (he tested it on Canva's SEO case studies), feed the source text into NotebookLM to generate a two-host podcast.
- Download flywheel: run cheap Twitter traffic with global targeting to the podcast URL, which lifts chart rank, which brings discovery, which brings more downloads.
- He knows people running about 100 podcasts at once, one per long-tail keyword, with roughly 10-minute episodes, mostly affiliate marketers.
- His own background: starting in 2012 with Amazon affiliate sites (around 20 sites). He says growth marketers come either from degenerate SEO/affiliate or from product, and end up in the same place.

chunks.heading: Picking app ideas: small scope, proven categories, undercut on price
chunks.text:
- Cody's focus is products with a very small scope, in spaces already proven at a high price point that he can undercut. He says many teams fail by trying to build a whole platform.
- Distribution: free views on TikTok for good content. He says average paid TikTok CPM is about $8-9, while paying Clippers (college editors, often through Discord networks) runs about $1 per 1,000 views, with bounty-style bonuses.
- Coaching apps: replace a formerly expensive human service with an AI version. Example: a running coach app that plugs into Strava for about $29/month (or $7.99/week) versus a human coach at roughly "400" a month (he says the figure loosely). Even at 80% as good it is competitive and an impulse purchase.
- He says the most effective form adds a voice agent that keeps context. He cites Bardy (an AI business coach with voice) as having raised $8M. Nutrition coach AI is another idea.
- Skip "AI therapist": "nobody wants an AI therapist"; people want a coaching mechanism toward a goal.
- Trackers: he praises retention from trackers, citing a friend's app, Sunflower Sober, which he says has among the fastest daily active user growth he has seen. The friend came up in the era of free Facebook traffic.
- Lock-in: data lock-in matters. In Record Book AI, 365 journal entries plus insights create switching costs. He contrasts this with API-wrapper clones.

chunks.heading: Exact-match domains, tool pages and spinning out features
chunks.text:
- Exact-match domain play: buy a domain matching a long-tail tool keyword. He bought aiinfographicgenerator.com for $10, with about 10,000 monthly searches. The tool ingests a blog post URL and outputs a downloadable, embeddable PDF.
- He says exact-match domains are easy to rank, then a "link magnet flywheel" compounds. A real tool people use after a Google search also reads as a legitimate product, so the site is less likely to get hit as a niche site.
- Tool pages for clients: for a construction company he built a remodel cost calculator, embedded an AI-generated app on the page, built links to it, and ranked page one.
- Build out the rest of the site around the head keyword with long-tail blog pages (e.g. "infographic template 4"), which feed users into the tool. Display ads such as AdSense are another option.
- Spinning out features: customers of his transcription product (Swell AI) said the transcription was the best they had tried and all they needed was transcription. He bought an exact-match domain with about 22,000 monthly searches, will copy that feature's code into a new brand and price it separately.
- General rule: build one product, find the killer feature, spin it out as its own standalone.

chunks.heading: B2B vs B2C, and building then selling small software businesses
chunks.text:
- Cody advises that if you aren't great at marketing, there is "zero percent chance" of making it in B2C, where you compete against the most aggressive marketers. B2B buyers are less price sensitive.
- Audience pricing example: podcasters have little money, YouTubers have more, and webinar hosts have more still. He chose webinar hosts for Swell AI because of that.
- Even so, he is building B2C Record Book AI, and says a modest outcome (about $20K MRR, sold for around $1M) would be fine.
- Quick-flip pattern he describes: build a site to about $2K MRR in a three-month sprint, sell it on MicroAcquire for about $100K (he cites up to a 50x multiple with no employees), and repeat a few times a year. Keep the ones that keep growing.
- B2B tip: do consulting for a specific group, find a shared pain point, build software that automates it, then offer it as software (e.g. a $1,500 custom job becomes $99/month).
- App stores give a sticky, shareable base if ASO, TikTok and SEO start working.

chunks.heading: Cold email setup that Cody sees working
chunks.text:
- Infrastructure: he uses Mailreef (spins up a dedicated AWS server for cold email). About $400/month sends 50,000 emails/month, and he says a million sends a month costs about $8K. He also mentions Hypertide and Thor's Hammer as similar tools.
- He reports deliverability on par with Gmail or Microsoft inboxes.
- Setup: buy about 30 domains on Porkbun, create 5 inboxes per domain, and send 20-30 cold emails per inbox per day.
- Lists: scrape Apollo using one of the Apollo scraping companies, then validate emails.
- Email format: short, about the length of a tweet. First line sets context ("saw you host webinars"), second line gives social proof ("we helped X company do Y in Z time"), then a hard offer or call to action ("want us to do this for you?").
- Female sender names: he says they tested and worked "100%." He knows a company running about 25 fictional female sales reps on LinkedIn, run by an AI agent, that is "absolutely crushing it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains how he learned growth by doing, why distribution beats product, and how AI makes long-tail SEO content nearly free. He also covers his Twitter system and a layered growth stack (podcast SEO, iOS Facebook ads, email/SMS newsletters) for podcast growth.

chunks.heading: Early path into marketing and the lesson from his first company
chunks.text:
- Cody started by figuring out how to make money on the internet at 16, selling things through e-commerce, back when free clicks from Facebook pages were available.
- He started a company that took off, dropped out of school and traveled, then watched it implode because he "wasn't building a brand."
- He calls that failure the best thing that could happen early, with low stakes: when building companies, "focus on brand because that's the only thing that actually has value long term."
- He later studied business economics and worked at a B2B marketing agency serving Fortune 500 manufacturers (wood, windows). He designed strategy, built processes, and built the analytics infrastructure so teams had a North Star for what was working.

chunks.heading: Where his specialty sits and how his career moved
chunks.text:
- A friend at Rupa/e.l.f.-style beauty growth company showed him a graph of word-of-mouth growth with ads layered on top, compounding about 30% month over month. Cody saw it as blue ocean, moved to San Francisco a week later, and scaled it for about a year.
- He then joined a DeFi savings-account crypto company growing about 3x month over month for four months. The Terra Luna collapse eroded the business model overnight.
- Takeaway he drew: his expertise is companies that already have product-market fit and an audience and need distribution. He went back to consulting for early-stage startups, building initial growth infrastructure (what others call "fractional head of growth," which he calls "dumb"; it is a stopgap to get the first 100 users).
- With co-founder Max he built side projects, then launched Swell AI in September 2022 (AI writer for podcasters). It took off as ChatGPT hit in December 2022 / January 2023.
- Draft Horse AI launched about 45 days before this interview (June 21): an AI SEO engine where you plug in your website and it writes content at scale. Long-term vision: "have your blog grow itself" toward a business goal like signups.

chunks.heading: How he learns marketing and how to start
chunks.text:
- He learned from YouTube videos and Reddit threads. He argues digital marketing "can't be taught" in a classroom because it changes so fast; a university program is two years stale.
- "You're either in the pit or you're not": either you do it daily and understand what's going on, or you don't.
- His starter exercise: make a blog about a topic you're interested in, figure out how to get traffic to it, and figure out how to sell something to that traffic. Do that and "you're in the top one percent of marketers."
- Learning loop: follow one topic, note unfamiliar terms in each video, research those, repeat. Document what you learn in public to attract people with the same interests (inbound).
- He talks weekly with growth friends (heads of growth, CMOs), swapping what's working and where the arbitrage is. Example: a friend ran the same strategies across Facebook ads at Deliveroo, Snapchat ads at Depop, and TikTok ads at a new company.

chunks.heading: Niche sites, then and now with AI
chunks.text:
- Traditional niche site: rank a site around product searches (e.g. "best binoculars for birding") and monetize traffic via ad networks (AdSense), affiliate commissions (e.g. Amazon, roughly 4-8%), or selling your own products. One friend runs a gardening site with ad income plus a newsletter list and periodic PDF how-to guides.
- Big media agencies also run thousands of niche sites and sell the traffic to consumer packaged goods brands.
- The shift: writing content was the biggest cost. A thousand articles at about $100 each meant roughly $100K for okay-quality writing. With AI, he says a thousand articles through Draft Horse costs about $500.
- In July 2022 AI content became "good enough" to be usable from a marketer's view.
- His workflow: find a niche, pull low-difficulty, low-competition keywords, feed them into Draft Horse, publish 2,000+ word articles (e.g. "how to start a [X] business" variations). Low-competition keywords start ranking immediately. He builds initial sites in about 10 hours.
- Cheap content makes the long tail viable in a way that was previously cost-prohibitive.
- He expects the window to last about 18 to 24 months before it is built into every tool and CMS. He calls it a land grab.

chunks.heading: Differentiating when content costs nothing
chunks.text:
- If AI writes the average, experts become more valuable. His view: companies will capture expert knowledge (Fireside chats, podcasts, PDFs), load it into a vector database, and have AI write only from that corpus, so the output is unique because nobody else has the data.
- Roles shift: instead of fresh grads repurposing content, you need a curator who feeds good material in and reviews the output; the middle is automated.
- Stack he uses for this: Pinecone (vector database) and LangChain. The same approach could produce news-style articles by loading 10 sources and writing against them.
- Draft Horse mechanics: it generates a blog post outline (what an SEO manager would hand a writer), then writes to it, tracking what it has written, is writing, and will write, to stay cohesive.
- Roadmap he describes: Search Console data feeding back to Draft Horse to refresh underperforming content, a tracking tag to report signups, automatic internal linking, automatic indexing, and images with exact-match alt text.
- Scale example: on one day he was writing 3,000 articles across three properties (1,000 on marketing for his personal site, 1,000 on WordPress for Draft Horse, 1,000 on podcasting for Swell), live in about two hours.

chunks.heading: Publishing workflow: ship rough, polish what gets traffic
chunks.text:
- Upload text first, get it live, then add images, video, CTAs, and rewrites after an article starts getting traffic.
- His reasoning: if nobody sees it, it doesn't matter if it's not perfect. This depends on company stage; startups can tolerate imperfection, while regulated firms like accounting must be more careful.
- Even for a media brand with no software, he would still use AI content at scale. He describes companies producing 10,000+ articles with CTAs to a newsletter or show.
- Marketing split: transactional marketing (paid ads, cold email: act now, results soon) vs long-term investment marketing (SEO: effects show about 12 months later).
- Math he uses: if about $5K buys 10,000 articles and even a fraction rank, you get an inbound engine. Spending 50 cents now to create one free signup within 12 months "pays for itself," so he does it until it stops working.

chunks.heading: Twitter growth system
chunks.text:
- In early 2023 he saw an arbitrage: Twitter was giving unusual free reach, like Facebook in 2012. He went in to sell tools through it.
- Results: about 400 followers at the start of 2023 to about 8,000, and 2.2 million impressions per month for the $5/month Twitter Blue fee, which he calls "the cheapest CPM on the internet right now."
- Process: same as all marketing: pick a channel, turn it into a system, read the data, do more of what works.
- Concretely: 10 tweets per day (70 per week), written every Sunday over a glass of whiskey. He reviews the past three months of top tweets by impressions, then writes 70 new ones remixing those ideas. This creates a loop that learns what his audience engages with and feeds more reach.
- Style: bare-bones, just the essence of an idea, documenting what he is doing.
- He is half-automating it with AI and thinks the full loop (write from vector database, publish, read impressions, write more from winners) can be automated, but Draft Horse is the focus.

chunks.heading: Distribution over product and the two moats
chunks.text:
- "I see worse products win all the time because they have better distribution." He says product-first founders (especially in SF) assume a great product gets found; good product is just table stakes now.
- With software and content easy to clone, he says only two things create a moat: owned media (an audience nobody else can reach) and proprietary customer data.
- His own apps are Tailwind components plus an OpenAI API wrapper, yet he tweeted that the site is worth more than his townhouse because of distribution.
- He cites the book The Innovation Stack: stacking about 8 to 11 ideas creates something new. Unit economics pitch for Draft Horse: content that cost about $100 before costs about $1 now, "a no-brainer."

chunks.heading: Podcast growth stack: SEO, iOS ads, newsletters, SMS
chunks.text:
Used for zero-to-one podcasts (biotech, marketing, insurance examples). Layer four things:
- **Podcast SEO**: keywords in show name, description, episode titles and show notes drive ranking inside Apple Podcasts and Spotify, where he says roughly 90% of downloads happen. Downloads act like domain rating. Rewriting old show notes on a 500-episode show has produced about 30% week-over-week growth in some cases.
- **Facebook ads to iOS-only devices**: use a clip from the show as the ad, test around 20 clips, put spend behind the lowest CPC. Link to the Apple Podcasts episode URL (a deep link that opens the app) so a play becomes a download. He also uses a podcast subscribe deep link ("podcast://" followed by the RSS feed URL) which prompts a subscribe, making each new episode an instant download.
- **Newsletters**: for a biotech client he scraped industry emails, added about 200 per day via automation, and sent the best-performing episode first, then each new episode weekly. Reported results: roughly 40% opens and 5% CTR on these cold emails. He calls it a gray-hat arbitrage that will go away.
- **SMS** (Klaviyo-style bulk texting): he reports about 90% open rates and 40 to 50% clicks on new-episode texts. A friend is testing WhatsApp in Europe.
- Flywheel: more downloads give better podcast SEO and chart position, charts are scraped by aggregators like Chartable straight from Apple categories, and that brings more downloads.

chunks.heading: Growing a newsletter from 33K toward 330K
chunks.text:
- Starting point: use paid ads and work the math backwards: if a subscriber costs $1 and the newsletter earns more than that per subscriber over its life, buy them. He notes Sam Parr built The Hustle largely on Facebook ads and sold it for $40M in about two years (his figures as stated).
- A friend gets $1 signups from Facebook using a screenshot of an Apple Note as the ad image for an AI newsletter.
- He suggests pairing paid ads with a newsletter cross-promotion network (a tool he could not name on air; sellers add "newsletters you might like" to their emails). He has seen about 20,000 subscribers added in seven days that way.
- With capital, he would test every channel (likely TikTok for a millennial/Gen Z audience), compare cost per signup, then scale the cheapest.
- Without capital the playbook differs; his advice depends on starting capital.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains how podcasts act as a sales and content engine, why feeding AI human expert source material beats generic prompting, and how he layers every growth channel (cold email, paid, programmatic SEO, TikTok networks). He also shares his "can we do this forever?" marketing filter and career advice to start a blog, get traffic and learn technical skills.

chunks.heading: Starting a content-led company by turning podcasts into a repeatable sales channel
chunks.text:
- Cody's route into this: e-commerce, then a BD marketing agency doing digital strategy for Fortune 500 manufacturers (doors, windows, "very unsexy businesses"), then Rupa Health as employee six.
- At Rupa, he helped take the company from a $20 million to a $110 million valuation in about six months.
- Rupa marketed to practitioners (doctors), who are high income, hard to reach and marketed to from every angle. His team concluded early that they had to build a media arm to create a relationship and drive demand generation.
- That arm became a live class series, a podcast series and thousands of blog posts, which produced strong SEO.
- Lesson he drew: podcasts, especially in B2B, are a way to produce media on a regular cadence that can be chopped into clips, blog posts, newsletters and more.
- Swell AI started in July 2022. Cody was consulting, had spun up a podcast for a client, and saw AI was "good enough". His co-founder Max, already deep in embeddings, built a first version within 24 hours.
- That MVP was a Google Drive folder where friends uploaded MP3s. Cody sold it to about 10 people, ran the files locally on laptops and emailed the generated content back by hand. There was no website; he emailed friends who used webinars and podcasts to grow and said "send us the recordings, we'll handle the rest."

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping and defensibility choices at Swell AI
chunks.text:
- Swell is self-funded. Cody owns other companies that cash flow it, and Max had exits that cover him.
- They were approached by VCs early and chose to build "something that's sustainable" and profitable instead.
- His reasoning: something new drops in AI every week, so it was unclear what raising would mean for long-term defensibility.
- Defensibility now comes from a complex workflow product: take raw media, turn it into any form and publish it anywhere.
- Pricing: a free tier, then usage based. Cost is based only on the upload time of the source file (effectively the transcription), with unlimited clips and unlimited text afterwards. He says this works because model costs are now low.
- Positioning: a prosumer product, not a high-end enterprise one. The initial wedge was podcasters; the target is now "your AI content marketing team".
- Customers include local news channels as well as individual creators.

chunks.heading: Why human source material beats prompting an LLM
chunks.text:
- Cody's view: an LLM is trained on the average of the internet, so its output is average. Unique ideas still require talking to experts, and "thought leaders are actually now more valuable than they ever were."
- Workflow he describes: record conversations with experts (e.g. five hotel marketing experts), drop the recording in, get a transcript, then prompt for a blog post outline, then a post written from the outline.
- Tell the AI to reuse the vocabulary in the transcript so the tone, style and voice match the recording. He says this lands you in the top ~5% of content versus a bare prompt like "hotel marketing strategies for 2024".
- General principle: give the AI a "walled garden" of source material to work from, which orients its context and raises quality.
- Other source material he cites: PDFs and reports, or scraping everything on page one of Google for a target keyword (blog posts, YouTube videos) into the context window. He says this gives output "10x better" than prompting the LLM alone.
- Experts often dislike writing but are happy to talk, so interviews, fireside chats and webinars all work as sources.
- Cody says the prompt-chain is the real product. He argues "I don't think anybody actually wants to chat with AI". Chat is a sandbox for finding the prompt chain, and the value is in templated, automatic outputs.

chunks.heading: Podcasts as "sales in disguise" for early-stage companies
chunks.text:
- Cody's quote: "Podcasts are one of the most effective sales tools that exist currently."
- He advises early-stage companies to create a show.
- Outreach tactic: invite your target ICP onto the show. For clients using Swell, with a 10,000-subscriber newsletter and clips offered back to guests for their socials, he cites a roughly 20% response rate on that outreach.
- Result: you are suddenly in a relationship with your target customer.
- Distribution: email the episodes to a newsletter. People open it and spend an hour with you each week, which he says you could not pay them to do. Industry experts on the show act as "almost this honeypot" that creates inbound.
- Byproducts include clips, social posts, blog posts and newsletters.
- He says video podcasts are taking over and that YouTube looks like the winner, based on the data Swell sees.

chunks.heading: Repurposing webinars into long-tail SEO and clips
chunks.text:
- Example: clients with 500+ webinars from the last three years and no plan for them.
- Tactic 1: turn each webinar into blog posts. Prompt for 10 long-tail keywords related to the webinar, write a post per keyword, publish and embed the webinar in each post to drive more views.
- Tactic 2: cut the hour-long webinar into 5-10 minute insight clips for YouTube.
- Cody says the clips often outperform the source: a webinar with 97 views versus a clip with a hook at the start that did close to 1,000 views from the same content.

chunks.heading: AI "employees" and custom models as the next layer
chunks.text:
- Cody is focused on automating whole marketing roles. Example under construction: a social media manager agent, internally called "Jenna".
- Its loop: take a long-form upload, make clips, schedule and publish them to social platforms, analyze performance, find more clips like the top performers in the back catalog, and repeat as a growth flywheel.
- He sees the same pattern for Google Ads, Facebook Ads and programmatic SEO (keyword research, write posts, check what drove signups, write more).
- His view: even if an agent is only ~50% as good as a human, at a price like $149 a month it still creates impact, and it improves over time. Agents would "show up in your slack, and they start working."
- Differentiation will come from custom models trained for a specific outcome. Clip selection is his example: general models are trained on average Shorts, TikToks and Reels, whereas training on the top 1% of clips would improve selection.
- Cost: Swell was quoted about $1.2 million to train such a model. He says it was closer to $9-10 million about 18 months earlier, and that on-demand GPU rental (he names sfcompute.com, e.g. 10 H100s for four days) and distributed compute are lowering the barrier.
- Prediction: in a couple of years a model could be trained for roughly $100-150k, creating defensibility for a company.

chunks.heading: Layering every growth lever, including a TikTok account network
chunks.text:
- Cody describes his background as "degenerate growth tactics". Swell's mix includes:
  - cold email at close to 100,000 emails a month
  - paid ads across all channels
  - programmatic SEO for inbound traffic
  - a "TikTok cloud network" of about 100 accounts posting daily
- TikTok network mechanics: virtual machines plus proxy networks per account so they are not shadow banned. AI writes scripts, HeyGen avatars read them, background is removed, and a product recording is placed behind the avatar.
- Numbers: each video gets about 600-700 views, which across 100 accounts adds up to about 3.2-3.5 million views a month. He says branded searches for the platform rise over time.
- Principle: "take every growth lever that exists, wherever your target customer is," then layer the strategies on top of each other to "break the laws of physics" in marketing. Be present everywhere with educational content, media content or an offer.

chunks.heading: For You pages make content a numbers game
chunks.text:
- Cody's argument: TikTok invented "for you" content that the platform picks for you; YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, LinkedIn and Twitter have since copied it.
- Implication: you cannot predict what the algorithm will favor, so volume matters. Posting once a week gives four at-bats a month; more posts means more chances.
- Example: a friend posts 5-6 short videos a day on LinkedIn with about 7,000 followers and gets about 2.7 million views a month. One of those five videos usually goes much more viral than the rest.
- Baseball analogy: "if I hit 100 times, I'm gonna get on base 20 times."
- He applies this to B2B: produce many variations rather than a few precise pieces.

chunks.heading: Marketing advice: only start what you can repeat, and learn by doing
chunks.text:
- Best advice he received: "Don't even start the thing" unless it is repeatable. Ask whether you can do it indefinitely, every day, week or month, for two years or more. If not, "don't even start the thing because it won't make impact for your company."
- He contrasts this with "campaigns", a term he says came from the military via post-WWII advertising, with a start and an end. He prefers sustainable cadence.
- Advice for aspiring marketers: start a blog, get traffic to it, and sell something to that traffic. He says doing that puts you "in the top 1% of marketers in the world".
- He says the information is free on YouTube now (he runs a tactical YouTube channel), so courses are unnecessary. Imitate what others do and be a practitioner: "trial by fire", because tactics change fast (he was troubleshooting cold email that morning because what worked three days earlier had changed).
- Use AI to learn: ask Perplexity ("complexity AI" in the transcript) for a Google Ads curriculum and a YouTube video list per item; he estimates about 10 hours of study.
- Get technical: if a marketer can prompt AI to write Python scripts they become "god tier".
- Example: for a friend's company he scraped Toast's site for lead data, used a proxy to Google each company name and address to find its website on Google Maps, saved results to a folder, then ran a spreadsheet through Hunter.io and Phantombuster to find emails. He says this was hacked together with AI-written Python and no-code tools like Zapier, and would previously have needed engineering talent.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues that as AI drives feature parity and the cost of building software toward zero, distribution and brand are the only durable moats. He covers owned media (a16z, Arrow Electronics, Red Bull, Rupa Health's podcast), tracking branded search, bottom-up AI adoption, guardrails and domain vocabulary for AI output, and using social as a public idea-testing ground.

chunks.heading: Distribution beats product when feature parity is the default
chunks.text:
- Cody says "product is shit" is a deliberate provocation: he argues distribution is more important than product, and "product always wins" is a Silicon Valley mistake.
- If product A and product B have feature parity but A has better marketing and distribution, "product A is going to win every time, full stop."
- NetSuite is his go-to example. People who use it "despise it" with "a visceral hate," yet it still wins because of distribution and a switching-cost moat.
- He argues AI is pushing the cost of creating digital products toward zero. Competitors can copy any feature quickly and cheaply, so feature parity becomes universal. Engineering bandwidth used to be the biggest constraint in organizations.
- With no software differentiation left, he says the only way to win is better distribution.
- He notes this applies to digital products; physical and retail products have different constraints.

chunks.heading: Owned media as a moat (a16z, Arrow Electronics, Red Bull)
chunks.text:
- Cody says the best companies build owned media brands that sell to a well-defined target customer. "Our target customer is everyone" produces terrible media.
- **Method:** define exactly who you sell to, their pain points and the outcomes they want, then work back to the media to make.
- **a16z:** he says it sells a commodity (money) and differentiates through media distribution, by acquiring podcast networks and YouTubers across technology and VC.
- **Arrow Electronics:** a massive electronics components reseller. In the early 2000s it bought electronics blogs for their email lists and engineer audiences, then sponsored them to market directly to the engineers who asked which components to use. He calls it a flywheel for new customer acquisition.
- **Red Bull Media House:** treated as its own company that has to survive on its own.
- He advises running owned media like a separate company with its own P&L and sustainability.
- With a 400,000-person email list and a weekly podcast with 30,000 downloads, "you almost do whatever you want within an industry." Any new product line already has rails to launch on.
- **Cost of the grind:** he says it is hard, like "a diet" or "a lifestyle choice." Unlike a product built once and sold many times, media needs fresh ideas every week.

chunks.heading: How owned media funded itself and gave leverage at Rupa Health
chunks.text:
- Rupa Health was a marketplace aggregating specialty lab tests so people could order from multiple labs through one portal.
- Cody's team sold sponsorships on their podcast to the labs. Selling those slots covered production and the whole marketing and distribution operation, so it was cost-neutral on the line items.
- It also gave negotiating leverage with labs much larger than Rupa. When a lab pushed back on the percentage Rupa took per test, they offered a media package instead:
  - the lab's CEO on the podcast
  - 3 live classes
  - 20 posts across Rupa's social channels
  - 4 email write-ups sent to the full list
- He says this changed the leverage in the deal: "it allows you to punch above your weight."
- His point is that owned media is both distribution and negotiation leverage, and it is hard for competitors to copy.

chunks.heading: Media partnerships and the "digital gravity" model
chunks.text:
- Cody coined "digital gravity" and owns digitalgravitybook.com. The idea is to build digital mass on the internet so you have gravity in your category.
- A small mass has little pull. A larger mass catches more of the "comets" passing by and gets them into orbit around your brand. "You're Jupiter, you're not the Earth."
- **How to build it:** content engines and owned media that widen your footprint, so you are discoverable in social feeds and AI chat answers. He says people now discover products mostly on social media and AI chats.
- **Partnerships example:** with Alex Lieberman (co-founder of Morning Brew), who sells to a similar audience, he set up a marketing partnership. They run a shared webinar series every 6 weeks and share all leads. He plans 10 to 15 more deals like it over 12 months. He says this is only possible because he has an owned media network. With a 1,000-person list he'd be uninteresting to someone with 200,000.
- **Funnel view:** he says the funnel isn't clean. People sit at different stages at different times, so a large content library gives many touchpoints. His example was a company selling shower bases to hotel chains, where deal cycles ran 3 to 5 years. Keeping them top of mind meant making entertaining and educational industry media and weaving pains and outcomes into it.

chunks.heading: Brand as the only moat, and why content beats rising ad costs
chunks.text:
- Cody started in print-on-demand dropshipping, scraping Etsy, Redbubble and Amazon for winning products and remixing designs. It made money, but he built zero brands, so when the market shifted he had nothing to lean on.
- **His 2026 metric:** branded search volume. He tracks it in Google Search Console, looking at searches for the Graphed name each month, and builds a dashboard on it. The question is whether it rises month over month.
- He lives by "patience, persistence, and compound interest."
- **Why content:** in a paid ads category, cost per click might start at $1 and drift toward $5 as the arbitrage disappears. The way to combat that is to get more people searching for your company by name instead of competing for the same clicks.
- Education, thought leadership, and talking to pain points and desired outcomes are the best-performing content in his experience.
- Content makes organic customer acquisition cost slide toward zero, which offsets rising ad costs. He calls the rise in costs "the law of worsening click-throughs."
- He says to tell internal teams that brand is the number one filter, because eroding it prices you out of the market over the long term.
- **Suggested first step:** take a small share of budget already going to SEO or PR, pick one thing to do well (a weekly webinar or podcast plus an email newsletter), and run it for 12 months, then measure the impact. He says he has seen PR budgets spent spinning stories, and that the same money in owned media gives far more leverage.

chunks.heading: Using social as a testing ground for ideas
chunks.text:
- Cody's process: publish ideas, check impression data, and see what resonates.
- He says "For You" feeds (TikTok was the originator) show content based on what keeps people on platform, with no need for a social graph or followers. That gives an immediate feedback loop he treats as a "stress test" of an idea in public.
- When an idea gets traction, he goes deeper: a dedicated podcast episode, a 5,000-word blog post, or other formats.
- He says blogs and newsletters give slow, vague feedback (an email or two from friends).
- Podcasters can find the common thread across their top 20 episodes of the last 2 years, put the transcripts into an AI context window, and ask for a book outline and section drafts to beat up.
- He says average ideas are now a commodity. "Good ideas are now the hardest thing to come by."
- **His writing process:**
  - dictate stream-of-consciousness thoughts with SuperWhisper (Option+Space on his MacBook)
  - run them through software he built that reorganizes the logic and applies examples of his past writing
  - polish the final output himself, as a curator
- He was taught to write with "martial respect for the economy of words."

chunks.heading: Rolling out AI: bottom-up tooling, status incentives and an internal newsletter
chunks.text:
- **Bottom-up over mandate:** Cody says large "digital transformation" pushes are a mistake. Companies should give individual contributors the tooling to automate their own daily workflows. He says companies that lock down tooling lose, and those that supply it win.
- **Example of lockdown:** a friend's former SDR left a company that gave him an Apollo API key (a data enrichment tool for prospecting) for one that refused, which made him far less effective.
- **Example of a bad mandate:** a software company set a weekly minimum token usage, so one employee had AI split and recombine spreadsheet columns just to hit the limit.
- **Automate what people hate:** nobody likes lead enrichment in a CRM. Give them a HubSpot API key and a Perplexity API workflow to do the research and write it into HubSpot. He says this reduces burnout.
- **Share and incentivize:** create a Slack channel or fireside chat where people post "here's the thing I built," with a Notion tutorial so others can deploy it. This creates status, and status creates a flywheel.
- **What drives people:** "money, time, and status." Status is the easiest lift for organizations (a call-out from a boss or leader, a badge of honor).
- **Internal newsletter:** at a previous company he sent one every Tuesday morning documenting what they saw working. It made him a thought leader internally and gave him leverage to get more resources. His point is to market internally like you market externally.
- He suggests asking employees to write LinkedIn posts about how they use the product.
- **Measure outcomes, not activity:** a high performer's leading indicators (messages, conversations) may look subpar while revenue is strong. The hard part is defining the outcome. Early-stage companies often can't say if success is signups, revenue, pipeline or closed deals. His line: "I don't care how you get there. As long as you get there."
- **Automate what exists first:** look at what you do manually and replicate it with the tool. Treat AI like Excel or PowerPoint, a tool in the belt, and avoid "pie in the sky" ideas.

chunks.heading: AI guardrails, domain vocabulary and token abundance
chunks.text:
- **Set "nos," not "yeses":** it is easier to list lines you can't cross and let people experiment inside them than to list approved actions. Anything that could get the company sued should not be in the team's vocabulary. He says to hire people who love the game of finding arbitrage within the rules.
- **Codebase guardrails at Graphed:** their code base spells out what agents may do (only TypeScript for front end and back end, and defined UI specs, e.g. what a "card" is). He says typed languages suit AI because it is discrete and must pass checks.
- **Speed example:** he asked Cursor for a hover-isolation feature on a line chart legend, and it wrote the code and opened a PR. He reviewed and shipped it within an hour. He says this is only possible with that infrastructure set up from the start.
- **Standardized data:** a Google Analytics 4 connection looks the same for customer A and B, so the agent can be good at it once. He says messy data warehouses make it hard to build a semantic layer or knowledge graph.
- **Average output problem:** LLMs trained on the internet give the average, and value sits in the top 10% or top 1%. Test: ask Claude to write a sales email as a top 1% direct response copywriter, then ask it to edit as a 40-year veteran newspaper editor conscious of the economy of words. The result is far higher quality.
- **Vocabulary:** he says the hardest part is having the words to describe the outcome. He built a podcast for himself to learn graphic design terms, e.g. describing a TV-fuzz texture as "5% opacity" with "a compounding split of dots that are growing in size."
- **Domain experts get more valuable.** Deep technical knowledge lets you direct AI the way you would brief a VA, but with far better results.
- **Token abundance:** he says the cost of intelligence is heading toward zero. He cites an open-source model from China that benchmarked just below Claude Opus 4.6 at 1/20th of the cost within weeks. "How do I not think from a what-we-can-do constraint?" With everything possible, deciding the right thing becomes the hard part.
- **PM example:** a friend's product managers were each building internal products with Claude Code and pitching them, but nobody wanted to buy them. It "looks like work is happening."

chunks.heading: Cody's background and what he's building
chunks.text:
- About 7 years in early-stage startups, after e-commerce and a B2B marketing agency where his boss had been through Y Combinator and taught him to invest in brand.
- At the agency he worked with Fortune 500 clients on digital adoption in their marketing organizations: design the process, educate the teams, deploy it internally.
- He joined Rupa Health as employee 9 or 10, and says he helped take it from a $20 million to a $110 million valuation in about 6 months. The team grew from about 10 to about 150 in 18 months.
- He is founder of Graphed (graphed.com), an AI data analyst for growth teams that unifies data sources, builds charts, live dashboards and reports, and answers questions about data. It recently released an MCP so it works inside Claude Code, Claude Cowork, ChatGPT or other chat apps.
- His specialty is early product adoption: first 10, 100 and 1,000 customers.
- He is active on Twitter and LinkedIn, and hosts a podcast interviewing people in his industry about what is working now. He says that content can be packaged and cold-emailed to prospects, who see it as free knowledge.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains how solopreneurs and creators can build trust and revenue with long-form content (podcast, newsletter, YouTube) fed by short-form clips, and how to use AI as a task automator grounded in expert source material rather than generic LLM knowledge. He also covers high-volume posting on "for you" feeds and remixing top performers.

chunks.heading: Using AI to produce content: audit tasks, then feed it source material
chunks.text:
- Cody's rule for adopting AI: audit your current systems and workflows, then automate the parts AI can handle so the team focuses on high-impact work. He estimates "80% of them can probably be automated in some way."
- He says not to pay consultants such as McKinsey or Gartner to rebuild everything "AI ready". Ask which tasks AI can take over today and implement those.
- Example: a friend consults for real estate firms, audits their workflows, builds AI-enabled operations, and automates about 60% of daily tasks.
- AI's core strength, in his words: taking unstructured data and structuring it. Example: give it a 45-90 minute transcript and ask for 10 insights on digital marketing.
- He aims for AI to get work 80-90% of the way there, with a human doing the last 10%.
- He treats AI as a tool "like Excel", good for some jobs and bad for others, and doubts AGI is near. His reason is that the compute needed to mimic a human brain's neurons doesn't exist yet.
- Even automating 10% of your own work puts you "so much farther ahead" in five years. He calls AI automation skills the most desired skill set, and says "AI automation" is the fastest-growing keyword he has seen. His tip: if you're a coach with nothing to sell, build an AI automation course and "a 1000% sell."

chunks.heading: Why AI content sounds average, and the fix: a walled garden of source material
chunks.text:
- Cody agrees that AI content is average when it writes from the model's general knowledge. LLMs learn from the whole internet, and "the average is pretty average."
- The target is top-10% or top-1% content. To get it, give the AI constraints and source material, "a walled garden that it can work from."
- Podcasts and calls make ideal source material because they capture real human expertise.
- Example: asking AI to write "Google Ads for apartments" gives useless output. Interview someone who only runs Google Ads for apartments, then extract their knowledge from the transcript into a blog post, LinkedIn posts, a Twitter thread and clips. He says the output is "10x" better.
- For coaches and creators: record every call and conversation, then repurpose it into clips, blog posts and other formats. Coaches use Swell AI to turn calls into follow-up next steps and one-pagers for clients, plus clips and keyword-based blog posts.

chunks.heading: SEO playbook: AI blog posts built from what already ranks
chunks.text:
1. Pick a target keyword. His example: "social media management for fintech startups."
2. Collect everything ranking on page 1 for it: YouTube video transcripts and blog post text.
3. Put it all into one context window.
4. Prompt 1: write a blog post outline for the keyword, based on the source material.
5. Prompt 2 (chained): write the full article from that outline and the same source material.

- He calls the result "top 5%" of content writers you could hire.
- His test results: this type of content reached page 1 "in like 24 hours." His personal blog (domain authority about 12) ranks around position 3 for "Google Ads for apartments," with about 30 minutes of dwell time.
- His reasoning: the content works because it draws on information already shown to provide value, not on the AI's general knowledge.

chunks.heading: Content funnel for creators, coaches and course sellers
chunks.text:
- Cody says short-form (TikTok, Shorts, Reels) can't sell high-ticket offers directly. The trust-building formats are podcasts, email newsletters and long-form YouTube.
- The playbook he sees working:
  - Short-form is top of funnel: it introduces people to you.
  - It leads into owned media: email plus long-form content.
  - You stay in front of them on social every day.
- Why long-form wins: an hour a week in someone's ears is a one-to-many conversation that builds deep trust. Buyers arrive ready: "you don't have to convince them of anything." He cites a sales call that morning where the prospect said they'd watched all his videos and just wanted the link.
- Symbiotic loop he describes:
  - Record a weekly long-form podcast with guests.
  - Chop it into short-form clips.
  - Email episodes to every contact in your target audience.
  - Send clip viewers to a lead magnet, then into a drip nurture of more content.
- He says the $3k-style purchase usually follows about six weeks of emails, episodes and social exposure.
- His "digital gravity" analogy: gravity is the byproduct of mass, and digital mass is content. More content means more gravity, which means more influence and inbound. He says funnels don't work like a top-to-bottom slide. People "fly by," enter your rotation for weeks, then buy.

chunks.heading: Sustainable content production for a solo founder
chunks.text:
- Content is a grind. He says to optimize for longevity: posting daily for 30 days won't move a business, but posting daily for 2 years will.
- Lean on other experts for source material. Interviews with guests cost about 2 hours a week (roughly an hour of prep and an hour of talking), and the knowledge comes from them.
- Build long-form content that gets chopped into clips, then repurposed into blog posts and newsletters, and automate as much of that as possible.
- Time saved goes to human work: sales and client-facing time.
- Distribution test he poses: know exactly where your buyers spend time, online and offline, and be in their lives daily, weekly and monthly. His example: marketing to photographers only on LinkedIn, when they're on Pinterest, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. If you can't answer, "drop everything else" until you can. Knowing this puts you in the top 10%.

chunks.heading: Social posting: volume, remixing winners, and the For You page
chunks.text:
- Cody's logic against "saturation": TikTok-style For You feeds (now on Instagram, YouTube, Twitter and increasingly LinkedIn) reward content by consumption, so only good content gets shown. You aren't clogging a followers' feed. A TikTok video can hit 1M views with no followers.
- On Instagram, he says you can post 4-6 reels a day and one will take about 80% of the views.
- His Twitter routine:
  - Posts about 70 tweets a week, scheduled in advance.
  - Weekly, reviews the last 3 months of data and takes the top 10% performers.
  - Remixes those winners with new angles. Some tweets resurface every 6 weeks and reliably get about 100,000 impressions.
- Claims from the transcript: 85% of his account growth came in the last 12 months. He says to "get back to the basics": hooks plus interesting ideas.
- On repetition: "short memories," so reposting a tweet from 3 months ago goes viral again. He says the posting ceiling is "2x or 3x higher than what people think." Once a day is the minimum, and the ceiling is roughly 4-6 per day on Reels.
- More posts mean more at-bats and more data for deciding what to make next.
- "Chicken and rice" analogy: same core ideas, different seasoning per channel (Twitter, shorts, blog posts).
- Each channel gets one action to drive: Twitter, read and click to something you own; shorts, click or go Google the brand name (what influencer/UGC content has become); blog posts, sign up or download. Write more of the 20% of posts that produce 80% of sign-ups.

chunks.heading: Automating job roles with AI agents
chunks.text:
- His view: automate tasks, and a job role is a bundle of tasks. Example: a social media manager's loop is publish, see what works, find top performers in the back catalog, make more.
- Swell AI is testing an internal agent (called "Jenna") that does clip identification, captions, auto-cropping for active speaker, scheduling and publishing, data analysis, and re-clipping top performers from the catalog.
- He expects solopreneurs to hire AI agents like employees. The price he gives: about $150 versus $1,800/month for good offshore talent. Even at roughly 50% of a human's quality he'd take it, and one agent could manage 100 accounts.
- An SEO agent could do keyword research, verify volume, write, publish and index, check which posts produce sign-ups, then write more from the best performers.
- He thinks AI avatars aren't something people want to interact with, but an AI phone-answering service for restaurants (plugging orders into Toast or Square POS) is a likely standard, and he's working with a company in that space.
- Host's example (not Cody's): automated outreach to new trial signups.

chunks.heading: Cody's career path and background
chunks.text:
- Parents both owned businesses. He started with graphic design, then t-shirts, print-on-demand and ecommerce, then marketing ecommerce, then a B2B marketing agency doing digital strategy for Fortune 500 manufacturers (windows, doors, wood paneling).
- His advice: follow whatever opportunity presents itself, and "walk through it or run through it." The best things happened by pulling the string rather than planning.
- Agency lesson: successful agencies do one thing well and say no to more than they say yes to. His full-service agency work was hard to systematize.
- Rupa Health: he joined as employee 6 and says the company went from about a $20M valuation to $110M in about 6 months. Headcount went from 6 to 70 over 18 months. Rupa is a marketplace for specialty lab test ordering, taking a 7% rate on top of margin.
- His bet there: content is the only durable differentiation when product and global talent are easy to copy. They launched a weekly podcast and weekly live classes and turned each into blog posts, clips, social posts and newsletters.
- Results he cites: the podcast went from nonexistent to a top-20 US medical podcast in about 6 months (around 180,000 downloads a month when he left). Live classes became a revenue center by charging for continuing education credits. At peak his content marketing ops team was 15-20 people.
- AI turning point: he says around October 2023 outputs got "80% of the way there" to usable. He left Rupa and co-founded Swell AI with Max to productize that workflow: one expert conversation becomes a week of media, so a one-person marketing team can function like ten.
- His Twitter bio: self-funded startup beating VC-backed companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider explains how he built an owned-media content engine at Rupa Health and turned it into Swell AI. He argues for interview-led podcasts chopped into clips, automating 5% of your process at a time with AI, and treating your content library as the differentiator while marketing becomes a profit center.

chunks.heading: Why Cody built an AI content engine: owned media, social discovery, and the erosion of search
chunks.text:
- Cody started in e-commerce (print-on-demand), then worked at a B2B agency doing digital strategy for building-materials manufacturers (windows, wood paneling, shower bases). That taught him marketing when purchase decisions have a very long time horizon.
- At Rupa Health he joined as person six and ran content from zero. He says the company went from a $20 million to a $120 million valuation in about six months, by building owned media channels with their own distribution.
- He describes three trends behind Swell AI: search eroding as the default way to choose vendors; buyers knowing more than the salesperson; and social becoming the place discovery starts.
- The agency lesson: the biggest customer feedback was that buyers "knew more than the salesperson" about the product. His response was to create owned media channels to cut through the noise.
- His thesis for Rupa, which marketed to physicians (high purchasing power, hard to reach): start from what the audience wants to hear (other practitioners talking about their businesses and research), then record those conversations and publish them.
- At peak the Rupa content team was about 25 people including freelancers and writers. Content operations became a headache to manage, which is what pushed him toward AI automation.

chunks.heading: The content engine: one long-form interview feeds every channel
chunks.text:
- Cody's core workflow: publish a long-form podcast weekly, chop it into clips, and schedule the clips to social platforms daily. That covers every place people discover a brand.
- Younger people increasingly begin discovery on Instagram, LinkedIn and TikTok, using social as a search engine for awareness content, and may then go deeper into blog posts. He expects this to flow up the age ladder, as Facebook did from colleges to "my grandma".
- Rupa repurposed podcasts and live classes into clips, blog posts, newsletters and white papers.
- Swell AI's first version was a Google Drive folder: customers uploaded MP3s, Cody ran the software locally and manually emailed back show notes and blog posts. It started with podcasters because friends already used podcasts to grow their businesses.
- Outputs Swell templates can produce: show notes, newsletters, 2,000-word blog posts, keyword identification, takeaway recaps, course structuring (coaches drop in a two-hour recording and ask for 5-10 minute sections), and email copy for podcasters to paste into their ESP.

chunks.heading: Why social beats search for trust
chunks.text:
- Cody argues there is distrust of content "that doesn't have a face to it". Incentives are aligned on social: if a creator recommends a bad bar, people stop trusting that creator. Websites face no repercussion for bad information; they mostly just want a sign-up.
- Test he uses: ask someone to name the author of the last article they read from Google; most can't.
- He still runs programmatic SEO as one of Swell's marketing strategies. He does not say to abandon search, only to shift more resources to social because that is where people increasingly begin.
- AI-written SEO content has flooded results. He cites Google's recent content quality update, after which hundreds of sites dropped to near zero overnight while Reddit and Quora (user-generated forums) benefited.
- Example for B2B: if the ICP is interior designers, a founder who hosts a weekly podcast interviewing interior designers about their careers and mistakes, emailed to them each week, builds large trust.
- Warm audiences improve outbound: he says open and response rates on cold emails rise when prospects have already been receiving your content, so a BDR reaching out lands on a warm lead.

chunks.heading: Becoming a media company: results and examples
chunks.text:
- Cody's biotech client (about 20 people): built an email list of biotech founders in the US and started a weekly podcast about 12 months earlier. Result: nearly everyone in the industry listens weekly, investors send inbound for their portfolio companies, warm intros arrive from people wanting to be guests, and ICPs he says could not be reached by cold email now come inbound.
- The same media asset gave the small company leverage in negotiating with large organizations such as Roche and Genentech.
- Marketing becomes a profit center: at Rupa they built a top-20 medical podcast in about six months, reaching about 150,000 downloads a month. They sold ad space to Athletic Greens, and that deal paid the entire salary of the growth department.
- Long-standing examples he points to:
  - Arrow Electronics (a $6 billion market cap component reseller): selling a commodity, so differentiation comes from content.
  - Red Bull: "selling sugar water" but built one of the coolest brands through content, including its F1 team sponsorship. He says its media house makes more money than product sales.
  - Refine Labs / Chris Walker: a weekly podcast pair (one interview show, one solo deep dive) chopped into clips and distributed on social; he has done it for 10 years.
  - Comedians: sit down for conversations, chop clips, distribute across channels.
- He calls this "still a blue ocean". He and his team only stumbled on the process in 2020; AI tools now let it scale for the first time.

chunks.heading: How to adopt AI in marketing without a company overhaul
chunks.text:
- Cody pushes back on "AI transformation" framing. His method: find 5% of your current process to automate, then 10%, 15%, 30%, 60%, until about 80% is automated, without changing company structure or workflow.
- He says companies that swing to the overhaul end of the spectrum tend to fail at implementation.
- The team's role shifts from "grunt labor" to curator, focused on high-touch work humans do better.
- Claim: a team of five "10x marketers" given these tools becomes "100x marketers".
- Example: a team writing two articles a week can write 20 a week because the first draft takes about two minutes from source material. Saved templates also lock in brand voice, which makes output more consistent.
- Swell's "text sources" feature lets a team supply a raw unstructured text file, extract insights, write a LinkedIn post per insight in the brand's tone, and save the sequence as a reusable template.

chunks.heading: How Swell AI works under the hood
chunks.text:
- Transcription: audio is chopped into pieces and transcribed in parallel, then stitched together, so a 60-minute episode doesn't need 60 minutes of compute. The transcript then acts as a "walled garden" the AI writes from.
- Clip identification mimics a human editor: find the core ideas in a 45-minute episode, extract the core insight for each (using "entity identification"), write a roughly 10-word hook for it, then find a roughly 30-second clip that supports the hook.
- Product progression: MP3 first, then MP4 (video clips), then text sources. Recent additions: auto-cropping, and on-brand caption templates with overlays.

chunks.heading: Content library as the differentiator, books from interviews, and the roadmap
chunks.text:
- Cody's view: building products and doing distribution are both getting easier, so the differentiator is a content library only you have (industry experts, proprietary data).
- Vision: query your full back catalog (white papers, internal docs, hundreds of episodes), use results as source documents, and repurpose into a LinkedIn post or other asset. Swell would also pull trend data from TikTok and YouTube Shorts APIs and surface clip and content ideas, like a "Pinterest" of your own library.
- Book workflow: a customer with about 150 episodes consolidated them into categories and is producing about 20 micro-chapters. He uses a template with his tone, style and voice plus the whole-book outline, then combines sections in post. The goal is a first draft to the publisher to get the advance. Cody compares it to how "How to Win Friends and Influence People" was written (five journalists interviewing 300 people over about a year and a half), with the first research pass automated.
- As model token limits grow, an entire back catalog could go into one source document: generate an outline, edit it, then draft the book.
- Roadmap: send clips straight from Swell to scheduling (starting with YouTube Shorts), then pull social performance data to find best performers and suggest similar content from the library (about a year out), plus SMS and email management. The aim is one place for source content, repurposing, distribution and analytics, in service of testing, doing less of what doesn't work, and more of what does.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains his Claude Code setup for growth work: one env file of API keys, five parallel terminals, and Claude building software to automate everything. He shares concrete builds: 100 landing pages in 30 minutes, 40 Facebook ads from code templates, and a LinkedIn engager to cold email pipeline built in 15 minutes.

chunks.heading: Claude Code as the GTM engineering stack: replacing N8N and "middle work"
chunks.text:
- Cody says all his work now starts in Claude Code. He opens five terminals and runs growth activities in parallel.
- Setup is simple: one environment file holding the API keys for his entire software stack. For whatever he is working on, he has Claude build software to automate it.
- If something can't be automated, he has Claude do the "middle work" instead. He borrows the term from the Linear founder: (1) you have an idea, (2) you do all the work of materializing it, (3) you polish the final output. Claude now does step 2.
- To get started: make a directory, open a terminal and cd into it, run Claude Code, and describe what you want to automate. In his words, "It is seriously this easy."
- He replaced all the AI automations he ran in N8N with code. He deployed a server to Railway and did not build it himself; Claude built it using the Railway API. Now he goes straight to code with "no N8N middleware."

chunks.heading: Building 100 landing pages in 30 minutes for Google Ads
chunks.text:
- His Google Ads strategy: find the converting keywords, then build a dedicated landing page for each one. This raises the campaign's conversion rate.
- The manual process was to extract converting keywords and build each page by hand, with the target keyword as the H1 and repeated in the first paragraph of the hero section.
- Now he gives Claude the list of target keywords and tells it to make a landing page for each. The pages are built "literally seconds later."
- Under the hood, the pages are hosted in the Strapi CMS, and Claude Code generates them by hitting the Strapi API.

chunks.heading: "All design is just code": generating 40 Facebook ads in minutes
chunks.text:
- Cody had an epiphany at 4am that all design is just code. Figma's foundation is code, so Facebook ads can be made with code too.
- He gave Claude a design example and had it build a Facebook ad template out of React components. The template is exported as an image using HTML to canvas.
- He then had Claude Code iterate over the template to produce 40 variations.
- His testing strategy: make many variations that each focus on a different positioning or messaging concept, then move the winners into their own campaigns.
- At the time of writing he was building a connection to the Facebook Marketing API with Claude Code, so the 40 ads could be bulk uploaded to an ad set.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn engager extraction to cold email pipeline
chunks.text:
- The idea: viral LinkedIn posts are often engaged with by his exact target customer, so he mines those engagers.
- He had Claude wire up a Slack function where he drops in a LinkedIn post URL. The flow:
  1. The URL goes to Phantom Buster, which pulls the profile URLs of everyone who engaged.
  2. Apollo.io enriches those profiles with emails and first names.
  3. Million Verifier validates the emails.
  4. Valid contacts are added to an Instantly AI campaign that cold emails them.
- He says this whole pipeline was built in about 15 minutes.

chunks.heading: Business idea: portfolio of "Best Exercises for X" digital downloads
chunks.text:
- Cody sees a big opportunity in building a portfolio of "best exercises for X outcome" products, each one a digital download.
- The real value comes from scale: build tens of thousands of them, then bundle the aggregate and sell the IP, which he thinks would be a very good business.
- Distribution would be only Amazon and Amazon ads.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues AI answer engines mostly scrape Google's first two result pages, so brands must flood their niche with content and media placements to build "digital gravity". He also covers YouTube as the top social channel, free apps as lead gen for services, and cheap ad tactics.

chunks.heading: AI answer engines scrape Google page 1 and 2, so the play is "digital gravity"
chunks.text:
- Cody says he was asked more about AI chat search in two weeks than in the prior 12 months. It is now top of mind for founders and marketers.
- He spoke to the founder of Profound (Answer Engine Optimization software), who told him 95% of the searches they see are web based. Those web searches get scraped from Google.
- His own internal data shows AI answer engines scraping page 1 and page 2 of Google.
- The job for a brand: publish more content in its niche and earn more media placements on page 1 and page 2.
- Scale needed: "I'm not talking about 10x content, I'm talking about 1000x. You need surface area, a lot of surface area to show up in AI search engines."
- Mental model: more surface area makes more digital mass, more digital mass makes more digital gravity, and digital gravity makes more influence in your niche.
- His timing view: "Make a plan, the arbitrage is now."

chunks.heading: YouTube as the most valuable social platform
chunks.text:
- Cody has been investing heavily in YouTube, based on two observations:
  - YouTube is now streamed more than Netflix. On Netflix's recent earnings call they were asked about YouTube as a threat.
  - Someone sent him a photo of them watching a podcast he appeared on through their smart TV in their living room.
- His argument: you can now be in a person's home, talking to them daily, weekly or monthly, as much content as you can get out the door.
- Comparison he draws: "cable news brainwashed my grammy from her living room, you can now do this too."

chunks.heading: Free small apps as lead gen for higher-priced services
chunks.text:
- Cody highlights Relay Commerce (relaycommerce.io), which builds many small-scope Shopify apps and gives them away free.
- The goal of the free apps is lead gen for the company's main consulting services.
- Apps he lists that they own: relo, peel, smartrr, flocker, fomo, salespop, smartrmail, bookthatapp. All of them push toward the consulting services.
- Takeaway: many cheap, narrow free tools act as a distribution funnel into a higher-priced service.

chunks.heading: Cheap paid traffic tactics: Twitter and TikTok
chunks.text:
- **Twitter ads for AI music discovery:** he audited an ad where a company makes music with AI and uses cheap Twitter ad traffic to create discovery. For these ads he suggests global targeting with a CPC bid cap of $0.01; he reports seeing $.005 link clicks.
- **TikTok ads with a $2 CPM bid cap:**
  - Clippers are being paid about $1 per 1000 impressions.
  - TikTok lets you set a bid cap of $2 CPM. When he tested it he got a $1.64 CPM.
  - Benefit: no headache managing clippers who may bot farm views to drain a dedicated budget.
  - He calls it an easy way to build top-of-funnel discovery.

chunks.heading: Building 100+ ad variants with AI automation
chunks.text:
His thesis: more ad variant testing means cheaper CPCs. Two workflows:

**1. Video ads**
- Prompt Perplexity for 10 pain points related to the product.
- Ask for 10 thirty-second ad scripts per pain point, each using a hook from a hook list.
- Sample hooks: "You won't believe how easy this is…", "What happens next will shock you…", "Struggling with [problem]? Here's a solution.", "Tired of wasting time on [task]? This will save you hours.", "Say goodbye to [pain point] once and for all.", "Stop wasting money on [ineffective solution]! Try this instead.", "3 simple steps to solve [common problem].", "If you [describe your target], stop scrolling!"
- Use n8n to take the transcripts, upload them to the HeyGen API, then upload the ads to Facebook Ads.

**2. ChatGPT image API ads**
- Prompt Perplexity for 10 pain points, then 10 ad concepts per pain point.
- Pull competitor ads from the Facebook Ad Library.
- Feed competitor ads, your product images and the 100 concepts to the ChatGPT image API via an n8n flow to generate an ad per concept.
- Upload all ads to Facebook Ads.

chunks.heading: n8n as a marketer's lever, and product ideas around it
chunks.text:
- Cody calls n8n "might be the most OP thing ive used as a marketer."
- Insight: n8n flows are just structured JSON, so he asks Perplexity to write n8n JSON for him.
- Tooling note: he deploys self-hosted n8n on Railway.com for $5 per month.
- Idea he drew from this: an app that works as an n8n flow-building assistant you chat with, which writes the code. He says search volume for "n8n json" is "going nuclear."

chunks.heading: Go-to-market ideas he shared
chunks.text:
- **AI study podcast:** people want a podcast built from what they are supposed to learn. Build it on the Nari Labs Dia model, turning user-supplied source material into an engaging podcast. Go-to-market is TikToks with the hook "this app saved my brain".
- **AI music generator:** use cheap Twitter ad traffic to get the first listeners (see the Twitter tactic above).
- **n8n JSON generator:** the chat-based flow builder described above.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues ad-supported media is a grind (constant outbound, budget cuts, advertiser management) and the real money comes from using media as a vehicle to sell a product you own. He gives B2B and DTC examples plus quick distribution ideas like short-form LinkedIn and AI-written long-tail blog posts from webinars.

chunks.heading: Media is a vehicle for selling an owned product, not the product itself
chunks.text:
- Cody calls media "a terrible business" if the revenue comes from selling ads.
- A friend who owns a big email newsletter makes great money, but "selling ads is a grind": constant outbounding for sponsors, managing advertiser expectations, and budgets that get cut overnight.
- Cody says every media business owner he has talked to says "the juice is just not worth the squeeze."
- His fix: sell a product you own through the media.
- Key takeaway in his words: "Media isn't the product. Media is the vehicle to sell something."

chunks.heading: Owned-media-plus-product examples (B2B and DTC)
chunks.text:
- Cody cites Logan Paul doing Prime as proof: "ads don't make you a billionaire." He makes the same point about Jimmy (MrBeast) selling chocolate.
- **B2B example: Workweek.** It builds podcasts for B2B niches. Example: the Wolf of Franchises podcast sells Krokit.com to its audience. Cody says that from back channels he heard "they print."
- **DTC example: DearMedia.** It builds podcasts for consumers, then builds DTC brands on top of them. Example: The Skinny Confidential sells body shaping devices to its audience.
- Pattern: build the audience first (podcast, newsletter), then launch a product the audience already trusts you to recommend.

chunks.heading: Short-form LinkedIn: pick a format and let it rip
chunks.text:
- Cody says short-form LinkedIn content is "still just going" and tells people to just do it.
- The tactic: find a format and repeat it consistently.
- He notes that when new content goes viral, it resurrects old content, so a back catalog keeps paying off.

chunks.heading: Turn webinars into long-tail SEO traffic with AI
chunks.text:
Cody's workflow for getting more views on webinar recordings:
1. Get the transcript of the webinar.
2. Have AI list 20 long-tail keywords related to the webinar.
3. Have AI write a blog post for each keyword.
4. Post the blogs to your site and get them indexed.
5. Embed the webinar recording on each page.

His summary: "simple."

chunks.heading: Business ideas and distribution plans
chunks.text:
- **YouTube thumbnail library subscription.** Distribution: blog posts targeting long-tail keywords. Also scrape YouTubers' emails from their About pages (he suggests using Fiverr for the scrape) and cold email 100,000 people a month.
- **AI job description writer.** Growth: an exact-match domain plus backlinks, and Google Ads on job description writer keywords.
