chunks.heading: Content marketing and podcast tools Cody recommends
chunks.text:
- **Swell AI:** an AI content marketing team that turns videos into clips, blog posts and newsletters. His pitch is to make your company a media company to grow your brand, build trust and get more inbound leads.
- **PodcastGuestLaunch.com:** books you as a guest on podcasts. Cody says they have booked him on 30+ shows.
- **Acclaim Podcasting:** podcast newsletter growth, claiming to add 5,000+ subscribers a month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues software signup-to-paid activation works like a YouTube video: the homepage is the thumbnail/title promise and onboarding must deliver the lightbulb moment fast. He also shares concrete tactics: a high-volume Twitter plus DM automation that nearly doubled his newsletter in 4 weeks, a directory-link plus indexing playbook for local SEO, and a "Google Ads for XYZ" YouTube idea.

chunks.heading: Software activation mirrors a YouTube video: the promise, then the delivery
chunks.text:
- Cody drew this from reviewing the signup flow with the engineering team of a seed-stage startup he was consulting for. He says YouTube videos and software activation to paid have "the same biology."
- A good YouTube video needs a thumbnail and title combination that earns the click. Then it must deliver on that promise as soon as possible so the viewer actually consumes the media.
- In software, the homepage is the thumbnail/title. It makes a promise.
- Immediately after signup, the product has to deliver on what the homepage promised. That delivery is what produces activation to paid.
- Activation is the user's "lightbulb moment." The goal is to reach it as fast as possible, so build the signup-to-activation flow to instigate that moment.
- The promise is an opportunity for trust. If it isn't delivered, it "erodes all trust instantly."

chunks.heading: Business idea: summary newsletters of podcasts people select
chunks.text:
- Cody found a company that summarizes podcasts a user selects into a newsletter for them.
- After backchanneling with friends, he heard it was doing about $50,000 a month.
- He says AI is "for sure" writing the summaries.
- Its acquisition strategy is ranking for podcast-related keywords.

chunks.heading: Business idea: "Google Ads for XYZ" YouTube channel
chunks.text:
- Thousands of keywords follow the pattern "google ads for XYZ."
- When searched on Google, YouTube videos rank on the front page for them.
- The play:
  1. Start a YouTube channel and make videos that target these keywords.
  2. Monetize the channel.
  3. Promote Google Ads-related software and earn affiliate commissions.
  4. Upsell Google Ads as a service.

chunks.heading: Local SEO playbook: directory links plus an indexing bot
chunks.text:
- Building the first foundational links for a local business is hard. Cody's answer is directory links.
- The problem: directory links don't get seen easily because the directory sites are huge. Example: Mapquest has 12M pages. An indexing tool is needed to get the linking pages seen.
- The process:
  1. Buy directory links on Fiverr.
  2. Submit the links the Fiverr seller provides to the SpeedyIndex Telegram bot for indexing.
- Result: he did this for a friend's website and got 118 links built in 7 days.
- SpeedyIndex is a Telegram bot that indexes links you built for your site.

chunks.heading: Personal newsletter growth: Twitter cadence, thread CTA and DM automation
chunks.text:
- Cody decided to grow his newsletter and almost doubled it in 4 weeks, reaching about 100 new subscribers a day.
- The system:
  1. Post 70 tweets a week: 10 per day, one every hour from 7am to 5pm.
  2. Add a call to action to subscribe to the newsletter on every post, as a thread reply on a 10-minute delay.
  3. DM every new follower asking them to subscribe to the newsletter. He automated this entirely with Phantom Buster.

chunks.heading: Tools Cody lists and uses for content, bookings and outbound
chunks.text:
- Swell AI: an AI content marketing engine that turns videos into clips, blog posts and newsletters. Cody's framing: make your company into a media company to grow your brand, build trust and get more inbound leads.
- PodcastGuestLaunch.com: gets you booked as a guest on podcasts. Cody says they've booked him on 30+ shows.
- Acclaim Podcasting: podcast newsletter growth, which Cody describes as growing a podcast email newsletter by 5,000+ subs a month.
- SalesQL: a LinkedIn email scraping tool that finds anyone's personal email and the emails they've had at previous jobs.
- SpeedyIndex: the Telegram indexing bot used in the local SEO playbook above.
- Assembly: scheduling software from a friend that Cody likes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A May 2024 newsletter issue where Cody argues newsletter values are crashing (a consolidation opportunity), that founders should build in public as media companies, and shares business ideas (an unlimited influencer outreach agency, an exact-match ebook domain) plus AI-written SEO articles and affiliate bounties.

chunks.heading: Newsletter values are heading toward zero, creating a consolidation opportunity
chunks.text:
- Cody says a friend who owns one of the big AI newsletters told him he is "scooping up newsletters for next to nothing."
- His reasons for the collapse:
  - Beehiiv and Substack made starting a newsletter easier than ever, so the market got saturated.
  - Content is a grind. Most people can't make it sustainably, so burnout is imminent.
  - There is more ad inventory than people who want to buy it.
- His prediction: "This space is going to crash."
- The opportunity he sees is for brands to buy these newsletters cheaply and consolidate them.

chunks.heading: Creator-first founders: build in public becomes the norm
chunks.text:
- Cody argues startups have become "a spectator sport." He says he wishes he had written that line first.
- About 200M people in the US want to start a business, and they want to watch and obsess over startups like Formula 1.
- Ride-alongs, build-in-public posts and vlogs of startup life are a "blue ocean strategy" and a differentiator.
- He says this gives founders leverage with customers, investors and marketing partnership negotiations.
- He predicts doing investor updates in public will become the norm.
- His summary: "Every company will be a media company. Start now or die on the vine."

chunks.heading: Business idea: an "ebook generator ai" site
chunks.text:
- Cody stumbled on the keyword "ebook generator ai" and calls it "easily a $10k a month product."
- Plan:
  - Buy an exact-match domain.
  - Build links.
  - Rank for the keyword.
  - Get paid.

chunks.heading: Business idea: an agency that does unlimited influencer outreach
chunks.text:
- The idea came from a founder client of Acclaim Podcasting, who wanted to reach out to YouTubers for marketing partnerships for their software but found it very time-consuming.
- The model: unlimited influencer research, outreach, negotiation, tracking and affiliate reporting, charged at $3,000 a month.
- How to run it:
  - YouTube channels show the creators' emails.
  - Hire a person on Fiverr to scrape them.
  - Buy domains similar to the client's company name.
  - Use Instantly for cold email.

chunks.heading: Using Perplexity Pro to write articles that rank
chunks.text:
- Cody saw a tweet about Perplexity Pro one-shot writing "how to" articles, and tried it with "how to shopify xyz".
- Results:
  - It one-shot wrote an 1,100 word article that was classified as 82% human written.
  - It even wrote code that rendered perfectly when copy-pasted into WordPress.
  - He published 5 articles as a test, and they reached page 2 of Google within 24 hours.
- His conclusion: "Search as we know it is so done."

chunks.heading: Affiliate bounties to get social content about your software
chunks.text:
- Cody gets emails like this from Descript and calls it a great way to get people to make social content about your software.
- Elements that make it work:
  - A specific thing they want you to do.
  - A time limit, which creates urgency.
  - Stated expectations of quality.
- His advice: make your own version of this.

chunks.heading: Generating 1,000 ads with AI (content he recommends)
chunks.text:
Cody calls a video showing a creator's process of making 1,000 ads with AI for a client "one of the most insane things I've ever seen." His takeaways:
- Stack: Midjourney, DALL-E and a Figma workflow that builds thousands of display ad variations in seconds, both on-brand and unique in message.
- Customization: AI can adjust ads to specific locales or demographics, accounting for cultural and regional nuances, which increases effectiveness.
- Scaling: ad production scales without a proportional increase in resources, so businesses can run larger campaigns or more clients at once.
- Testing: AI makes testing ad variants "feel like nothing," so you can quickly find and deploy the best ads and improve ROI.
- Future: he expects more personalized, interactive and contextually relevant advertising.

chunks.heading: Content marketing and tools Cody uses
chunks.text:
- Cody appeared on Greg Isenberg's Startup Ideas Podcast, which "went a little viral."
- He also went on an IBM podcast (Making Data Simple) to discuss how B2B marketing is changing because of AI-powered content marketing.
- Tools he lists:
  - Swell AI: turns videos into clips, blog posts and newsletters, so a company becomes a media company to build brand, trust and inbound leads.
  - PodcastGuestLaunch.com: has booked him on 30+ shows.
  - Keywords Everywhere: shows keyword search volumes and average CPC, a cheap alternative to Semrush or Ahrefs.
  - Phantom Buster Email Extractor: scrapes emails from the whole website for a list of target customer sites, good for B2SMB marketing.
  - Acclaim Podcasting (his company): grows a podcast's email newsletter by 5,000+ subs a month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues teams need an AI brand voice document just like a style guide, and pitches small-tool-for-big-ecosystem businesses built on long-tail keywords and programmatic landing pages. He also shares growth tactics: controversial hidden-result LinkedIn polls that convert to an email course, and cold email measured on signups rather than replies.

chunks.heading: Brand voice documents for AI-generated content
chunks.text:
Cody argues that teams need AI brand voice guides the same way they have brand style guides. A style guide covers fonts, colors and iconography so media looks consistent, and "consistency builds trust, and that's the cornerstone of effective marketing." When teams use AI to create content, outputs often drift and feel off-brand.

His process:
- Collect media the brand has already produced.
- Ask AI to define the brand voice and persona from that content.
- Refine and finalize the document, then share it with the whole team.
- The document contains prompts that keep tone consistent no matter who generates the content.

Pro tip: instruct the AI to pull specific vocabulary from the brand's existing content. This builds a corpus of brand-specific terms so AI output always sounds on-brand. "Each person has words they tend to use more often than others. Brands should have this too to make them feel human."

Related tool he lists: CSS Peeper, a Chrome extension that reads a site's CSS and builds a brand style guide (fonts, hex codes, icons).

chunks.heading: "xyz QuickBooks integration" tool idea
chunks.text:
Cody's favorite business type is "small tools for big ecosystems." He thinks this one could be a $10M ARR company.

- There are over 4,000 keywords of the form "xyz quickbooks integration."
- A quick analysis found roughly 40 to 50% of these potential integrations have no current solution.
- The product: a tool that helps other software connect with QuickBooks.

Go-to-market:
- Build a long-tail landing page for each integration.
- Build links to those pages to earn organic traffic.

chunks.heading: Programmatic SEO agency for Shopify collection pages
chunks.text:
Cody's logic: Etsy is a billion-dollar company because it has millions of long-tail landing pages (he cites 13M). "This is how marketplaces actually grow." Previously this required a team of engineers; now AI can do it.

The service: generate programmatic long-tail collection pages for Shopify stores with many SKUs.

How he would find customers:
- Use BuiltWith to find all sites running Shopify.
- Use a Python script to crawl them and count products.
- Cold email owners of stores with high SKU counts.
- Find the emails with Hunter.io.

Validation: a beta test of this had customers pay $2,000/mo for it to be run for them. He says he doesn't have time to build it himself and wants someone else to.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn polls that turn into email course leads
chunks.text:
Cody runs LinkedIn polls built to generate leads:
- Ask a controversial question and hide the results until someone votes. Voting (a click) is needed to see outcomes, which drives engagement.
- More engagement on a post means more reach.
- Everyone who votes gets a push notification when the poll ends, which brings them back to the post for a second round of engagement.
- Before they return, he edits the post to add a call to action to join his 7-day email course. That converts returning voters into leads.

chunks.heading: Cold email as a signup channel (Swell AI test)
chunks.text:
Cody sent about 2,000 cold emails to Swell AI prospects, optimizing for opens and signups rather than replies.

- Open rates went above 50%.
- About 1% of the people emailed signed up for Swell AI, which he found by comparing signup data against cold email data for the same period.
- Extrapolation: 100,000 emails would yield around 1,000 signups, and about 5% of signups convert to paying customers.
- He says he doesn't fully believe the math but plans to try scaling it and share the data.

chunks.heading: Newsletter referral reward ideas
chunks.text:
Cody shared takeaways from a 45-minute podcast on newsletter growth that he hadn't considered before. Referral reward types:
- Digital products (eBooks, checklists, exclusive articles) as immediate rewards for 1 to 3 referrals.
- Personal shoutouts in the newsletter, such as for a referral or a birthday.
- Swag (stickers, hats, shirts) for higher referral counts, though it may be less effective than it used to be, so keep rewards fresh.
- Access to private groups, extra content or special Q&As, to create exclusivity.
- Giveaways where each referral earns an entry for a desirable item (AirPods, tablets).
- Cross-promotions: promote a subscriber's content or services if they hit a referral count, appealing to creators and businesses in the audience.

chunks.heading: Tools Cody recommends
chunks.text:
- Create.xyz: AI text-to-app builder, "think Retool but I prompt AI." Helps PMs build internal tools.
- CSS Peeper: Chrome extension that extracts a site's fonts, hex codes and icons into a brand style guide.
- Swell AI: AI content marketing engine that turns videos into clips, blog posts and newsletters. His framing: turn the company into a media company to grow brand, trust and inbound leads.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider borrows startup tactics (be where customers look, solving problems) and applies them to large corporations with no digital footprint. His "digital gravity" model grows online influence in sequence: brand first, then product questions, then industry questions, so the internet recognizes a company as big as it is offline.

chunks.heading: Digital gravity: the model
chunks.text:
- Cody defines digital gravity as "the sphere of influence you have on the digital world." Like real-world size and reputation, it has to be earned.
- Analogy: gravity is about relative size. The moon orbits the Earth and the Earth orbits the Sun because of relative mass.
- Unlike planets, digital planets can grow. Cody names three growth levers: brand, answering questions about the product, and answering questions about the industry.
- He says it is simple in concept but complex in practice. It takes smart teams, investment in digital marketing infrastructure, an understanding of how the internet works as a whole, and daily discipline. "It's a grueling, multi-year process. But the most impactful things are hard."
- Context: he wrote this in 2019 as Director of Digital Strategy at R+M, which helps large corporations move from traditional to digital media.

chunks.heading: Why big companies have to teach the internet they're big
chunks.text:
- Cody came to R+M in early 2018 from bootstrapped startups, where the early problem is finding product-market fit and getting people to trust you.
- Startup formula for looking bigger and more trustworthy: be where your target customers expect to get information about a company like yours. That could be Google, Medium, YouTube or LinkedIn, and every industry has a different mix.
- His rule: your customers spend time somewhere online, so be there as much as you can, "solving problems and providing value."
- He was surprised that R+M's clients (publicly traded, international supply chains, vertically integrated "from mine to table") were at the same starting point online as young startups.
- Core point: a real-world footprint does not translate online. "You have to teach the internet you're big" by growing your digital footprint.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Make the website market the brand
chunks.text:
- Cody's rule: a website exists "to market brand. Period."
- Most companies already have a website when they start with R+M. He says these sites are often confused about why they exist and are not optimized for brand.
- First investment: make the website take the real-world brand online.
- The goal is to make search engines, social media and the internet at large understand the who, what and why of the brand, so the brand exists online as it does in the real world.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Answer questions about the product
chunks.text:
- After brand, the next phase is answering the questions people ask about the client's products.
- People ask these questions in the real world, so the answers should be published online in a form that both people and search robots can find.
- He notes that robots map the gravity of the web and that human language alone is hard for robots to understand.
- This is the client's first real content. It comes as text, video and sound bites, often several media combined, to create the best answer to each product question.

chunks.heading: Step 3: Answer questions about the industry
chunks.text:
- Once brand and product questions are exhausted, move to higher-level industry questions that are not directly about the product but relate to "the DNA of the brand."
- Purpose: signal to the digital world where the company sits in the digital universe.
- Order of work is specific to generic, and brand to industry. Cody says this order lets you "clone the company's real world size online."

chunks.heading: Results and why the early investment matters
chunks.text:
- Cody reports that cloning real-world size online had a large effect. Clients needed to add another shift (staffing) and had their best sales quarters ever, after only 6 months of work.
- He shared a graph of one client metric, one of hundreds tracked, showing online gravity growth.
- Why do it: the brand gains "digital mass to throw around online in its industry."
- Early investment in digital footprint puts the brand so far ahead of competitors that, he argues, 20 years later it will be impossible for other firms to catch up. "It is hard to stop a star once it's burning."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues that the most important business moats are marketing moats built from owned media. He shows how he dominates the front page for a handful of keywords across blogs, YouTube and free tools, then backstops it with email. He frames marketing as a portfolio of risk-weighted bets, with owned media as the bonds.

chunks.heading: Marketing moats and owned media as a portfolio
chunks.text:
- Cody argues the most important defensible moats are marketing moats, not the ones usually discussed in business school. He says people keep talking about "the least important moats": product, economies of scale, high NPS.
- Owned media is how he builds a marketing moat. Channels you don't own are variable, higher risk and easier to duplicate.
- His closing frame: think of marketing as "a portfolio of bets with risk premiums." The portfolio holds riskier bets and short and long-term bets, and should adjust to where the company is in its life cycle.
- His one-line summary: "owned media is the bonds of your portfolio."

chunks.heading: Owning every result for the few keywords that drive acquisition
chunks.text:
Cody's example is a software product in his portfolio for the Etsy Sellers niche.

- Only 10 keywords create all of its new customer acquisition.
- He works to own the front page for every one of those keywords with several assets at once:
  - Multiple blogs on separate domains ranking for them.
  - YouTube videos from multiple channels ranking for them.
  - Free Chrome extensions that do a lesser version of what the software does.
- The goal is that a searcher sees his assets however they browse the results page.

chunks.heading: Why SERP ownership is still not fully owned
chunks.text:
- Cody notes that even a fully owned front page carries risk, because Google and YouTube could change their ranking algorithms.
- His hedge is email collection from the same audience, so he can communicate directly whenever he wants.
- The pattern: rank across many surfaces, then pull the audience into a direct channel (email) that no platform controls.

chunks.heading: The B2B scenario: how rented channels fail
chunks.text:
Cody walks through a B2B software company that gets customers through paid ads.

- Say it found two channels that work and raised a Series A on that marketing arbitrage.
- Three months after the raise, Y Combinator accepts two companies doing exactly the same thing.
- CPC doubles and CAC triples.
- Channels you don't own are variable, higher risk and easy to copy, "especially now with ad spy tools."

chunks.heading: Examples of owned media
chunks.text:
Cody's list (he notes they all still carry some risk):

- Email newsletters.
- The company website, when people go to it directly.
- SEO content for organic traffic.
- Podcasts.

His observation: they are all old, tried-and-tested technologies. If companies were doing it in 2000 and are still doing it now, there is probably an owned media strategy built around it.

chunks.heading: How to apply this
chunks.text:
- Find the small set of queries that drive acquisition, and put multiple assets (blogs, videos, free tools) on each one.
- Add email capture to every owned surface, to protect against algorithm changes.
- Treat paid ads as the risky part of the portfolio and owned media as the stable base, then rebalance as the company matures.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody defines FOMO marketing as deciding based on what you could be doing instead of what is working. He frames marketing as a portfolio (80% on proven channels, 20% on exploration) and says to keep scaling a winning channel until returns diminish, using a 13x ROAS Google Search example.

chunks.heading: Portfolio framing: 80% on what's working, 20% on exploration
chunks.text:
Cody defines FOMO marketing as "when we make marketing decisions based on what we could be doing rather than what is working."

- He thinks of marketing as a portfolio: about 80% of resources on what is already working and about 20% on exploring new initiatives.
- The split is short-term bets versus long-term bets.
- He is not against testing new things. He says to allocate only a small percentage of resources to them.

chunks.heading: Shiny object syndrome distracts from the job of marketing
chunks.text:
Cody says many marketing teams get shiny object syndrome, which pulls them away from why they exist: "to increase revenue."

- The failure mode is expanding into new channels (his example list: TikTok, Pinterest, SEO) before the current channels are exhausted.
- His rule: "If you have a winning horse, bet on that winning horse until it stops winning."
- Summary principle: do more of what is working and less of what isn't.

chunks.heading: Case study: the 13x ROAS ecom brand that wanted to add channels
chunks.text:
An investment banker friend asked Cody about channel expansion for an ecom brand he was working with.

- The brand already had a lot of success on its current channels and wanted to expand into TikTok, Pinterest and SEO.
- The friend mentioned the brand was getting a 13x ROAS on Google Search Ads. Cody called that ROAS "insane."
- Cody asked whether they had exploited that arbitrage as far as it could go. The answer was no.
- His advice: put as much money into that channel as it takes until you see diminishing returns. "Go to that ATM until it quits printing."

chunks.heading: How to decide where the next dollar goes
chunks.text:
A practical sequence implied by Cody's argument:

1. Find the channel with the best return (here, 13x ROAS on Google Search).
2. Keep scaling spend into it until marginal returns diminish.
3. Only then look at new channels as the main bet.
4. In the meantime, run new-channel experiments with a small slice of resources (roughly the 20%).

chunks.heading: Winning horses for B2B brands (as of late 2022)
chunks.text:
Cody lists what he was seeing work for B2B brands at the time:

- Cold email
- Customer match lists into ad channels
- Remarketing product demos
- Podcasts
- Repurposing podcast content
- Educational content posted to LinkedIn pages

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody starts B2B engagements by asking what the sales team wishes prospects knew before the first call, then maps marketing tactics to those gaps. He pairs purely educational, team-hosted expert content (trust, brand) with ungated product demos remarketed to scraped customer-match lists (product understanding).

chunks.heading: Educational content as the foundation of B2B marketing (digital gravity)
chunks.text:
Cody argues that most B2B brands now know they need content, but much of it is "just sales BS in disguise and provides zero value to prospects." His instruction: "Give this up. Do it right now." Instead, make purely educational content with a strong call to action to learn more about the product.

- He calls giving without expecting anything back "digital gravity."
- Increasing your "digital mass" online gives you more influence in your target market.
- Educational content works because it builds trust before a prospect ever talks to sales.

chunks.heading: Start from what the sales team wishes prospects knew
chunks.text:
When Cody works with B2B clients, one of the first questions he asks is: what does your sales team wish prospects knew before ever talking to you? He says he already knows the answers, but the exercise is valuable regardless.

Typical answers: the product exists, what the product is, the problem it solves, what it does, who the company is, and that the company and its people can be trusted. In other words, the sales team wants leads to be "buyer ready."

- His closing challenge: talk to your sales teams, ask what they wish leads knew before talking to them, then build marketing initiatives that solve those gaps.
- He pairs two tactics (below) to create buyer-ready leads with "low mental energy input."
- He scores each tactic against the list to see which gaps it closes.

chunks.heading: Tactic 1: Educational content hosted by a team member
chunks.text:
The easiest way to make highly educational content, per Cody, is to bring thought leaders from your industry in and have them share their expertise, with someone on your team "hosting."

- **Offboards idea generation.** Your job shifts from creating unique ideas to curating and sharing them.
- **Elevates your brand.** Hosting the content associates you and your brand with it.
- **Builds an owned media library.** It becomes a content engine you can mine whenever you want to repurpose content elsewhere.
- **What it solves on the list:** who the company is, and trust in the company and its people. It does not solve what the product is, the problem it solves, or what it does.

chunks.heading: Tactic 2: Remarketing ungated demos to B2B audiences
chunks.text:
Cody says it "literally blows my mind that there are still gated demos in 2022." His view is that B2B customers want to learn everything they can about a product before they talk to anyone, so "give the people what they want."

Steps he lays out:

1. Scrape the emails of your target customers.
2. Import the lists as customer match lists on every platform where people spend time online.
3. Create product demos.
4. Remarket those demos to the customer match audiences, plus anyone who touches your website (install the pixel).

- B2B purchase decisions have a long time horizon, so demos that show how the product improves people's lives educate buyers over time.
- Result: customers who "deeply understand your product before they even talk to your sales team."
- **What it solves on the list:** that the product exists and what it is, the problem it solves, and what it does. It does not build trust in the company or explain who the company is.

chunks.heading: Why the two tactics work as a pair
chunks.text:
Cody's scorecard approach shows the tactics are complementary, covering opposite halves of the buyer-ready list:

| Gap | Hosted educational content | Remarketed demos |
|---|---|---|
| Product exists / what it is | Partly | Yes |
| Problem the product solves | No | Yes |
| What the product does | No | Yes |
| Who the company is | Yes | No |
| Trust in company and people | Yes | No |

Together they leave prospects knowing the product, the problem, the solution, and the people behind it before the first sales call.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody recounts a friend's B2B SaaS experiment paying one creator $5K/month to run the brand's TikTok, yielding 375K views for $15K and a 3x ROAS. He argues for hiring channel-native specialists who build trust through consistency, tell product-in-the-journey stories, and are measured on channel growth, with simple referral-link tracking.

chunks.heading: A hired channel specialist beats rotating UGC creators
chunks.text:
- Cody sees brands moving toward one specialist creator per channel instead of rotating UGC models.
- Specialists know the channel, own it entirely, and build consistency and trust because the same person delivers the information every time.
- Rotating UGC models feel unnatural on the platform. His analogy: "imagine if your favorite YouTuber, Tiktoker, or podcast host just switched every upload or episode. Like it would feel strange."
- Specialists are measured on channel growth, unlike social media managers who often keep "posting to no one".
- His advice: mimic what happens naturally on each channel and run a version that serves business goals.
- His 2023 prediction: more companies hiring for titles like "YouTuber", "TikToker" and "Podcaster".

chunks.heading: Case study: $5K/month TikTok hire for a B2B SaaS
chunks.text:
- A friend who owns a B2B SaaS company hired one person at $5K per month to run the brand's TikTok.
- Results so far: 375K views for $15K spent, and a ROAS of 3x.
- Cody drew his insights below from conversations about this experiment.

chunks.heading: Make content native, personality-led and consistent
chunks.text:
- **Consistency builds trust:** seeing the same face repeatedly makes people more likely to click when it appears in the feed. The more value they keep providing, the smaller the ask feels when it's time to buy.
- **Native content:** content must be built for the specific channel. Each channel has its own nuances, and a one-size-fits-all approach has less impact than a tailored version.
- **Needs a personality:** the friend tested generic product-focused content with no face against content featuring the TikToker. Videos with the person included went viral 10x more.

chunks.heading: Tell stories where the product is part of the journey
chunks.text:
- The best performing videos told a story in which the product was included in the journey, rather than the journey being about the product.
- Cody calls this "a really nuanced but important detail and a classic content mistake".
- Focus on the goals people are trying to accomplish, and show the product as an essential tool for getting there.

chunks.heading: Measure ROI with a dedicated link and a self-reported field
chunks.text:
- Create a dedicated referral or signup link for each channel. It's an easy way to measure the ROI of hiring these people.
- Combine it with a required "how did you hear about us?" form field to gather enough data to prove the value.

chunks.heading: Post more and double down on winners (80/20)
chunks.text:
- In this experiment, 63% of impressions from the organic strategy came from 20% of posts.
- Cody calls it "a numbers game": post more, see what works, make more of what works and less of what doesn't.

chunks.heading: Treat it as an owned media strategy
chunks.text:
- Followers gained on the channel give the brand a direct line of communication.
- Cody frames this as building a marketing moat and diversifying the company's marketing bets.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues the hardest part of a scraped email list is knowing what to send, and his answer is a podcast. A client's cold list, sequenced into an ESP and only promoting the podcast, got a 40% open rate and 5% CTR. The podcast hit 5K+ monthly downloads in 60 days because people see podcasts as education, not sales.

chunks.heading: Cold email list → podcast promotion as the first newsletter send
chunks.text:
Cody frames the hard part of a scraped email list as "what do I send them?" His answer: promote a podcast.

- Business emails are effectively public now: they sit in directories, can be scraped, or can be found with lookup tools.
- If you have a defined target audience and a product that sells easily to them, email is one of the fastest and easiest ways to reach them, "ESPECIALLY if you're an early-stage startup."
- The problem comes after you have and have validated the emails. Deciding what to send is, in his experience, one of the hardest parts of this channel.

chunks.heading: The process and the results he reports
chunks.text:
- For a client, he loaded a cold list of their target audience into an ESP as a sequence.
- The only content sent was promotion of the client's podcast.
- Results on that cold list: a 40% open rate and a 5% click-through rate. He says it "literally blows my mind" and that it is hard to hit those numbers even on a warm list.
- The podcast reached 5K+ downloads per month within 60 days and 8 episodes, which he says puts it in the top 1% of podcasts.

chunks.heading: What the email says
chunks.text:
- The email is educational in tone and is essentially "Go learn this today on this podcast."
- It has no direct product pitch. The product ask lives inside the podcast, as a call to action at the start of each episode to sign up for the product.

chunks.heading: Why it works: the psychology
chunks.text:
- For the target customer, a podcast is a small lift because it is passive: they can listen without doing anything.
- People don't see podcasts as sales tools yet. They see them as educational vehicles, so the call to action feels soft instead of aggressive.
- Recipients don't find it salesy, even with the signup CTA at the top of the episode.

chunks.heading: Customer interviews as disguised testimonials
chunks.text:
- Cody tells clients to interview their own customers on the podcast.
- That makes each episode a customer testimonial packaged as education.
- The content "doesn't have to be perfect, it just has to exist so it can be distributed."

chunks.heading: Where it applies
chunks.text:
- He says the process can be done for every industry.
- The takeaway: pair a validated cold list with a podcast so the list has something worth sending, and treat distribution of imperfect content as more important than polishing it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues every B2B software company should own a database of all its target customers, then use GPT-3 to qualify leads instead of relying on brittle keyword matching or manual SDR review. The workflow is simple: scrape each lead's site, feed the text to a yes/no prompt, and loop over the list. He frames AI as making top performers 100x rather than replacing people.

chunks.heading: Lead validation with GPT-3: prioritizing a large lead database
chunks.text:
- Cody says every B2B software company should own a database of all its target customers, sourced from anywhere possible. His examples: directories and scraping Google Maps.
- Investor angle: an early-stage startup that has a list of all its target customers when raising its Series A will make investors "stoked."
- The problem: with, say, 50K collected leads, it is unclear which ones the sales team should work first.
- Traditionally, SDRs comb the database and validate leads manually.
- Keyword filters help only a little. Companies that fit a product often use language that signals it, but keywords are "super limited because people talk about the same thing differently pretty often."
- Cody says GPT-3 removes that limitation, because it can judge fit from the meaning of a company's own site copy instead of matching exact terms.

chunks.heading: The four-step GPT-3 lead validation process
chunks.text:
Cody heard about this from a friend who uses GPT-3 for lead validation and thought it solved a massive problem. The process:

1. Use Python to request a potential lead's URL.
2. Ingest all the text on that person's site.
3. Run a GPT-3 prompt asking a qualifying question. His example: "Does this company have multiple mental health professionals or are they a solo practitioner?"
4. Loop this through all the leads.

His summary: "And you just validated your list."

chunks.heading: Writing the qualifying prompt
chunks.text:
- The prompt is a plain yes/no or either/or question about a trait that decides whether the lead fits your product.
- His example question separates multi-provider mental health practices from solo practitioners. It is a firmographic distinction that is hard to catch with keywords but easy to read from a site's team pages and service descriptions.
- The same pattern works for any ICP criterion that shows up in a company's website text. Cody only gives the mental health example.

chunks.heading: AI makes strong people far more productive, not redundant
chunks.text:
- Cody does not think AI tools like this will replace people. He thinks "it will make 10x people 100x people."
- His stated goal: make teams "super human, so that one really good person can work like they're 100 people."
- Applied to sales: the manual lead-vetting work SDRs used to do is automated, so reps spend their time on leads already validated as good fits.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues email should be judged by cost per click, including labor and CRM costs, rather than as a transactional blast channel. Because people return to old emails months later, email works as a user's personal search engine and database, so every relevant email you send seeds long-term, SEO-like assets in their inbox.

chunks.heading: Email as a cost-per-click channel
chunks.text:
- Cody argues email marketing is measured wrongly: "We should be measuring email clicks on a CPC basis," the way search and display are measured.
- Historical framing: advertising started with "eyeballs" (impressions), then added vanity metrics like recall, retention and likeliness to buy. Cost per click (pioneered by Bill Gross at Idealab/goto.com, popularized by Google) shifted the metric from impressions to user actions.
- Simple version: monthly price of the email sender divided by the clicks email creates.
- Better version: compare the conversions that come from email against conversions from paid ads.
- Cost is not only money. Time and mental energy count too, so they belong in the CPC calculation.

chunks.heading: The true email CPC formula
chunks.text:
- Formula: Email CPC = (initial labor setup costs + CRM cost x months) / total clicks in the time frame.
- Cody's worked example from client data: ($2,500 setup + $99/month x 24 months) / 2,500 clicks = $1.95 per click.
- Compared with paid ads at about $0.10 per click, email carries a large premium.
- He argues the premium is worth paying because people revisit emails months later, so one send keeps producing clicks long after it goes out.
- The same lens applies to the true cost of email nurture campaigns, which include the build labor, not just the software bill.

chunks.heading: Email as a personal search engine
chunks.text:
- While digging through client email data, Cody saw people open an email in the month it was sent, then return months later and click again.
- He connected this to his own habit: he emails himself links all the time, using his inbox as a database and search engine.
- His conclusion: people use their inbox as a "hacked database" they can search later, so sending an email adds your brand, content and ideas to that database.
- He describes email accounts as "personal search engines" for their owners.

chunks.heading: Permission to seed a user's database
chunks.text:
- When someone shares their email (a PDF download, a newsletter signup, a product purchase), they give permission to add to their personal database.
- That lets a company seed the inbox with information relevant to the person and related to the brand, which they may return to later.
- Cody frames this as the reason email is "the most valuable marketing asset."
- Email is not a transactional campaign. It is a long-term marketing strategy, similar to SEO.

chunks.heading: Email compounds like SEO
chunks.text:
- The more relevant content a company has sitting in people's inboxes, the bigger the network of information that links back to its site.
- Each email is a durable, searchable entry point rather than a one-time blast, so value accumulates over time.
- Practical implication: judge email on lifetime clicks and conversions per dollar and hour invested, not on first-week open and click rates.
- He also notes email still works despite being disrupted by free services like Gmail: it drives traffic, nurtures leads and re-engages audiences. He cites the quote "You'll change more street addresses than you will email addresses in the 21st century."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues digital ads should work like evolution: a process of elimination, not a search for one right answer. Instead of A/B testing single components, combine many photos, headlines and body copy into hundreds or thousands of ad units and let CPC and conversion data show the winners. He also ties this to AI-built ads drawn from media libraries.

chunks.heading: Nature selects by elimination, and Cody argues digital ads should too
chunks.text:
- Cody argues that "nature doesn't A/B test." Evolution tries many combinations at once and the last organism standing wins. It is a process of elimination, not a search for the right answer.
- He says digital advertising should work the same way: search for what doesn't work rather than what does.
- He acknowledges this is counterintuitive, since "every digital ad blog, agency and guru" says to A/B test methodically. He calls that approach "utterly archaic."
- His alternative is "A-through-Z testing," which takes A/B testing a step further by testing everything at once.

chunks.heading: Big number theory: use ad volume to find outliers
chunks.text:
- Cody's premise is that with enough data, trends emerge. They let you identify independent and dependent variables, see patterns and, most importantly, find outliers.
- He notes that outliers live in the tails, and the tails are typically where the most interesting things happen.
- Print media (magazines, newspapers) limits you to physical ad slots. Digital offers a relatively infinite inventory of ad slots, so you can make tens, hundreds or even thousands of ads.
- Instead of running a single ad to an audience, he says to run every ad creative idea you can think of.
- Trusting big number theory lets you separate the average ads from the ads in the tails, then put your time, money and mental energy behind the ads that create the most organizational impact.

chunks.heading: What A-through-Z testing is and how to run it
chunks.text:
- A-through-Z testing combines three ideas: each ad unit is its own entity, big number theory, and letting the algorithm decide the winner.
- The algorithm shows the winner through CPC and conversion data, which reveal the most effective ad units.
- Example setup for Facebook ads: combine 10 photos, 10 headlines and 10 body texts. That creates 1K combinations (1,000).
- Run all of them and let the platform, and the people on it, decide which combination gives the greatest return on ad spend.
- Cody frames this as "teasing a message out of the audience" with the message they want to engage with most, rather than forcing a message on them.

chunks.heading: Why not dissect ad components
chunks.text:
- Cody describes working at a previous agency where executives at big public companies would ask how testing worked and try to dissect ad components: the photo, the copy, the call to action. They then looked for trends within each.
- He says this is wrong, because combining creative elements produces a whole new piece of media.
- His analogy: "Hydrogen and oxygen apart are naturally combustible, together they're naturally cool."
- So the unit of analysis is the full ad (the combination), not its individual parts.

chunks.heading: Feeding learnings back into the next round
chunks.text:
- Once certain ad units succeed, you use that knowledge when refreshing the ads: which media and copy go well together.
- This shapes which components you use in the next round, but it does not split the ad units back into separate parts.

chunks.heading: The path to AI-based advertising
chunks.text:
- Cody concedes that making 1K ad units by hand is probably not a good time investment for most organizations.
- His answer: take the human out of making the ads. He expects companies to have media libraries from which AI-based software generates ad units.
- Firms will then be able to test thousands of ad units and advise creative teams on what media to make next for the library.
- He calls A-through-Z testing "the bridge to the future of AI-based advertising" and says this is what his company, Audience Eye, was pursuing at the time (2020).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues digital marketing should drop campaigns with start and end dates (a military idea from Madison Avenue) and instead run an always-on portfolio. Spread resources across short and long term assets, favor things that compound, and simply do more of what works and less of what doesn't.

chunks.heading: Marketing budgets should work like a financial portfolio, not a series of campaigns
chunks.text:
Cody argues digital marketing should not run on campaigns. A campaign is a military idea with an objective, an initiative and a timeline, borrowed by the "Mad Men of Madison Avenue" from their time in the service. It made sense when firms had to send one message to as many people as possible and needed timelines to measure success or failure and to limit ad fatigue.

- Digital gives instant feedback loops, so it is "insane to fix things that aren't broken."
- He wants start and end dates eliminated.
- "If your agency is flighting digital ads you should fire them." Flighting means they are not learning and getting better with every growth cycle.
- Agencies that assign arbitrary budget amounts to communication goals and start from zero each year are running a structure designed for an 80-year-old constraint set.

chunks.heading: The financial life analogy: stop restarting from zero every year
chunks.text:
Cody compares the campaign model to a person who, every year, burns their savings, quits their job, bombs their house and starts each January homeless. Nobody would run their financial life that way, so he asks why an agency would do it to a marketing budget.

- A financial portfolio holds both short-term and long-term initiatives, and so should a marketing budget.
- Funds in a portfolio are distributed by age, income level and appetite for risk.
- He says more important than short- versus long-term thinking is doing things that compound in value.
- The goal is marketing initiatives built into portfolios that mitigate risk and grow in value over time.

chunks.heading: Three marketing resources and risk tolerance by digital maturity
chunks.text:
Cody names three types of marketing resources: money, time and mental energy. Each should be allocated along a spectrum of short-term and long-term needs, and each organization should have a different portfolio composition.

- Companies early in adopting digital have less to lose, so they should take on higher risk.
- Companies further along in their digital evolution have more to lose, so they should have lower risk tolerance.
- Example he cites: Fortune 500 companies that launched new websites and wiped out organic traffic by not understanding SEO fundamentals and erasing content that was ranking. In one case, about half of organic traffic was lost in under 14 days because the IT team deleted the site map, unpublished content and changed the XML structure.

chunks.heading: What goes in the portfolio and the job each channel does
chunks.text:
Cody's example portfolio splits budget across search ads, display ads, content production, email marketing and SEO. The pieces are separate but work together as one unit.

- **Search ads:** target people who are buyer-ready and closest to a purchase decision, so the goal is getting them to choose you.
- **Display ads:** educate the target segment about the brand. They reach people still in discovery who do not know the product exists. This changes if display is used for remarketing.
- **Content production:** "the foundation of an organization." It educates customers and grows what he calls digital gravity.
- **Email marketing:** both short- and long-term. It nurtures a lead close to buying, and the CRM list is an asset that gains value over time.
- **SEO:** the long-term investment, comparable to the 10% of yearly income that goes into accounts with compounded growth.
- Print is not excluded on principle and makes sense for some clients, but for many it is more cost-effective to put resources into digital, where it is easier to track what works.

chunks.heading: Operating rule: no end dates, do more of what works
chunks.text:
The campaigns in the portfolio have no end dates. The decision rule is simple:

- If something isn't working, stop it.
- If it is working, do more of it.
- Don't flight ads and don't do unnecessary work; shift effort toward what works and away from what doesn't.

He calls the idea "so simple that it's deceiving how powerful it is," and says that done right it makes massive impacts for organizations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody argues that storytelling marketing hides the product inside a narrative where it is a character, letting people sit in someone else's problem and see how the product improves life. Every story needs a problem, a journey and a solution, and it works across Facebook ads and email by tapping the human urge to share stories that make us feel.

chunks.heading: What storytelling marketing is
chunks.text:
Cody defines storytelling marketing as "the process of creating story narrative where the product is a character." The product is hidden inside a story rather than pitched directly.

- His example: a rainy camping scene in Glacier National Park where a "whisper light camp stove" warms the group with Guatemalan coffee. The product sits in the narrative without being announced.
- The story casts a vision of the product in someone's life, typically in an aspirational way.
- It lets people "sit in someone else's shoes, in someone else's problem" and see how the product would make their life better.

chunks.heading: Why storytelling works for marketing
chunks.text:
- He says storytelling is "a part of the fabric of being human." People connect with stories.
- Marketing is the expression of how a product helps people solve a problem. A story paints a portrait of the moment that problem happens and shows the product as the solution.
- He calls storytelling "a cheat" for three jobs at once: capturing a person's interest, illustrating a problem, and showcasing the product or service as the solution.

chunks.heading: The three-part story structure
chunks.text:
Cody says storytelling marketing is always composed of three things:

1. **A problem**
2. **A journey**
3. **A solution** (the product)

- Example: Google's first real commercial, "Parisian Love." It shows someone trying to impress a French girl (problem), their falling in love (journey), and Google Search helping the protagonist (solution).

chunks.heading: Storytelling in Facebook ads
chunks.text:
- Facebook is already a place where users tell stories digitally through text, video and images, so he sees it as a strong fit for storytelling marketing.
- Ads that cast a vision of people facing a challenge and overcoming it with a product, using the problem/journey/solution model above, "will get the cheapest traffic from Facebook."

chunks.heading: Storytelling in email marketing
chunks.text:
- He notes email is one of the oldest forms of digital marketing, and people are notorious for forwarding stories (his example: a grandmother forwarding an elaborate story that made the reader feel something).
- The tactic is to tap into the natural desire to share stories that make us feel.
- He names three sources of feeling to build emails around:
  - Learning something new.
  - Hearing about someone overcoming an impossible obstacle.
  - Sparking irritation at a frustrating fact of life.

chunks.heading: Books he recommends for marketing storytelling
chunks.text:
- **Stories That Stick** (Kindra Hall): the bridge for any gap in a business is a good story. Hall shows leaders the four unique stories they already have to captivate and convert audiences.
- **Brand Storytelling**: using a narrative to connect a brand to customers by linking what it stands for to shared values.
- **Unleash the Power of Storytelling**: a practical roadmap for crafting and delivering more persuasive stories to get more of what you want in career and life.

chunks.heading: How to hire a storytelling marketing agency
chunks.text:
- Look for people with "a large volume of empathy." Empathetic people make the best storytellers because they can identify other people's problems and write narratives from those people's perspective.
- The agency must also understand how stories get distributed through social media.
- His rule: if they can't empathize and also distribute those stories with modern media, "don't hire them."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody explains that when a customer won't buy within about 48 hours, your marketing goal is branding: owning an association in their mind. Continued branding raises mental switching costs by deepening the customer's emotional relationship with you, making it very hard for a competitor to uproot.

chunks.heading: Branding vs. planned purchase cycles: when the goal is branding
chunks.text:
Cody starts client conversations by mapping the customer's journey, specifically the questions a customer asks throughout the purchasing decision. He says an agency's job is to understand the brand, understand the customer, and build the bridge between them.

- Clients usually underestimate the purchase cycle. They think customers decide much faster than they do.
- Simplified model: purchases are either impulse (within the next 24 hrs) or planned (a more deliberate process).
- His rule: "If your customer won't make a purchase within the next 48 hrs your marketing goal is branding."

chunks.heading: What branding is: owning an idea in the customer's head
chunks.text:
Cody defines branding as associating your company name with an idea, a moment, a feeling or a need. The aim is to be synonymous with that idea in the person's mind.

- Example: a physical therapy clinic. Not everyone it markets to needs care today, but they will get hurt at some point. The goal is that when a customer tears a shoulder, they immediately think of the clinic (his example name: Boise Physical Therapy).
- Big-brand examples of the same association: Gillette is razors, Dawn is dish soap, Kleenex is Kleenex.
- Practical takeaway: for products bought on a delay or triggered by an event, market to people before the need arises so your name is the first thing they think of when it does.

chunks.heading: Branding raises mental switching costs
chunks.text:
Cody argues you don't stop branding once the association is established, because "branding increases mental switching costs."

- Switching costs are what you pay when you move from one product to another (iPhone to Android, Tropicana to concentrate, Whole Foods to Trader Joe's).
- Each brand has physical pros and cons, and each customer weighs them differently. What gets forgotten is that mental switching costs also exist.
- People build relationships with brands the way they build relationships with people, using the same emotions. The deeper the emotions, the harder it is to switch.
- Switching is hard because it takes a lot of mental energy to uproot the association with a brand, and the idea that brand has attached itself to, and then attach a new brand to that idea.

chunks.heading: How associations get lost, and how to defend yours
chunks.text:
Cody says associations are most vulnerable when a brand does something that hurts the relationship it holds with the customer's idea. That opens a gap for a competitor to replace the associated brand.

- Defense: keep developing customer relationships, grow the level of affinity, and talk to customers regularly about things they want to hear.
- Done well, this makes the brand-and-idea association hard, "if not impossible," to uproot.
- Opportunity side: if a competitor stumbles, a rival brand can take over the association.

chunks.heading: Checklist for branding clients or your own projects
chunks.text:
Cody's three things to think through:

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cody Schneider describes the V3 SEO Model his agency used on powerful, aged domains to find keywords worth targeting. By combining Value, Verge and Volume, the team built landing pages for search intent and reports a client gaining 51% more organic clicks and 29% more impressions in 30 days.

chunks.heading: The V3 SEO model: three filters for picking keywords
chunks.text:
Cody's V3 SEO Model is a keyword selection framework. He developed it at Reynolds + Myers, where the team works with high-authority domains. One client's domain was older than google.com (21 years old at the time of writing) and had a backlink portfolio to match.

- On domains this powerful, he says "Google 'tells' us what it wants us to rank for."
- The three V's are **value**, **verge** and **volume**.
- A keyword that meets all three is called a **V3 keyword**. In his diagram, V3 keywords are the overlap of the three circles.

chunks.heading: Value: keywords that create value for the business
chunks.text:
Cody's first filter is whether ranking for a keyword can create value for the organization.

- Keywords related to the company's products.
- Information prospects search for at different stages of the buyer's journey.
- Keywords important to brand identity.

Ranking for keywords that fail this filter produces traffic but no business impact, so they are excluded even if they rank easily.

chunks.heading: Verge: keywords already on page two or three
chunks.text:
Cody's second filter is that the keyword is on the verge of page one.

- The keyword already ranks on page two or three of Google.
- He argues Google signals what a site can rank for. A keyword already showing up on pages two or three is one Google considers the site relevant for.
- These keywords "can often be lifted to page one with just a little work."
- This makes verge keywords the cheapest wins. It is incremental effort on existing rankings, not a new ranking built from zero.

chunks.heading: Volume: keywords big enough to move the needle
chunks.text:
Cody's third filter is that the keyword has a monthly search volume that is relatively large for the industry.

- The keyword must have "the potential energy necessary to create impact to our current search analytics."
- Volume is judged relative to the industry, not as an absolute number.
- Without this filter, lifting a verge keyword to page one would barely register in clicks or impressions.

chunks.heading: Executing the model: build landing pages for V3 keywords
chunks.text:
Cody's process once V3 keywords are identified:

1. Find keywords that satisfy value, verge and volume at the same time.
2. Build landing pages that best answer search intent for each new target keyword.
3. Wait about 30 days.

chunks.heading: Result: +51% organic clicks and +29% organic impressions in 30 days
chunks.text:
Cody reports that applying the V3 model for a client at Reynolds + Myers produced these results within 30 days:

- 51% more organic clicks.
- 29% more organic impressions.

He notes the client had a very old, powerful domain, which is the context in which he says Google tells you what it wants you to rank for. He shows the result as a Search Console style chart in the original post and invites questions, saying he will answer "hastily."

The REDACTED cloud agent is a **scheduled Cursor Automation**: every day at **9:00 AM ET** Cursor spins up a cloud VM on this repo, gives it `REDACTED/AUTOMATION .md` as its job, and lets it operate the Google Ads account with no human approval step.

## What it is

It is not the ads loop itself. It is a daily **account manager** sitting on top of the loop.

- **Cursor cloud agent** (9:00 AM ET) — reads the account, decides, ships code, triggers jobs, reports.
- **Graphed job `google-ads-daily`** (7:00 AM ET) — the actual Testing → Winners mutations.

The agent’s own trigger is outside its control. Everything else in `REDACTED/graphed.yaml` is its to change.

## How a morning run works

1. **Recall.** Read Memories: baselines, watch items, last changes, schedule ordering.
2. **Check the 7am loop.** `graphed logs` for `google-ads-daily`. Quota fail → re-trigger later. Code bug → fix, test, push `main`, deploy, re-run.
3. **Read the scoreboard** from the Graphed warehouse (free; Google Ads API quota is shared and scarce): 7- and 30-day spend, clicks, conversions, CPA by campaign/ad group.
4. **Hunt what the rules missed.** Zero-conversion terms, competitor/nav patterns, broad-match drift. The loop already auto-negates proven waste ≥$25; the agent looks for *patterns* worth a standing negative, a seed change, or new code.
5. **Check watch items** (brand serving, demotions staying paused, tCPA effects, etc.).
6. **Act**, in this order:
   - re-trigger `google-ads-daily`
   - ship a config/schedule change
   - write new loop code if the system can’t do the thing yet
7. **Record.** Update Memories. End with health vs targets, what shipped, what’s being watched, and **URGENT** if Kyle needs to act today.

## What it is allowed to use

Cloud setup is `.cursor/environment.json`: install the Graphed CLI and `npm ci` in `REDACTED/`.

Always available: `GRAPHED_TOKEN` (warehouse, jobs, deploys). Direct script runs also need Google Ads + OpenRouter keys; if those are missing, it falls back to triggering the already-deployed jobs.

Preferred tools, cheapest first:

1. Warehouse SQL (no API quota)
2. Existing npm/Graphed jobs with `--apply` (`daily`, `negate`, `promote`, `prune`, `budget`, `expand`, …)
3. New scripts under `REDACTED/jobs/google-ads/src/` — test, commit, push `main`, `graphed deploy`

It only touches files under `REDACTED/`. Commits are supposed to explain *why*.

## Hard rails

These do not move, no matter what it finds:

- Never touch Brand Protection (`24031728127`)
- Never raise total daily budget (~$540)
- Never create/remove/re-type campaigns
- Never delete `DRY_RUN` (live = `"0"`; `"1"` is the emergency brake)
- Never weaken safeguards (classifier fail-safe, promotion gate, atomic mutates, API budget, brand guard)
- Config moves ≤25% per run

Emergency: spend spike → re-run the loop / add a standing negative. Serving collapse → `cleanup-negatives`, or set `DRY_RUN=1` and escalate.

## Success definition

Winners CPA trending toward **$250** with impressions recovering; Testing’s zero-conversion spend share falling; total conversions not collapsing

- cap at roughly five conversion events, more than that is noise

server-side lead qualification

- facebook conversions api fires events from a server
- enrich the lead in real time, score 1 to 10, send back only leads above threshold (~6)
- b2b signals: headcount, crm in use, site traffic (apify similarweb endpoint), branded search volume
- smb signals: google review count and velocity
- consumer signals: zip code
- solves the lead quality complaint, the algorithm optimizes for form fills unless you tell it otherwise

marketing api

- create a system user, assign it the app, page, ad account, instagram account

- use the api for writes only: uploading creative, turning off losers, moving ads between adsets

- mcp exposes only a handful of endpoints and breaks at scale, go direct to the api

campaign structure

- two campaigns: testing and winners
- testing campaign holds multiple adsets, five ads per adset competing for budget
- facebook concentrates budget on the likely winner on its own
- signal window is two days to a week depending on spend and cost per action
- winners move into the winners campaign and compete against each other there
- watch for ad fatigue in the winners campaign
- remix winners into new variations, push back into testing
- optional: higher funnel event in testing, deeper event in winners

- open source stack: airbyte for the pipeline, clickhouse for the warehouse
- postgres and supabase are not built for this, 100m rows takes minutes instead of milliseconds
- facebook ads alone is about 42 tables with hundreds of columns
- warehouse access enables conversational analytics and live dashboards
